title: A/B Testing & Experimentation
one: The one tool that tells you what would have happened anyway — and all the ways that comparison gets ruined.

terms.d: Two versions of the same thing run at the same time, with people split randomly between them, so any difference in results is caused by the change and not by luck, weather or timing.
terms.c: Your café has two front doors. Same street, same coffee, same hour. Half of the arrivals go through door A, half through door B, and at closing time you compare the two tills.

terms.d: The version you already have. It exists to tell you what would have happened anyway, which is the one number you can never get from a launch.
terms.c: The old door. You are not testing it — you are using it as a ruler.

terms.d: The changed version. Ideally it differs from the control in exactly one meaningful way, so a result points at a cause.
terms.c: The new door. If you also repaint the sign and hire a busker, a win tells you nothing about the door.

terms.d: A single sentence that can be proved wrong. Format: because we observed X, we believe doing Y will change metric M by about N%, and we will know within T days.
terms.c: “Because 40% of people hesitate at the old door, a wider door will lift coffees-per-visitor by about 5% within two weeks.” Now the test can embarrass you, which is the point.

terms.d: Chance, not judgement, decides who gets which version. This is the whole trick: it makes the two groups similar on everything you thought of and everything you didn't.
terms.c: The host flips a coin for each arrival. They don't send the regulars through the nice door and the tourists through the old one — that would be a survey, not an experiment.

terms.d: The thing you flip the coin on: a person, a session, a device, an account, a city. Pick the unit that matches the thing you are changing, and keep it consistent for the whole test.
terms.c: Flip the coin per person, not per visit. Otherwise Tuesday-you and Thursday-you walk through different doors and end up in both columns.

terms.d: Run the identical experience against itself. You should find nothing. If you find a winner, your measurement is broken — better to learn that now than after a launch.
terms.c: Two identical doors. If the till says one of them sells 4% more coffee, the problem is your till.

terms.d: Start with a small slice of traffic (1–5%), check nothing is on fire, then increase. It limits the damage of a bad variant without slowing you down much.
terms.c: Open the new door to a trickle first. If the frame collapses, you'd rather it happened to nine people than nine hundred.

terms.d: A small group deliberately kept on the old experience for months, so you can measure the real cumulative effect of everything you shipped.
terms.c: One table of regulars who always use the old door, all year. They tell you whether the year of renovations actually added up to anything.

terms.d: How many people you need in each group before the numbers can be trusted. Decided before the test, from your current rate and the smallest effect you'd act on.
terms.c: Four customers per door proves nothing. Seventy thousand per door proves something. The maths tells you where the line is.

terms.d: The moment a person is assigned to an arm and starts counting. Count people from the moment they could have seen the change, not from the moment they succeeded.
terms.c: Anyone the host waves through the doorway is in the experiment — including the people who turn around and leave.

terms.d: You asked for a 50/50 split and got 52.6/47.4. With big numbers that gap is far too large to be chance, so something is broken — and any result is untrustworthy.
terms.c: The coin came up heads 526 times in 1,000. That is not a coin. Stop reading the till and go find out what the host is doing.

terms.d: A temporary lift caused by the change simply being new and attracting attention. It fades. Tests that stop early bank it as if it were permanent.
terms.c: Everyone tries the shiny new door on day one because it's shiny and new. By next month it's just a door.

terms.d: The opposite: a temporary dip because existing users have to relearn something they already knew. It also fades, which is why very short tests punish good redesigns.
terms.c: The regulars grumble for a fortnight because their hand goes to the wrong handle. Then they stop noticing.

terms.d: The arms leak into each other, so the groups aren't independent. Common with anything social, shared, marketplace-based or inventory-limited.
terms.c: Door B customers tell their friends in the Door A queue about the new door. Or both doors compete for the last croissant.

terms.d: A subgroup: mobile, new users, one country, one plan. Useful for explaining a result, dangerous for finding one, because there are always enough slices for something to look impressive.
terms.c: Split the day's takings by weather, tourists, regulars, morning, evening. Look at enough slices and one will always sparkle.

terms.d: The overall number moves one way while every subgroup moves the other, because the mix of subgroups changed. A signal to investigate, never to pick the number you prefer.
terms.c: Door B beats Door A overall, yet loses with tourists and loses with regulars — because Door B happened to get more of the high-spending regulars.

terms.d: A number that summarises behaviour: conversion rate, orders per visitor, minutes watched, seven-day retention. Define exactly how it's computed before you look at it.
terms.c: What you write in the ledger at closing time. Coffees per visitor, not “vibes at the counter”.

terms.a: OEC, north-star metric for this test
terms.d: The one number that decides the call, chosen before launch. One. If you have three primary metrics you have none, because you'll pick whichever one won.
terms.c: “Coffees sold per person who walked in.” Written on the wall in ink before the doors open.

terms.d: Things that must not get worse, each with a stated limit: page speed, refunds, complaints, retention, revenue per user. Guardrails are how a “win” gets caught out.
terms.c: The complaints book, the queue length and the average bill. A door that sells more coffee but doubles complaints is not a better door.

terms.d: A fast stand-in for something slow to measure. Useful, but only as far as the two things really move together — check that link before trusting it.
terms.c: Counting how many people pick up a menu, because you can't wait a year to see who becomes a regular.

terms.d: Where the metric sits today, measured over a full weekly cycle. Every sample-size and impact calculation depends on it, so get it right first.
terms.c: Last month's ledger: 3.2 coffees per 100 people through the door.

terms.d: 3.2% to 3.5% is +0.3 percentage points absolute, and +10% relative. Both are correct; mixing them up is how a modest result gets reported as a triumph.
terms.c: Three more coffees per thousand customers, or a tenth more coffee than before. Same fact, very different-sounding email.

terms.d: The natural bounce in a metric when nothing has changed. Noisy metrics need far more traffic; revenue per user is noisier than conversion rate because a few big spenders dominate.
terms.c: Tuesday is never exactly Wednesday, even with the same door. Rain, paydays, a coach party — noise.

terms.d: Using each person's own past behaviour to cancel out predictable noise, so the same traffic detects smaller effects. Roughly the same result, sooner.
terms.c: You already know what each regular usually spends, so you compare them to their own average instead of to strangers. Much less guessing.

terms.d: A verdict that the gap you measured is larger than random splitting usually produces. It says “probably not luck”. It does not say the effect is big, lasting or worth having.
terms.c: The gap between the two tills is bigger than the day-to-day wobble you'd expect from two identical doors.

terms.d: If the two versions were truly identical, how often would pure chance produce a gap this big or bigger? p = 0.03 means about 3 times in 100. It is not the probability that you're right.
terms.c: “If both doors were the same, I'd see a gap this dramatic on 3 days out of 100.” Suspicious enough to act on, not proof.

terms.d: Your false-alarm budget, set in advance, usually 0.05. It is a business choice: how often are you willing to crown a winner that isn't one?
terms.c: “I accept being fooled by coincidence once every twenty tests.” Cheap doors, loose budget. Expensive rebuild, tighten it.

terms.d: The range of true effects consistent with your data, usually 95%. The most honest single output of a test: it shows the size and the uncertainty together.
terms.c: “The new door is somewhere between 4% and 16% better.” Far more useful than “the new door won”.

terms.d: The chance your test will notice a real effect of the size you care about. Convention is 80%. A low-powered test mostly produces shrugs, and occasionally a lucky lie.
terms.c: How good your till is at spotting a genuinely better door. A bad till misses good doors — and once in a while crowns a bad one loudly.

terms.d: The smallest effect your test can reliably catch, given traffic, baseline and power. Halving the MDE roughly quadruples the traffic needed — this is the single most expensive dial in experimentation.
terms.c: With 400 customers a day you can spot “much better”. To spot “slightly better” you need a much busier street or a much longer test.

terms.d: You declare a winner that isn't better. You then ship it, book the gains in a plan, and quietly never see them.
terms.c: You knock through a wall for the new door, and takings stay exactly where they were.

terms.d: You miss a real improvement, usually because the test was too small or too short, and conclude the idea doesn't work. Nobody writes this one up.
terms.c: The new door really was better, your till couldn't tell, and you bricked it up.

terms.d: Approaches designed for people who want to look at results early. They adjust the bar so repeated peeking is legitimate — a fix for peeking, not a licence to stop at the first good number.
terms.c: A till designed to be checked hourly: it just demands a bigger gap before it will say “winner”.

terms.d: Checking repeatedly and stopping the moment it looks significant. Every look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so your real false-positive rate ends up far above 5%.
terms.c: Reading the tills every hour and closing the test the first time Door B is ahead. You'll find “winners” on days when both doors are identical.

terms.d: Test twenty things at 5% and roughly one wins by luck. Applies to metrics and segments as much as variants. Either decide in advance or correct the threshold.
terms.c: Twenty slices of the day's takings, one looks brilliant, and you build a strategy on the coincidence.

terms.d: Real, but too small to matter. A significant +0.2% that costs three engineer-months and adds a permanent maintenance burden is a loss, whatever the p-value says.
terms.c: The new door genuinely sells one extra coffee a week. It cost forty thousand pounds.

terms.d: Any figure that looks interesting or surprising is usually wrong. The bigger the result, the harder you should look for the bug before you celebrate.
terms.c: Door B is up 300%. Check the till, check the coin, check whether Door A was locked. It's almost never the door.

terms.d: The three legitimate endings. Write which one you're taking, the expected impact with its range, and what you learned — before the result gets retold in a meeting as something it wasn't.
terms.c: Keep the new door, brick it up, or try a wider one. Then write it in the ledger, because in six months nobody will remember.

terms.d: After shipping, check the real world matched the forecast. Effects usually shrink; knowing by how much makes your next forecast believable.
terms.c: A year later, compare the ledger to the promise you made on the day you knocked the wall through.

steps.t: Start from a decision, not an idea
steps.out: One sentence: the decision this test unblocks
steps.b: Before anything else, write down what you will do differently depending on the outcome. If both answers lead to the same action, you have found a very expensive way to feel busy. Also check an experiment is even the right tool: for tiny traffic, brand-new products, one-way doors, or anything where you need to know why, judgement plus research beats a test that can never reach significance.
steps.do: Write: “If it wins we roll out to all markets; if it loses we keep the current flow and stop the redesign.”
steps.no: “Let's test it and see” — the phrase that produces underpowered tests nobody can act on.
steps.snip:
Decision  → Do we replace the 3-step checkout for everyone?
If B wins  → roll out to 100%, cancel the redesign track
If B loses → keep current flow, reallocate the two engineers

steps.t: Write a hypothesis that can be wrong
steps.out: A falsifiable statement with a number in it
steps.b: A hypothesis has four parts: the evidence, the change, the predicted effect on one named metric, and roughly how big. The size matters more than it looks — it is what you will feed into the sample-size maths, and it forces you to say out loud whether you expect 1% or 30%.
steps.do: “Because 68% of mobile users abandon at the account step, removing forced sign-up will lift visitor-to-order by ~8%.”
steps.no: “The new checkout will improve the user experience.” Nothing there can ever be shown to be false.
steps.snip:
Because we saw   [evidence from data or research]
we believe that  [specific change]
will cause        [one primary metric] to move by ~[N%]
We'll know when   [n per arm] users have been exposed.

steps.t: Choose one primary metric and your guardrails
steps.out: 1 primary metric + 3–5 guardrails, each with a limit
steps.b: Pick the single number that decides the call, and write down exactly how it's calculated, including who counts as being in the denominator. Then list what must not get worse, with a threshold on each. Guardrails are the difference between a team that ships wins and a team that ships numbers.
steps.do: Primary: visitor→order rate. Guardrails: average order value (no worse than −2%), refund rate, p95 page load, support contacts per 1,000 orders.
steps.no: Three primary metrics. You will end up reporting the one that happened to win, which is cherry-picking with extra steps.

steps.t: Size the test before you build it
steps.out: n per arm and a planned end date
steps.b: Four inputs decide everything: your baseline rate, the smallest effect worth acting on (MDE), your false-alarm budget (α, usually 5%) and power (usually 80%). Out comes the sample per arm, and dividing by daily traffic gives the run time. Do this before engineering starts — it's the moment you discover that detecting a 1% lift would take eleven months.
steps.do: Round the run time up to whole weeks so every arm gets the same number of weekends, and add follow-up time for any guardrail measured over 7 or 30 days.
steps.no: Building first and sizing later. If the answer is “nine months”, you've just spent a sprint on an unanswerable question.
steps.snip:
n per arm ≈ 15.7 × p × (1 − p) ÷ (absolute lift)²
   p = baseline rate, α = 0.05 two-sided, power = 80%
Example: p = 3.2%, want to detect +8% relative (+0.256 pts)
   n ≈ 15.7 × 0.032 × 0.968 ÷ 0.00256² ≈ 74,000 per arm

steps.t: Build the split, then try to break it
steps.out: A QA'd experiment, signed off before launch
steps.b: This is where most bad results are actually created. Check the assignment is random and sticky per user, that both arms are logged identically, that the metric fires on both, and that nothing about the variant changes who is even eligible to be counted — a redirect that drops slow connections silently deletes your most impatient users from one arm only.
steps.do: Run an A/A test or replay historical traffic first, verify the split ratio, and check the variant on a slow 3G mobile profile.
steps.no: Trusting the platform. Instrumentation bugs are the single most common cause of exciting results.

steps.t: Launch small, ramp up, watch the guardrails
steps.out: A daily health check — split ratio and guardrails only
steps.b: Go to 1–5% of traffic for a day. Look at errors, latency, crashes, complaints and the split ratio. What you deliberately do not look at is the primary metric: watching it is how peeking starts. If the health checks are clean, ramp to the planned allocation.
steps.do: Set an automatic kill rule up front: “abort if error rate rises above X or revenue per user drops more than Y%.”
steps.no: Ramping straight to 50/50 on a payments change on a Friday afternoon.

steps.t: Let it run to the plan
steps.out: A test that ends on the date you said
steps.b: Run to your planned sample and at least one full week, ideally two — behaviour on Sunday is not behaviour on Wednesday, and novelty and primacy effects need time to decay. If you truly must monitor the primary metric continuously, use a sequential or Bayesian method that's built for repeated looks, rather than a fixed-horizon p-value you check every morning.
steps.do: Freeze the end date in the ticket. If you extend it, write down why before you look at the result.
steps.no: Stopping the afternoon it goes green. Peeking can push your real false-positive rate past 25%.

steps.t: Read the result in the right order
steps.out: Effect size with a confidence interval, not a verdict
steps.b: Read it in this order, and don't skip ahead. 1. Health: split ratio, sample as planned. 2. Primary metric: effect size and the confidence interval. 3. Guardrails. 4. Segments, last, and only to explain a result you already have. If the number surprises you, look for the bug before the story: the bigger the surprise, the more likely it's a bug.
steps.do: Report it as “+10% relative, 95% CI +4% to +16%, guardrails clean”. The range is the honest answer.
steps.no: Reading segments first. Enough slices will always hand you a headline.
steps.snip:
Health      SRM check 50.07 / 49.93  → pass
Primary     3.20% → 3.52%  (+10.0% rel)
            95% CI  +4.3%  to  +15.7%      p = 0.0006
Guardrails  AOV −1.0% (limit −2%) · refunds flat · p95 flat
Segments    consistent across mobile / desktop / new / returning

steps.t: Decide, write it down, then verify in the wild
steps.out: A one-page result note + a post-launch check
steps.b: Ship, kill or iterate — and record the decision with the effect range, the guardrail outcomes, and what you'd do next. Convert the range into money or users so the business can plan with the uncertainty rather than the midpoint. Then, weeks later, check reality against the forecast. Effects nearly always shrink; teams that measure the shrinkage are the ones whose forecasts get believed.
steps.do: Keep a searchable log of every test, including the losers. The losers are where the real product knowledge lives.
steps.no: Shipping and moving on. Untracked wins compound into a roadmap built on numbers nobody can reproduce.

cases.title: Guest checkout at a mid-size retailer
cases.sub: The boring, profitable kind of experiment: one change, one metric, run to plan, believed.
steps: Do we drop forced account creation for everyone? A win rolls out globally; a loss ends the checkout redesign track.
Because 68% of mobile abandonment happens on the account step, offering guest checkout with a progress bar will lift visitor→order by ~8%.
Primary: visitor→order rate. Guardrails: average order value (limit −2%), refund rate, p95 page load, support contacts per 1,000 orders.

Baseline 3.20%, MDE +8% relative, α 0.05, power 80% → 74,200 per arm. At 10,000 per arm per day that is 7.4 days, rounded up to 14 days so each arm gets the same two weekends — which delivers 140,000 per arm, comfortably past the minimum.
A/A test over one day found no difference (p = 0.71). Split ratio verified at 50.07 / 49.93. Variant checked on a throttled 3G profile.
1% for a day, then 50/50. Daily checks on errors, latency and split ratio only — the primary metric stayed hidden until day 14.

Control 4,486 orders from 140,196 visitors (3.20%). Variant 4,921 from 139,804 (3.52%). +10.0% relative, 95% CI +5.8% to +14.2%, p < 0.0001. AOV −1.0%, inside the guardrail. Refunds and load time flat. Consistent on mobile and desktop.
Shipped to 100%. Forecast +$1.6M a year, with an honest range of $0.9M–$2.2M from the confidence interval. A 5% holdout kept for six months.

charts.sub: The range is the result. The midpoint is just its most likely point.

charts.title: Guardrails — nothing broke

verdict.p: Nothing about this result is clever. One change, one metric, guardrails set in advance, the plumbing checked, and the team didn't look at the primary number until the date they'd committed to. That's why nobody in the room argued with it.
verdict.lesson: A confidence interval that sits entirely above zero and comfortably above your MDE is the cleanest ship signal you will ever get.

cases.title: Navigation redesign at a recipe site
cases.sub: Two failures stacked: a broken split, then a real effect that evaporated. The +14% was never there.
steps: Do we roll the new navigation across the whole site? Six weeks of design work is waiting on the answer.
Because 71% of sessions end after one recipe, a category-first navigation will lift the rate of reading a second recipe by ~5%.
Primary: sessions that open a second recipe. Guardrails: pages per session, ad viewability, p95 load time, bounce rate.
Baseline 22.0%, MDE +5% relative → 22,300 per arm, reached in about a day and a half. The team correctly planned 14 days anyway, for weekly cycles and novelty decay.
On day 5 the dashboard showed +14.2%, p < 0.0001. Someone posted a screenshot with three champagne emoji and asked to ship on Friday.

The split was 52.6 / 47.4 — 78,900 sessions against 71,100. Chi-squared ≈ 406, so effectively impossible by chance. Sample ratio mismatch: the test was invalid. Cause: the variant loaded via a client-side redirect that silently dropped slow mobile sessions, so the surviving variant users were on faster connections and inherently more engaged.

Redirect removed, split verified, full 14 days, 210,000 sessions per arm. Week 1 came in at +3.8%. Week 2 at −1.8%. Pooled: +1.0% relative, 95% CI −0.1% to +2.1%, p = 0.086 — not significant, and the whole interval sits below the +5% they said they'd act on.
Someone then sliced 18 metrics across 6 segments and found “tablet users +21%, p = 0.03”. That's 108 comparisons; at α = 0.05 you expect around five such findings from pure noise. It was not pursued.
Not shipped on this evidence. The novelty curve became the team's standard exhibit for why 48-hour tests don't count.

verdict.h: The dashboard was green twice, and wrong twice
verdict.p: Both traps here are ordinary. A redirect changed who got counted, which manufactured a 14% lift out of thin air. Then a genuine novelty bump looked like a win for three days. Neither would have survived a health check and a fixed end date — which is exactly what those two habits are for.
verdict.lesson: Check the split ratio before you read the result, and treat any effect that shrinks day after day as novelty until it proves otherwise.

cases.badge: Won the metric, lost the money
cases.title: A pushier paywall at a subscription app
cases.sub: A large, real, statistically bulletproof +20% on the primary metric. It would have cost about $540,000 a year.
steps: Do we move the paywall earlier and make it harder to dismiss? Growth has a trial-start target; retention has an opinion about it.
Because 82% of visitors never see the paywall, showing it on the second screen with a delayed dismiss will lift trial starts by ~10%.

Primary: visitor→trial-start rate. Guardrails: trial→paid at 30 days, refund rate, support contacts, 30-day retention. Crucially, the guardrail window set the timeline: 12 days of exposure, then 30 more days of follow-up.
Baseline 4.50%, MDE +10% relative → 33,400 per arm, about 11.1 days at 3,000 per arm per day, run for 12 — which gives 36,000 per arm.
1,620 trials from 36,000 (4.50%) against 1,944 from 36,000 (5.40%). +20.0% relative, 95% CI +13% to +27%, p < 0.0001. Comfortably the biggest primary-metric win the team had ever produced.

Trial→paid at 30 days fell from 42.0% to 33.0% (p < 0.0001). Refunds rose from 1.9% to 3.4%. Support contacts per 1,000 trials rose 18%. The extra trials were people who'd been cornered, not convinced.

Per 1,000 visitors — control: 45 trials × 42% = 18.9 subscribers × $96 LTV = $1,814. Variant: 54 trials × 33% = 17.8 subscribers × $88 LTV = $1,568. That's −13.6% revenue, or roughly −$540,000 a year at current traffic.
Rejected. Two things changed permanently: revenue per visitor became a guardrail on every growth test, and the team stopped treating trial starts as a goal in their own right.
A gentler variant — same earlier placement, dismissible immediately — went on to win +6% trial starts with trial→paid flat, and shipped a month later.

verdict.h: A real win on the wrong number
verdict.p: Nothing here was a statistical error. The +20% was real and would have survived any amount of scrutiny. The mistake available to this team was choosing a primary metric that sits three steps upstream of the money, and it was caught by a guardrail with a long enough measurement window to see the damage.
verdict.lesson: Pick guardrails that can contradict your primary metric, and give them a measurement window long enough to do it.

quiz.q: Your test reports p = 0.03. What does that actually mean?
o: There is a 97% chance the variant is better
If the two versions were truly identical, chance alone would produce a gap this big or bigger about 3 times in 100
The variant is 3% better than the control
There is a 3% chance the variant is worse
quiz.e: A p-value describes how surprising your data would be in a world where the two versions are the same. It says nothing directly about the probability that you're right, and nothing at all about the size of the effect — which is why you report the confidence interval alongside it.

quiz.q: You're testing a change to a page people visit several times a week. What goes wrong if you flip the coin per visit instead of per person?
o: Nothing — more coin flips means more statistical power
The same person sees both versions, so the two groups are no longer clean comparisons and the effect gets diluted
The p-value becomes impossible to calculate
You need exactly twice the sample size
quiz.e: Sticky, per-person assignment is what keeps the groups separate. Randomising per visit means Tuesday-you is in the control and Thursday-you is in the variant, so the experience gets blended, real differences shrink toward nothing, and the experiment quietly loses the ability to detect what you built it to detect.

quiz.q: You asked for a 50/50 split. With 160,000 sessions in, it's 52.6 / 47.4. What's the right move?
o: Read the result but mention the imbalance as a caveat
Weight the two groups to correct the imbalance and carry on
Stop and debug — a gap that large isn't chance, so the whole result is untrustworthy
Nothing, small imbalances are normal
quiz.e: That's sample ratio mismatch, and at this scale it's effectively impossible by chance. It means something is deciding who lands where, and whatever that something is has almost certainly also skewed who gets counted. Fix the cause, then rerun. A caveat is not a fix.

quiz.q: Your test can detect a 10% relative lift. Your VP wants it to detect 5% instead. What happens to the traffic you need?
o: It roughly doubles
It stays about the same, the test just needs to run longer
It roughly quadruples
It halves
quiz.e: Sample size scales with the inverse square of the effect size, so halving the MDE multiplies the required traffic by about four. This is the most expensive dial in experimentation and the reason small-traffic products genuinely cannot test small changes — no amount of enthusiasm fixes it.

quiz.q: You're testing a pushier upgrade prompt. Which of these belongs as a guardrail metric?
o: Clicks on the upgrade button
Trial-to-paid conversion at 30 days
Number of prompts shown
Time spent on the pricing page
quiz.e: A guardrail has to be capable of contradicting your primary metric. Clicks and impressions move in the same direction as a pushier prompt by construction. Downstream quality — do these people actually convert and stay? — is the number that can tell you the win was hollow.

quiz.q: Day 3 of a planned 14-day test, the variant is significantly ahead. Why isn't stopping now a free win?
o: Because significance always disappears with more data
Because you have to run tests for exactly two weeks by convention
Because each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, and short windows bank temporary effects as if they were permanent
Because the p-value can't be trusted before 100,000 users
quiz.e: Two things bite at once. Repeated peeking with a fixed-horizon test inflates your real false-positive rate well beyond 5%. And a three-day window is exactly where novelty effects live. If you genuinely need to watch results continuously, use a sequential or Bayesian method built for it.

quiz.q: A variant is +14% on day 2, +7% on day 5 and +0.4% by day 12. Most likely explanation?
o: Novelty effect — the change drew attention because it was new, and that faded
Primacy effect — users were annoyed at first and then adapted
The variant is being degraded by later traffic
Sample ratio mismatch
quiz.e: A large early lift that decays toward zero is the signature of novelty. The mirror image — an early dip that recovers — is primacy, or change aversion. Both are real short-term effects and both are why a test that ends on day 3 systematically overstates redesigns.

quiz.q: After a flat result, you slice 18 metrics across 6 segments and find one significant winner at p = 0.04. How should you treat it?
o: As a win in that segment — ship it there
As a likely false positive: 108 comparisons at 5% will throw up several by luck
As proof the overall test was underpowered
As a guardrail breach
quiz.e: At α = 0.05, roughly one in twenty comparisons looks significant when nothing is happening. Run 108 and you should expect around five. Segment findings are for explaining a result you already have, or for generating a hypothesis you then test on purpose — never for rescuing a flat test.

quiz.q: Your result: +9% relative lift, 95% CI from −1% to +19%. What's the honest reading?
o: A 9% win, since that's the measured effect
A loss, because the interval includes negative numbers
Inconclusive and underpowered — the data is consistent with a small loss and with a large win
Significant, because most of the interval is positive
quiz.e: An interval that straddles zero means you cannot rule out the change making things slightly worse — and you also cannot rule out a substantial win. The useful conclusion isn't “no effect”, it's “this test was too small to answer the question”. Either get more traffic or accept you're making a judgement call, but don't report +9% as a finding.

quiz.q: A test comes back at +0.3% relative, p = 0.01, on 4 million users. Ship it?
o: Yes — it's statistically significant, which is the bar
No — significance with 4 million users is meaningless
It depends: significant just means real. Now weigh 0.3% against the cost of building and maintaining it
Yes, and forecast the gain from the top of the confidence interval
quiz.e: Statistical significance and practical significance are separate questions. With enough traffic, trivially small effects become detectable. A real +0.3% is worth having on a checkout flow for a large retailer and not worth having if it adds a permanent maintenance burden to a small team. That judgement is yours, not the statistics'.

sections.h: Two doors, one coin flip, and the only honest answer you'll get.
sections.lede: An A/B test is the one tool that tells you what would have happened anyway. Everything else in this topic — the sizing maths, the guardrails, the traps — exists to protect that single comparison from being ruined. Start with the panel: watch the interval narrow as traffic arrives. That intuition is worth more than any formula on this page.
Every term on this page maps onto one scene, so you have somewhere to put it. Same café, same street, same hour — two front doors, and a host who flips a coin for each arrival. Hover the labels.
Front of each card: what it means. Back: what it is in the café. Click or press Enter to flip. Filter by group if you're revising.

sections.h: From “I have an idea” to “we shipped it”
sections.lede: Nine steps in order. The first four happen before anyone writes code, which is the part most teams skip and then regret. Click any step to open it.

sections.h: How much traffic do you actually need?
sections.lede: This is step 4, live. Move the sliders and watch the run time. The lesson arrives quickly: detecting small effects is enormously expensive, and low-traffic products can't buy their way out of it.

sections.lede: Hover or tap any part of a diagram and it explains itself underneath.

cells: Type II — you binned a real win
A false negative. Usually an underpowered test, and nobody ever writes it up.
A real effect, detected. This is what power buys you.
Nothing there, and you said so.
A false positive. You book the gains in a plan and then never see them.

items.cap: Alpha controls the bottom-right box. Power controls the top-left one.
items.p: Your significance level is a budget for the bottom-right box; your power is how often you avoid the top-left one. Both are choices you make before the test, not findings from it.

Big, obvious changes are cheap to test. This is an argument for bolder changes.

title: Discovery & User Research
one: How to find out what is actually true about your users before spending a quarter building for a guess.

terms.d: The work you do to find out what is actually true before committing engineering time. Its output is not a decision to build — it is a reduction in how much you are guessing.
terms.c: The consultation. Nobody would take a prescription from a doctor who never asked what hurt.

terms.d: Research that finds problems you did not know about. Open questions, few assumptions, done before you have a solution in mind.
terms.c: “Tell me about the pain.” The doctor has no idea yet what is wrong.

terms.d: Research that checks whether a specific solution works. Narrow, task-based, done once you have something to react to.
terms.c: “Does it hurt when I press here?” Now the doctor has a hypothesis and is testing it.

terms.d: A standing habit of talking to a small number of customers every week, rather than a research project every year. Consistency beats scale here — the pattern shows up in the fifth conversation, not the fiftieth.
terms.c: A GP with a regular list, who notices the flu going round in week one instead of reading about it in an annual report.

terms.d: The short set of questions that decides who gets into your study. It is the highest-leverage thing in the whole process: the wrong people give you confident, useless answers.
terms.c: “Have you had this symptom in the last month?” Otherwise you spend the afternoon examining healthy volunteers.

terms.d: Ask about the person's life and past behaviour, never about your idea. Good questions are ones even your mother could not answer flatteringly — because they are about facts, not opinions.
terms.c: “When did this last happen, and what did you do?” instead of “would you take this pill if I made it?”

terms.d: A question that carries its own answer. It produces agreement, which feels like evidence and is not.
terms.c: “The pain is sharp rather than dull, isn't it?” The patient nods, and the notes are now fiction.

terms.d: Following an answer down to the motive underneath it by asking why, or up to the context by asking what for. Three or four levels is usually where the real job appears.
terms.c: “I need stronger painkillers” → why → “I cannot sleep” → why → “I lie awake worrying”. Different prescription entirely.

terms.d: The reliable difference between what people say they will do and what they actually do. Stated intent, especially about paying, is worth roughly nothing on its own.
terms.c: Everyone promises to take the full course of antibiotics. The pharmacy data disagrees.

terms.d: The problem space is what people are struggling with and why. The solution space is what you might build. Confusing them is how teams end up defending features instead of outcomes.
terms.c: Diagnosis versus treatment. You can change the treatment freely; changing the diagnosis means starting again.

terms.d: The progress someone is trying to make in a situation, independent of your product. People do not want a drill, a hole, or even a shelf — they want the room to stop looking chaotic.
terms.c: The patient's actual goal is getting back to work on Monday, not the specific medicine they came in asking for.

terms.d: “When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome].” Better than a user story because it carries the trigger and the context, which is where most design decisions actually get made.
terms.c: “When the pain wakes me at 3am, I want something I can take without food, so I can sleep until the alarm.”

terms.d: Listing everything that has to be true for an idea to work, then plotting each on how important it is and how much evidence you have. You test the top-right corner: important and unknown.
terms.c: Before surgery, listing what you are assuming about the patient's heart, allergies and recovery — then ordering only the tests that could change the plan.

terms.d: The smallest thing you can do to check the assumption that would sink the whole idea. Cheaper and faster than an MVP, because it deliberately builds nothing reusable.
terms.c: One blood test before you book the theatre.

terms.d: A tree with your outcome at the top, the customer opportunities that could move it underneath, and candidate solutions below those. It keeps a team honest about which problem a feature is meant to serve.
terms.c: The chart on the wall: recovery at the top, the contributing conditions beneath, treatments hanging off each.

terms.d: The point where new conversations stop producing new patterns. Usually five to eight people per meaningfully different segment — far fewer than teams expect, and far more than they usually do.
terms.c: By the sixth patient with the same symptoms, the doctor stops learning and starts treating.

terms.d: Turning raw notes into patterns in the open, with the team, so conclusions are traceable back to something a real person said. If nobody can find the quote, it is not a finding.
terms.c: Case notes on the table, grouped by symptom, with the patient's own words attached to each.

terms.d: Watching five people attempt a real task without help. Five is enough to find the majority of serious problems; it is not enough to measure anything, so never report percentages from it.
terms.c: Watching the patient try to open the child-proof cap. You learn more in ten seconds than from a survey.

terms.d: Noticing the evidence that fits the plan and quietly discounting the rest. Every researcher has it; the fix is process, not willpower — write your prediction down first.
terms.c: The doctor who has already decided it is a virus, and stops asking questions that could reveal otherwise.

terms.a: sample of one, the loudest customer
terms.d: One vivid story treated as a trend, usually because it came from someone important. Useful as a hypothesis, dangerous as a mandate.
terms.c: One patient reacts badly, so the drug is banned in that clinic while the evidence says otherwise.

terms.d: A customer telling you what to build. Treat it as a symptom report: valuable data about their situation, not an instruction. Always ask what they tried before asking you.
terms.c: “I need antibiotics.” Maybe. First, what has been happening, and for how long?

steps.t: Write the decision and the risk behind it
steps.out: One sentence: the decision, and what could sink it
steps.b: Research without a decision attached becomes a tour of interesting facts. Start with what you are about to commit — a quarter, a rebuild, a price change — and name the single belief that, if wrong, makes the whole thing a waste. That belief is what you are going to investigate.
steps.do: “We are about to rebuild onboarding. The thing that would sink it: people abandon because of the data import, not the sign-up form.”
steps.no: “Let's do some user research on onboarding.” You will get four weeks of material and no decision.

steps.t: Turn the idea into assumptions and rank them
steps.out: An assumption map with a top-right corner
steps.b: List everything that must be true: that the problem is frequent, that people notice it, that they will change behaviour, that you can build it, that someone will pay. Score each on importance and on how much evidence you actually have. The important-and-unevidenced ones are your entire research plan; the rest can wait.
steps.do: Include the commercial assumptions. Teams cheerfully validate desirability and then discover nobody has a budget line for it.
steps.no: Testing the assumption you are most curious about rather than the one that carries the most risk.

steps.t: Recruit the right people, not the available people
steps.out: A screener and six to eight booked sessions
steps.b: Define the segment by behaviour, not demographics: people who did the thing in the last 30 days. Screen out anyone who is friendly but irrelevant — including internal staff and the same three customers who always volunteer. If you can only find people by asking your sales team for favours, that is itself a finding.
steps.do: Recruit two or three people who churned or chose a competitor. They explain more in twenty minutes than ten happy users.
steps.no: Talking only to your most engaged users, then designing for a population that does not exist.

steps.t: Ask about the past, not the future
steps.out: Interview notes full of specifics and quotes
steps.b: Anchor every question in something that already happened: the last time, what they did, what it cost them, what they used instead. Never describe your idea in the first thirty minutes. When someone offers an opinion about the future, gently walk it back to the last real occurrence — and if there wasn't one, that is your answer.
steps.do: Ask “what happened next?” and then shut up. The silence is where the useful part arrives.
steps.no: Pitching, then recording enthusiasm as evidence. People are polite, and politeness is not demand.
steps.snip:
Good: When did you last need to do this?
      Walk me through what you did.
      What did that cost you — time, money, hassle?
      What did you try before that?
Bad:  Would you use a feature that did this?
      How much would you pay for it?
      Don't you find the current flow frustrating?

steps.t: Run sessions until the patterns repeat
steps.out: Saturation, or a clear reason to keep going
steps.b: Book five to eight per segment and run them close together, ideally within a fortnight, so the comparisons stay fresh. Write up within an hour of each session — memory decays faster than anyone believes. Stop when two consecutive sessions add no new pattern, and start again if you notice a new segment appearing.
steps.do: Have a second person on every call to take notes, so the interviewer can actually listen.
steps.no: Spreading eight interviews over two months. By the last one you are comparing notes with a stranger's product.

steps.t: Synthesise in the open
steps.out: Patterns, each traceable to real quotes
steps.b: Get the observations out of individual heads and onto one surface the team can see. Group them, name the groups in the customers' language rather than yours, and count how many people each pattern actually came from. A pattern with one source is a hypothesis; you can still act on it, but say so out loud.
steps.do: Label every finding with how many of the participants it came from. “5 of 7” carries information; “users say” does not.
steps.no: One person disappearing for a week and returning with a deck. Nobody else will believe it, and they will be right not to.

steps.t: Decide what you believe, and what you will still test
steps.out: A short note: beliefs, decision, next test
steps.b: Close the loop explicitly. Write what you now believe and how strongly, what you have decided as a result, and which assumption is still unresolved — then name the cheapest next test for it. Stated intent about money always stays on the unresolved list until behaviour confirms it.
steps.do: Keep a running list of retired assumptions. It becomes the fastest onboarding document your team has.
steps.no: Ending on “lots of interesting insights”. Insight that changes no decision is entertainment.

cases.title: Fourteen customers asked for bulk export
cases.sub: The request was unanimous, specific and wrong. Asking what they did with the file changed the roadmap.
steps: Do we build a bulk CSV export? Estimated at six weeks, and it was the top item in the customer request tracker.
The assumption worth checking was not “do they want export” — they clearly did — but “is export the job, or the workaround?”
Seven of the fourteen requesting accounts, screened for having actually exported something in the last 30 days. Two were admins, five were analysts.
Every session opened with “walk me through the last time you exported.” Six of seven described the same sequence: export, pivot by team and month, screenshot into a slide for a Monday meeting.
6 of 7 were rebuilding the same view by hand every week. Nobody wanted a file. They wanted a number their manager would accept, on a Monday, without them touching a spreadsheet.

Built a single saved report with team-and-month breakdown and a share link. Three weeks, not six. Bulk export was pushed down and eventually shipped much later for a genuine reason — an accounting integration.
Export requests from those accounts dropped roughly 80% within two months. The Monday report became the most-used view in the product.

verdict.h: The unanimous request was the workaround
verdict.p: Fourteen accounts agreeing on a solution feels like the strongest possible signal, and it is — a strong signal that something is broken. What none of them could tell you is that the broken thing was a weekly ritual, because they had stopped noticing it.
verdict.lesson: When customers agree on a solution, the finding is that they share a problem. Ask what they did before they asked you.

cases.title: Nine out of ten said they would pay
cases.sub: Every session was positive. The tier launched to near-silence, because nobody had been asked to actually do anything.
steps: Do we build a premium tier at $9/month? Growth was flat and pricing looked like the lever.
Ten interviews. The concept was described in the first five minutes, then participants were asked whether it was useful and whether they would pay. Nine said yes, several enthusiastically.

Two problems, both ordinary. Participants were recruited from the power-user community, so they were unrepresentative and unusually motivated to be encouraging. And every question was about the future, where nothing costs anything.
Eleven weeks of engineering. First month: 0.7% of eligible users upgraded, against an internal forecast of 6%.

A fake-door test — the pricing page and upgrade button live, capturing intent and then explaining it is not ready yet — would have cost two days. Or asking the nine enthusiasts to pre-pay, which is a question about the present.

The team re-ran discovery on the people who had not upgraded. The real blocker was that the premium features helped teams, and the product was priced and packaged per individual. Repackaged as a team plan, conversion reached 4.1% two quarters later.

verdict.p: Nothing in those ten sessions was dishonest. People were describing a hypothetical version of themselves, recruited from the group most likely to be generous, and asked a question that had no cost attached. The say-do gap did the rest.
verdict.lesson: Never let stated willingness to pay leave the room as validated. Convert it into a test where somebody has to actually do something.

quiz.q: A customer says “I need a bulk export feature.” What is the most useful next question?
o: Would you use it weekly or monthly?
Walk me through the last time you needed this — what did you do?
How much would you pay for it?
Should it be CSV or Excel?
quiz.e: A solution request is a symptom report. The last-time question gets you the actual job, the frequency, and the workaround they built — all of which might point at something cheaper and better. The other three questions all assume the export is the right answer.

quiz.q: You have eight interviews booked. Two people have churned recently, six are happy power users. What should you change?
o: Nothing — power users know the product best
Add more churned and competitor-choosing users; power users cannot tell you why people leave
Drop the churned users, they are biased against you
Interview only new signups instead
quiz.e: Power users are the least representative population you have: they have already adapted to every rough edge. People who left, or chose someone else, hold the information you are missing — and they are usually far more willing to talk than teams expect.

quiz.q: Nine of ten interviewees say they would pay for your new tier. What has this told you?
o: That there is real demand at that price
That the idea is worth building now
Almost nothing — stated future intent has a large and reliable gap to behaviour
That you should raise the price
quiz.e: This is the say-do gap, and it is one of the most expensive things in product work. Enthusiasm in a room where nothing costs anything is not demand. Convert it into an act: a pre-order, a deposit, a live pricing page, a signed pilot.

quiz.q: How many people do you usually need in one segment before patterns stop changing?
o: About 5 to 8
At least 30, for statistical validity
1 or 2 if they are the right people
100+, matched to your user base
quiz.e: Qualitative research reaches saturation quickly — five to eight per meaningfully different segment. That is nothing like a statistically representative sample, which is exactly why you never report percentages from it. Use interviews to find and explain patterns; use instrumentation and experiments to size them.

quiz.q: Which assumption should you test first?
o: The one you are most curious about
The one that is cheapest to test
The one that is both important and unevidenced — if it is wrong, nothing else matters
The one your stakeholders keep asking about
quiz.e: Assumption mapping exists to break the habit of testing whatever is easiest or most interesting. Sort by importance against how much evidence you actually have, and work the top-right corner. Cheapness matters — but only when choosing how to test the riskiest assumption, not which one.

sections.h: You are the doctor, not the pharmacist.
sections.lede: Customers arrive asking for a prescription. Your job is the diagnosis — and the two are only occasionally the same thing. This topic covers how to ask questions that produce facts instead of flattery, how many people you actually need, and why the most unanimous request in your tracker is usually a workaround for something nobody thought to mention.

panel.big: Ask about the past. The future is where people are polite.
items: “Would you use this?” is a question about a hypothetical person who does not exist.
“What did you do last time?” is a question about a real event with real costs.
Five to eight people per segment is enough. Doing it every week is what makes it work.

sections.lede: Almost every discovery failure comes from collapsing three different things into one: what someone asked for, what they are struggling with, and what would actually help.
sections.statement: A feature request is a symptom report written by someone who has already given up on the underlying problem.

cards.p: “Add bulk export.” Specific, actionable, and the only layer most teams ever hear. It tells you a workaround exists, and nothing about whether it is the right one.
“Every Monday I rebuild the same table for my manager.” This is where frequency, cost and emotion live. It is only reachable by asking about the last time.
“I need my manager to trust the number without me in the room.” Change the solution freely at this layer; you will usually find something cheaper than what was requested.

sections.lede: Front of the card: what it means. Back: what it looks like in the consulting room. Click or press Enter to flip.

sections.h: From “we should talk to users” to a decision
sections.lede: Seven steps. The first two are the ones that get skipped, and skipping them is how research becomes a hobby.

sections.h: Symptoms, risk and when to stop
sections.lede: Hover or tap any part of a diagram for the detail.

items: The request. Specific, actionable, and the only layer most teams ever hear.
“Every Monday I rebuild the same table”
The situation. Frequency, cost and emotion live here, and it only comes out if you ask about the last time.
“My manager trusts the number without me”
The job. Change the solution freely at this layer — the answer is usually cheaper.

items.cap: Fourteen accounts agreeing on layer one means they share layer three.
items.p: The unanimous request in your tracker is a workaround. Ask what they did before they asked you.

cells: Important and unevidenced. This corner is your entire research plan.
Important and already known. Stop researching it.
Neither important nor known. Genuinely fine to leave.
Low importance, plenty of evidence. This is where curiosity goes to hide.

items.cap: Assumption mapping exists to stop you testing whatever is most interesting.
items.p: Include the commercial assumptions. Teams validate desirability cheerfully and then discover nobody has a budget line.

curves.label: new patterns
curves.note: By the sixth conversation you are confirming rather than learning. Stop, or move to a new segment.

items.cap: Five to eight per segment. Far fewer than teams expect, and far more than they do.
items.p: This is also why you never report percentages from interviews. Use them to find patterns; use instrumentation to size them.

sections.h: One request refused, one validation that wasn't
sections.lede: Both started with strong, consistent signals from real customers. One saved three weeks; the other cost eleven.
Filterable. Try “bias”, “question” or “assumption”.
One attempt each, with an explanation either way.

title: Metrics & the North Star
one: Choosing numbers that describe value delivered rather than activity performed — and spotting the ones that quietly lie.

terms.d: The single number that best represents value delivered to customers, which the business also grows by. Not revenue — revenue is what you capture; the North Star is what you deliver.
terms.c: The bearing you are steering. Everything else on the panel exists to tell you whether you are holding it.

terms.d: The North Star broken into the multiplied or added parts a team can actually influence, level by level, until each leaf is something a squad could own this quarter.
terms.c: Speed comes from thrust and drag. Thrust comes from fuel flow and engine efficiency. Now there is a dial you can reach.

terms.d: What the customer gets and what you get, in one sentence each. If you cannot write both, no metric you pick will be the right one.
terms.c: The reason the flight exists at all: they arrive somewhere, you get paid for the seat.

terms.d: Outputs are the results you want and cannot touch directly. Inputs are the behaviours you can change this week. Teams should be held to inputs and judged on outputs.
terms.c: Altitude is the output. Throttle and pitch are the inputs. Pulling on the altimeter achieves nothing.

terms.d: Leading indicators move before the outcome and give you time to react. Lagging indicators confirm what already happened. You need both — and you should never manage exclusively by the lagging one.
terms.c: Fuel flow rising is leading. Running out of fuel is lagging.

terms.d: A number that reliably goes up, cannot go down, and changes no decision. Cumulative totals are the usual offenders: total signups, total downloads, total revenue since launch.
terms.c: A beautifully lit gauge that isn't wired to anything. Reassuring in the dark, useless in weather.

terms.d: A number that gets worse if you game the main one. Every goal needs at least one, chosen specifically because it can embarrass the goal.
terms.c: You can always gain altitude by climbing steeply. The airspeed indicator is what stops you stalling.

terms.d: A fast, measurable stand-in for something slow or invisible. Only as good as the link between the two, and that link needs re-checking every few quarters.
terms.c: Cabin pressure as a proxy for altitude. Close enough to fly by, until a seal fails.

terms.d: Averages hide the people having the worst time. For anything users feel — load time, wait time, support response — report the median and the 95th percentile, never the mean alone.
terms.c: “Average turbulence was mild” is no comfort to the two rows that hit the pocket.

terms.d: Someone who did a qualifying action in a window. The definition is doing all the work: “opened the app” and “completed a task” produce wildly different graphs from the same product.
terms.c: Counting passengers on board versus passengers who actually got where they were going.

terms.d: How many days a month a typical active user shows up. 20% means about six days a month. Useful only for products that should be daily habits — a tax tool with low stickiness is working perfectly.
terms.c: How often the same passengers reappear on the manifest.

terms.d: A group defined by when they started, then followed over time. Cohorts are the only honest way to see whether the product is improving, because they separate new-user growth from actual retention.
terms.c: Everyone who boarded in March, tracked as one group, so a busy April doesn't flatter their numbers.

terms.d: The percentage of a cohort still active at day 1, 7, 30, 90. The question is not how high it starts but whether it flattens: a curve that flattens has found a group of people for whom the product is genuinely part of life.
terms.c: Does the passenger list stop shrinking, or does the plane eventually empty?

terms.d: If the retention curve never goes flat, no amount of acquisition will build a business — you are refilling a bucket with a hole in it. Fix retention before buying traffic.
terms.c: A leak at altitude does not get better by taking on more fuel.

terms.d: The first point at which a new user has actually received the thing they came for, defined by behaviour rather than by finishing your onboarding. Best found by looking at what retained users did in week one that churned users did not.
terms.c: Wheels up. Everything before it is taxiing, and taxiing is not travel.

terms.d: Total gross profit you expect from a customer over their life. Always a forecast, always wrong at the edges, and dangerous when quoted to two decimal places. Use ranges.
terms.c: Estimated total revenue from a frequent flyer. An estimate, not a receipt.

terms.d: Total sales and marketing spend divided by customers acquired in the same period. Blended CAC includes organic customers and therefore flatters you; paid CAC is the one that governs decisions.
terms.c: What it cost to fill the seat, including the advert nobody remembers seeing.

terms.d: How many months of gross profit it takes to earn back the cost of acquiring a customer. Often more decision-relevant than LTV:CAC, because it tells you about cash rather than about a hopeful future.
terms.c: How many flights before the seat has paid for the advert.

terms.d: Any metric used as a target stops measuring what it used to. Not a reason to avoid targets — a reason to pair every target with a counter-metric and to expect creative compliance.
terms.c: Reward pilots for on-time arrival and the schedule gets padded. The planes are not faster.

terms.d: A ratio changes because the bottom of the fraction moved, not the top. Conversion rate improving because you started excluding bots is not the same as conversion improving.
terms.c: Your fuel efficiency looks better because you stopped counting the cargo.

terms.d: Predictable cycles — day of week, month end, holidays, school terms — that swamp real changes. Always compare like periods, and never draw a trend from a Tuesday.
terms.c: Headwinds every afternoon. Not a design flaw in the aircraft.

terms.d: Measuring only the users who stuck around. Engagement among survivors nearly always rises after a change that drove everyone else away.
terms.c: Interviewing the passengers who arrived, and concluding the flight was comfortable.

steps.t: Write the value exchange in two sentences
steps.out: “Customer gets X. We get Y.”
steps.b: Before choosing any number, state plainly what the customer receives and what you receive in return. Almost every bad metric comes from a team that only wrote the second sentence. If your product delivers value on Tuesdays and you get paid annually, that tension is exactly what your metric set has to hold.
steps.do: “A host gets a booked night. We get 15% of it.” Two sentences, and the North Star is now obvious.
steps.no: Starting from “what can we measure?” — you will end up with events, not meaning.

steps.t: Choose one North Star, and test it three ways
steps.out: One sentence with a number in it
steps.b: A candidate has to pass three tests. Does it go up only when a customer actually got value? Would it go down if the product got worse? Can a team meaningfully affect it inside a quarter? Revenue usually fails the first, cumulative totals fail the second, and company valuation fails the third.
steps.do: Prefer a metric with a unit of value and a time window: “weekly matched transactions”, “monthly reports shared”, “nights booked”.
steps.no: Picking two North Stars. You have then chosen nothing, and every argument will be settled by whichever is winning.
steps.snip:
Three tests for a North Star
  1. Does it only rise when a customer got real value?
  2. Would it fall if the product got worse?
  3. Can one team move it within a quarter?
Fails all three: “total registered users”
Passes all three: “weekly active teams with 3+ collaborators”

steps.t: Break it into a tree until you reach inputs
steps.out: A tree with owned leaves
steps.b: Decompose the North Star into parts that multiply or add — traffic × conversion × frequency × basket, or new + retained + resurrected − churned. Keep going until each leaf is something a specific team could move this quarter. The tree is also your best diagnostic tool: when the top number moves, you can see which branch did it.
steps.do: Write the arithmetic. If the parts do not reconstruct the whole, the tree is decoration.
steps.no: A flat list of twelve KPIs. A list cannot tell you why anything changed.

steps.t: Add counter-metrics to every goal
steps.out: Each target paired with something that can contradict it
steps.b: For each metric a team is chasing, ask how a clever, tired person would hit the number without delivering the value — then measure that. Sign-ups paired with activation. Speed paired with error rate. Volume paired with quality or complaint rate. This is the cheapest protection you will ever buy.
steps.do: Let the counter-metric be owned by someone who is not chasing the main number.
steps.no: Assuming your team is too principled to game a metric. Goodhart's law is not about ethics; it is about attention.

steps.t: Define every metric precisely, in writing
steps.out: A one-page definition per metric
steps.b: Name the numerator, the denominator, the time window, the exclusions, the timezone and the identity rule. Half of all dashboard disagreements are two correct calculations of two different things. Write it down once, link to it from every dashboard, and version it when it changes.
steps.do: Record the date of every definition change. A step in a chart is usually a definition, not the product.
steps.no: “Active users” with no definition. Three teams will build three numbers and each will defend theirs.

steps.t: Instrument it and reconcile against something real
steps.out: A number you would defend in a board meeting
steps.b: Implement the events, then check the result against an independent source: billing, the database, a manual count for one day. Expect a gap, find out why, and write down the acceptable margin. A metric nobody has ever reconciled is a rumour with a chart.
steps.do: Reconcile revenue metrics against the finance system before anyone forecasts from them.
steps.no: Trusting a funnel where each step is instrumented by a different team in a different quarter.

steps.t: Review on a cadence: number, diagnosis, action
steps.out: A weekly or monthly review with decisions in it
steps.b: Set a rhythm and a format. What did the North Star do, which branch of the tree explains it, what will we do differently, and what did we get wrong last time? The format matters more than the frequency — a review that only reads numbers aloud will be quietly abandoned within two months.
steps.do: Keep a log of predictions and outcomes. Calibration is the skill that separates a PM from a dashboard.
steps.no: Reporting the number without a diagnosis. If nobody can explain the move, nobody can act on it.

cases.title: A marketplace that optimised registrations
cases.sub: Two years of hitting the target, and the business did not move. The metric was measuring effort, not value.
steps: Total registered users, reported cumulatively to the board every month. It only ever went up, which everybody found reassuring.
Two years of work aimed squarely at the number: reduced sign-up friction, social login, an incentivised referral scheme, aggressive paid acquisition. Registrations grew 212%.
Weekly matched jobs — the point at which a buyer and a seller transact, and the only moment the business earns anything — grew 6%. Revenue grew 4%, which was inflation and a price rise.

The metric failed test one: it rose without anyone receiving value. It also failed test two — you could improve it by making the product worse, and they had, by burying the search experience under an account wall.
New North Star: weekly matched jobs. It broke into a tree with four leaves: new demand posted, supply liquidity in the category, match rate, and repeat rate. Each got an owner.

Within a quarter the roadmap was unrecognisable. The referral scheme was cut. The account wall came down. Work moved to matching quality and category liquidity — unglamorous, and the first thing in two years that moved revenue.
Match rate was paired with post-match cancellation rate, precisely so that “matching” could not be gamed by pairing people badly.

verdict.h: The team hit every target for two years
verdict.p: This is the expensive version of the mistake, because nothing looked wrong. Every review was green, every quarter beat plan, and the metric was rising for real. It simply was not connected to anyone receiving anything.
verdict.lesson: Run the three tests before adopting a North Star. A number that cannot go down when the product gets worse will quietly consume years.

cases.title: Two cohorts, one leaking bucket
cases.sub: Both cohorts looked identical at day one. One flattened at 31%, the other kept falling. Only one was a business.
steps: A consumer app, two acquisition sources: organic search (cohort A) and paid social (cohort B). Blended retention looked acceptable and nobody had split it.
Both cohorts started at 61% day-1. By day 30, A was at 38% and B at 12%. By day 90, A had flattened at 31%; B was at 4% and still declining.

A flat tail means a stable group for whom the product is part of life. Cohort A had roughly 31 people in every 100 who would keep coming back — the beginnings of a business. Cohort B had no floor at all.

Paid was two-thirds of new users and had a CAC of $18 with an effective LTV of about $6 on those retention curves. Every paid install lost roughly $12, and blended reporting had been hiding it for five months.
Paid social paused rather than optimised — the creative was working fine, it was bringing in people who did not want the product. Spend redirected into the activation step for organic users.

Total actives fell 22% in a month, which required an uncomfortable conversation. Cohort-A-equivalent actives rose, payback went positive, and the flattened curve moved from 31% to 36% over two quarters as activation improved.

verdict.h: Blended numbers hid two different products
verdict.p: Nothing was wrong with the measurement — the blended curve was arithmetically correct. It was just an average of a business and a leak, and averages of two different things describe neither.
verdict.lesson: Never judge retention on a blended curve. Split by acquisition source and cohort, and look for the flattening before you spend anything on growth.

quiz.q: Which of these is the strongest North Star candidate for a photo-printing service?
o: Total registered accounts
Monthly revenue
Photo books delivered per month
App store rating
quiz.e: Delivered photo books passes all three tests: it only rises when a customer got the thing they came for, it falls if the product gets worse, and a team can move it within a quarter. Revenue is what you capture rather than what you deliver, total accounts can never fall, and a store rating is neither controllable nor a measure of value delivered.

quiz.q: Your retention curve is at 40% on day 7 and 3% on day 90, still falling. What does that tell you?
o: Retention is weak but acceptable for consumer apps
There is no flattening, so there is no core of users the product is essential to — fix that before spending on acquisition
You need to improve day-1 onboarding
Nothing without a comparison to competitors
quiz.e: The flattening test is the useful signal, not the height of any single point. A curve with no floor means every user you acquire eventually leaves, so acquisition spend is a bucket with a hole in it. More traffic makes the leak bigger, not smaller.

quiz.q: A team is targeted on support ticket response time. What is the right counter-metric?
o: Number of tickets received
Reopen rate or resolution satisfaction
Team headcount
Average handling time
quiz.e: A counter-metric has to be capable of embarrassing the target. Response time can be improved dramatically by sending fast, unhelpful replies — which shows up in reopens and satisfaction, not in ticket volume or handling time. Volume is mostly outside the team's control anyway.

quiz.q: Conversion rate jumped from 2.1% to 2.8% overnight with no release. Most likely cause?
o: A competitor went down
A definition or filtering change moved the denominator
Seasonality
Genuine improvement from an earlier release finally landing
quiz.e: Overnight step changes with no release are almost always the measurement, not the product — a bot filter, a new exclusion, an identity change, a tracking fix. Twyman's law applies: the more interesting the number, the more likely it is a bug. Check the definition history before telling anyone good news.

quiz.q: Your average page load is 1.2s and users complain constantly. What are you probably missing?
o: The average is fine, the complaints are unrepresentative
The 95th percentile — a slow tail hurts real people and averages hide it
You need a bigger sample
Load time is not what they mean by slow
quiz.e: Averages are dominated by the majority who are fine. If p95 is 9 seconds, one in twenty page loads is genuinely painful — which, across a day, is most of your users experiencing it at least once. For anything a person waits for, report the median and p95 together.

sections.h: A dashboard is a cockpit. Most of the gauges aren't wired up.
sections.lede: Every metric problem is the same problem wearing a different hat: the number you can measure easily is rarely the number that means something. This topic is about picking one that does, breaking it into dials a team can actually reach, and pairing it with something that can contradict it.
