title: Prioritisation & Trade-offs
one: Deciding what not to do, defensibly, when everybody in the room has a different favourite.

terms.d: Deciding the order of work when there is more of it than there is capacity. Not deciding what is valuable — everything on the list is valuable to somebody, which is exactly why the job is hard.
terms.c: The triage desk on a Friday night. Every single person in the waiting room needs help, and there are four doctors.

terms.d: How much work your team can actually finish in a period, measured from history rather than hope. Prioritisation without a capacity number is a wish list with a running order.
terms.c: Four doctors, eleven hours. Not “as many patients as we can care about”.

terms.d: Support, incidents, compliance, dependency upgrades, migrations. Typically 20–40% of a team's real capacity, and if you do not subtract it before planning, you have already overcommitted.
terms.c: The beds permanently occupied by the patients already admitted. They come off the count before you plan the night.

terms.d: Deciding in advance what share of capacity goes to which kind of work — for example 60% core outcome, 20% platform and debt, 20% bets. Made once per quarter, it removes most item-by-item arguments.
terms.c: Two doctors on emergencies, one on the walk-in queue, one on ward rounds. Set at the start of the shift, not renegotiated per patient.

terms.d: The value of the best thing you did not do. It is the only cost that matters in prioritisation and the only one that never appears on a ticket.
terms.c: Every minute with this patient is a minute the person in bay four is still waiting.

terms.d: A scoring model: how many people it touches, how much it moves them, how sure you are, divided by how much work it is. Its real value is forcing four separate arguments instead of one vague one.
terms.c: The triage form: how many affected, how severe, how certain the diagnosis, how long the treatment.

terms.d: RICE without reach. Faster, cruder, and blind to how many people are affected — fine for comparing experiments within one surface, poor for comparing across a product.
terms.c: A quick look, no chart, no notes. Right for a sprained wrist, wrong for chest pain.

terms.d: How much you actually know, expressed as a percentage or a tier: measured data, research, informed guess, hunch. It is the number people fake most, and the number most worth arguing about.
terms.c: “Probably a virus” and “confirmed by test” lead to very different decisions and look identical on the form.

terms.d: A rough estimate in person-weeks or t-shirt sizes, from the people who will do the work. Precision here is false comfort — what you need is enough accuracy to distinguish a week from a quarter.
terms.c: Fifteen minutes, an hour, or the whole night. Nobody needs it in seconds.

terms.d: What it costs you per week to not have this yet. Some work is worth the same in June as in March; some loses most of its value if it misses a season, a contract or a regulation.
terms.c: Some conditions are stable for hours. Some deteriorate by the minute. That difference is the whole point of triage.

terms.d: Cost of delay divided by job size, from SAFe. Formally the right answer when you want to maximise value delivered over time, and useful mainly because it makes people estimate urgency separately from value.
terms.c: Treat the deteriorating patient with the quick fix first — you save more lives per hour that way.

terms.d: Your own criteria with your own weights — strategic fit, revenue, risk, effort. More honest than borrowing someone else's formula, provided you set the weights before you see the scores.
terms.c: A hospital's own protocol, tuned to the patients it actually gets.

terms.d: Sorting scope into four buckets for a fixed deadline. Its power is entirely in the fourth bucket: an explicit, written “won't this time” is the only part people remember.
terms.c: Treat now, treat tonight, treat if there is time, send home with advice.

terms.d: Sorts features by how satisfaction responds: basic expectations (absence hurts, presence is unnoticed), performance features (more is better, linearly), and delighters (unexpected, high upside, and they decay into expectations over time).
terms.c: Clean sheets are expected. Shorter waits are appreciated. Someone remembering your name is delight — until you come to expect it.

terms.d: Ranking is what matters most. Sequencing is what to do first, which also has to respect dependencies, one-way doors, learning value and who is available. The two lists are rarely identical.
terms.c: The sickest patient is the priority. But you still run the blood test first, because the treatment depends on it.

terms.d: A decision that is expensive or impossible to undo: data models, public APIs, pricing you have announced, migrations. These deserve far more analysis than reversible ones, and reversible ones deserve far less.
terms.c: Surgery versus a course of tablets. You can stop the tablets.

terms.d: How much a piece of work reduces uncertainty about everything else on the list. Sometimes the right first item is the one that tells you whether items two through nine are worth doing at all.
terms.c: Running the test that determines the whole treatment plan, even though it treats nothing.

terms.d: The senior view that skips the queue. Sometimes it carries information you genuinely lack; often it carries a recent conversation. The fix is not defiance but a scoring model everyone can see, including them.
terms.c: The consultant walks past the queue with a friend of a friend. Everyone notices, and the protocol is now optional.

terms.d: Continuing because of what you have already spent. The money is gone either way; the only question is what the remaining effort is worth from here.
terms.c: “We've already done four hours of this operation” is not a medical reason to continue.

terms.d: Producing a number to 2 decimal places from four guesses, then treating the ranking as objective. The model exists to locate disagreement, not to replace judgement.
terms.c: A triage score of 6.42 does not mean the patient is 3% sicker than the one at 6.24.

terms.d: Hundreds of items nobody will ever do, kept because deleting them feels rude. It hides the real list, and it quietly teaches stakeholders that “added to the backlog” means no.
terms.c: A waiting room with three hundred people in it, most of whom went home weeks ago.

steps.t: Work out what capacity you actually have
steps.out: A real number of person-weeks
steps.b: Start from the last two or three completed periods, not from headcount. Subtract holidays, on-call, support rotations, interviews, and the migration someone else has committed you to. Most teams discover 40–60% of nominal capacity is already spoken for, which explains a great deal about why last quarter felt like failure.
steps.do: Subtract keep-the-lights-on before planning, and show the subtraction to stakeholders. It is the most persuasive slide you own.
steps.no: Planning against headcount × weeks. You will overcommit by roughly a third, every time.

steps.t: Get everything onto one list
steps.out: A single list with a common unit
steps.b: Feature ideas, tech debt, compliance work, bugs, experiments, sales commitments. Anything kept in a separate list is really being kept out of the trade-off, and the trade-off is the whole exercise. Reduce every item to the same shape: what changes for whom, roughly how big.
steps.do: Include the work already promised verbally. Shadow commitments are what break plans.
steps.no: A separate “tech debt backlog” that never competes with features. It will never win a comparison it is not entered into.

steps.t: Score it — to find the disagreements
steps.out: Scores, and a list of things people disagree about
steps.b: Run RICE, WSJF or your own weighted model. The output you actually want is not the ranking; it is the three items where two people scored impact 3 and 0.5. That gap is a hidden disagreement about strategy or evidence, and it is far more valuable than the arithmetic.
steps.do: Score independently first, then compare. Scoring together produces consensus by anchoring on whoever spoke first.
steps.no: Treating the ranking as the decision. Then nobody has decided anything and the spreadsheet gets the blame.
steps.snip:
RICE   = Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort
ICE    = Impact × Confidence × Ease
WSJF   = Cost of delay ÷ Job size
Impact scale: 3 massive · 2 high · 1 medium · 0.5 low · 0.25 minimal
Confidence: 100% measured · 80% researched · 50% informed guess · 20% hunch

steps.t: Interrogate confidence, not impact
steps.out: Either better evidence, or a cheap test first
steps.b: Impact estimates are where optimism lives, but confidence is where you can actually act. For any large item scored at low confidence, the correct next move is usually not to build it or to drop it, but to spend a fraction of the effort finding out. A two-day test that raises confidence from 30% to 80% changes the whole ranking.
steps.do: Put the cheap test on the list as its own item, with its own effort estimate.
steps.no: Letting a big-effort, low-confidence item sit at the top because someone senior is sure. Confidence is not a mood.

steps.t: Turn the ranking into a sequence
steps.out: An ordered plan for the next few weeks
steps.b: Now bring in the things a score cannot see: dependencies, one-way doors, who is available, and what teaches you the most. Reversible decisions should move fast and get less analysis; irreversible ones deserve the extra week. Sometimes the second-ranked item goes first because it unblocks three others.
steps.do: Mark one-way doors explicitly. They are the only items that justify slowing down.
steps.no: Working strictly top-down through a ranked list. Rank ignores dependency, and dependency does not care about rank.

steps.t: Allocate by bucket, not by top-N
steps.out: A percentage split, agreed for the quarter
steps.b: Pure scoring quietly optimises for cheap and certain, which means platform work and genuine bets never win. Fix it structurally: decide up front that, say, 60% of capacity serves the main outcome, 20% goes to platform and debt, and 20% to bets that could be wrong. Then rank within each bucket.
steps.do: Agree the split with stakeholders once per quarter. It converts a hundred small arguments into one.
steps.no: Promising the bets bucket will also hit this quarter's targets. That is how it gets raided in week three.

steps.t: Publish the no's
steps.out: A visible “not this quarter” list, with reasons
steps.b: Write down what you are not doing and why — one line each, and name the thing it lost to. This is unpleasant for a day and saves you from months of re-litigating. It also lets people who disagree bring evidence rather than volume, which is a much better argument to be having.
steps.do: Delete anything older than two quarters that nobody has asked about since. It is not a plan, it is clutter.
steps.no: “It's on the backlog.” Everybody knows what that means, and it costs you credibility every time.

cases.badge: Big bet deferred · two small wins first
cases.title: The rebuild that lost to a checkbox
cases.sub: Everyone knew the billing rebuild was the priority. Scoring it separately from the things it was competing with produced a different order — and then a different decision.
steps: A B2B tool with 200,000 monthly users. The billing rebuild had been “next quarter” for three quarters. It was scored against ten other items, independently, by the PM, the tech lead and the support lead.

Impact scores on the rebuild ranged from 3 (massive) to 0.5 (low) — the widest gap on the board. Investigating it revealed the argument was really about who suffered: engineering hated the code, and support could name only 11 customers who had ever complained about billing.

Rebuild: reach 200,000, impact 3, confidence 40%, effort 12 person-months → RICE ≈ 20,000. Failed-payment retry emails: reach 9,000, impact 2, confidence 90%, effort 0.5 → RICE ≈ 32,400. Export column fix: reach 40,000, impact 1, confidence 95%, effort 1.5 → RICE ≈ 25,300.

Rather than accept a 40% confidence score on twelve person-months, the team spent four days measuring: how many users hit billing errors, how many churned within 30 days of one, and what support actually spent time on.
Billing errors affected 1.9% of accounts, and the churn correlation was real but small. Two of the four failure modes came from one retry bug, not from the architecture.

The two small items shipped in three weeks. The rebuild was descoped to fixing the retry path and the two worst failure modes — about five person-months instead of twelve — and scheduled after the quarter's main outcome work.
Failed-payment recovery rose from 34% to 61%. The remaining architectural work was still worth doing and is now sized honestly, rather than carrying the hopes of an entire quarter.

verdict.h: The score did not decide anything — the argument it started did
verdict.p: Nobody in the room was wrong. Engineering was right that the code was bad, support was right that customers rarely complained, and the PM was right that it mattered. The scoring model's only contribution was to make those three positions visible as numbers on the same row.
verdict.lesson: When two people score impact very differently, stop and find out what they each know. That conversation is worth more than the ranking.

cases.title: A quarter of eight cheap wins
cases.sub: RICE ran the roadmap, the team delivered everything, and the outcome the quarter was funded to move did not budge.
steps: A quarter with one funded outcome: raise new-team activation by 8%. The team prioritised strictly by RICE score, top-down, no allocation buckets.

Every item with a large denominator and a small effort. Copy changes, an empty-state fix, a settings reorganisation, two performance tweaks, an email nudge, and two bug batches. Median effort: half a person-month.

Effort sits in the denominator, so cheap items win almost automatically. Reach favours anything touching all users, and confidence favours anything already understood. The activation work — a guided setup flow with a data-import step — was 4 person-months at 50% confidence and ranked ninth.
All eight shipped. Activation moved +0.4% against a target of +8%. Every individual item had done roughly what was predicted; none of them was aimed at the outcome.
RICE has no concept of strategy. It ranks items against each other on efficiency, and eight efficient items pointed in eight directions produce a busy quarter and a flat graph.

Allocation buckets the following quarter: 60% of capacity reserved for the activation outcome, 20% for platform and debt, 20% for opportunistic wins. RICE still used — but only to rank within a bucket.
The guided setup flow shipped in eight weeks. Activation rose 6.2%, short of target and roughly fifteen times the previous quarter's movement.

verdict.h: A scoring model will always prefer cheap and certain
verdict.p: This failure looks like success right up until the review. The team was productive, the estimates were accurate, and stakeholders got things they had asked for. The model simply had no way to know which of those things the quarter was for.
verdict.lesson: Decide your allocation before you score. Rank within buckets, or efficiency will quietly outrank strategy every time.

quiz.q: Two people score the same item impact 3 and impact 0.5. What is the most useful response?
o: Average them to 1.75 and move on
Ask the more senior person to decide
Stop and find out what each of them knows that the other doesn't
Re-score with a bigger group
quiz.e: A wide gap on one dimension is the most valuable output a scoring model produces. It almost always means the two people are picturing different users, different failure modes, or different evidence. Averaging destroys exactly the information you needed.

quiz.q: Your team consistently prioritises with RICE and consistently ships cheap items. Why?
o: The estimates are wrong
Effort is the denominator, so low-effort items win almost automatically
Impact is being scored too conservatively
Confidence scores are too low on big items
quiz.e: This is structural, not a mistake. Dividing by effort means a small, certain item will usually beat a large, uncertain one — even when the large one is the only thing aimed at your actual goal. The fix is allocation buckets, with scoring used to rank inside each bucket.

quiz.q: A big item scores high on reach and impact but only 30% confidence. Best next move?
o: Build it — the upside justifies the risk
Drop it until someone brings evidence
Spend a fraction of the effort on a test that could raise confidence, and re-rank
Raise the confidence score, since the team believes in it
quiz.e: Low confidence on a large item is a signal to buy information, not to gamble or to give up. If two days of analysis or a small experiment moves confidence from 30% to 80%, the ranking changes legitimately — and the cheap test belongs on the list as its own item.

quiz.q: Which item deserves the most analysis before you commit?
o: The one with the highest RICE score
The most expensive one
The one that is hardest to reverse
The one stakeholders ask about most
quiz.e: Reversibility should govern how much analysis you buy. One-way doors — data models, public APIs, announced pricing, migrations — justify the extra week, because being wrong is expensive for years. Reversible decisions deserve less analysis than most teams give them.

quiz.q: Your team's nominal capacity is 12 person-weeks per sprint. What should you plan against?
o: 12 — that is the capacity
12 minus support, on-call, incidents and committed migrations, based on the last few sprints
14, to create healthy pressure
Whatever the last sprint delivered, exactly
quiz.e: Keep-the-lights-on work is typically 20–40% of real capacity and it does not negotiate. Planning against nominal capacity guarantees overcommitment, and overcommitment is what turns prioritisation into an argument about why the plan slipped rather than about what matters.

sections.h: Everyone in the waiting room is a priority. There are four doctors.
sections.lede: Prioritisation is not ranking things by how good they are — everything on the list is good, which is why it got on the list. It is triage: severity, treatability and capacity, decided out loud, with the no's written down. This topic covers the models, when each one is the right instrument, and the two ways they reliably mislead.

panel.big: The score's job is to locate the disagreement, not to end it.
items: Subtract keep-the-lights-on before you plan anything.
Decide allocation first, then rank within buckets — or cheap will always beat important.
Publish the no's with reasons. It costs a day and saves a quarter.

sections.lede: Most prioritisation arguments are three separate arguments having a fight inside one meeting. Split them and they mostly resolve themselves.
sections.statement: You are not choosing between good and bad. You are choosing which good thing waits, and telling that person to their face.

cards.p: Capacity after support, incidents and commitments. Almost every planning failure is an arithmetic failure that happened before anyone discussed value.
Allocation. Agree the split between the main outcome, platform health and bets before a single item is scored, or efficiency will eat strategy.
Score to find disagreements, then sequence for dependencies, one-way doors and learning value. Ranking and sequencing are different lists.

Four items to start with, or edit them into your own. Watch what happens to the ranking when you change confidence on the big item — and note how hard it is for anything expensive to win.

cells: Do them, but notice that a quarter of quick wins is still a flat quarter.
Where the outcome lives. Also where low confidence lives — buy information first.
Fine for a gap. Not a plan.
Expensive and marginal. The hardest ones to kill, because someone promised them.

items.p: This is why allocation comes before ranking. Efficiency and importance are not the same axis.

items: Ranked internally by RICE. Everything here points at one number.

items.p: Agreed with stakeholders up front, this converts item-by-item negotiation into a single conversation about proportions.

Cost of delay is hard to estimate and easy to inflate
A fixed deadline, fixed scope negotiation, launch or contract
Says nothing about relative value inside “must”
Deciding between table stakes, more-is-better, and delight
Needs survey work; delighters decay into expectations
Criteria are specific to your company and shift by year
Weights get tuned after the fact to justify a favourite
What is this worth per week of waiting?
Two items look equal and one has a deadline attached
Ignores effort entirely, so it cannot rank on its own

title: Strategy & Roadmapping
one: Turning a diagnosis into a sequence of bets somebody else can follow without you in the room.

terms.d: A diagnosis of your situation, a choice about how to respond, and the coherent actions that follow. If it contains no choice — nothing you are deliberately not doing — it is a plan with ambition attached.
terms.c: Looking at the mountain, the weather and your supplies, and choosing the north face because that is where your team's strengths actually are.

terms.d: A plain description of what is really going on, including the uncomfortable parts. Most strategy documents fail here: they describe an ambition and skip the situation.
terms.c: “The south route is shorter but the snow is unstable this month, and two of us have never used crampons.”

terms.d: The overall approach you will take in response to the diagnosis — the thing that makes some options obviously in and most obviously out.
terms.c: “We go slowly, high, and early in the day.” Now half the possible plans are eliminated without further argument.

terms.d: The specific, mutually reinforcing moves that follow. Coherent is the operative word: actions that each make sense alone but fight each other are the commonest form of strategy failure.
terms.c: Light packs, an early start, and camp below the ridge. Each decision makes the others easier.

terms.t: Where to play / how to win
terms.d: Two linked choices: which markets, segments and channels you compete in, and what advantage lets you win there. Answering one without the other produces either a target with no plan or a plan with no target.
terms.c: Which face you climb, and what about your team makes that face survivable.

terms.d: A meaningful chunk of work with an outcome attached and an explicit chance of being wrong. Framing work as bets is what makes it possible to stop things without anybody losing face.
terms.c: A supply cache placed high on the route. Useful if you get there, wasted if you turn back — and you accepted that when you placed it.

terms.d: Whether a piece of work makes your chosen advantage stronger. A profitable feature that pulls you toward a market you have chosen not to serve is a distraction with a business case.
terms.c: A shortcut that takes you off the route you trained for.

terms.d: The one thing actually holding back the outcome — a team, a technology, a channel, a licence. Improvements anywhere else produce very little, which is why finding it is the highest-leverage analysis you can do.
terms.c: The rope. Everything else can be world-class and you still move at the speed of the rope.

terms.d: Reversible decisions should be made fast and low; irreversible ones deserve seniority, analysis and a written record. Treating everything as one-way is how organisations get slow.
terms.c: Trying a route is reversible. Abseiling into the couloir is not.

terms.d: A communication artefact showing what you intend to work on, in what order, and roughly when. It is a route, not a railway timetable — and the honest ones get less precise the further out they go.
terms.c: The route drawn on the map, with the later days sketched rather than plotted.

terms.d: Organised by problems to be solved and outcomes to be moved, with confidence decreasing across three horizons. Trades false precision for the ability to change your mind without a crisis.
terms.c: “Today: reach the col. Next: the ridge, weather permitting. Later: the summit push.”

terms.d: A grouping of work around one outcome, used so that a roadmap communicates intent rather than a list of features. Themes survive re-planning; feature names rarely do.
terms.c: “Acclimatisation” is a theme. “Camp at 4,100m on Thursday” is a task.

terms.d: A milestone is a checkpoint you use to learn and adjust. A deadline is a date something must be true by, usually because of something external — a contract, a regulation, a season. Confusing them makes every date feel like a promise.
terms.c: Reaching the col by noon is a checkpoint that tells you whether to continue. The helicopter pickup on Friday is a deadline.

terms.d: How far ahead your plan can be honest given how much your world changes. For most teams that is one quarter of commitment, two of intent, and a year of direction. Planning past your horizon is fiction with Gantt bars.
terms.c: You can forecast tomorrow's weather. Next Thursday's is a guess in a nice font.

terms.d: The written version: situation, choice, why this and not that, what changes, how you will know. Prose forces coherence in a way slides actively prevent.
terms.c: The expedition brief everyone reads before they pack.

terms.d: Something you are deliberately not pursuing this period, written down. The fastest way to tell whether a strategy is real is to look for these.
terms.c: “We are not attempting the traverse this year.” Written on the brief, so nobody packs for it.

terms.d: A sentence naming what you gave up. It converts a strategy from a list of ambitions into a decision people can argue with productively.
terms.c: “We chose the longer route over the faster one, because we would rather be slow than exposed.”

terms.d: A team measured on shipping rather than on changing anything. Recognisable by roadmaps made of feature names, launches with no success metric, and nobody able to say what the last quarter achieved.
terms.c: Walking hard all day, in whichever direction the ground is easiest.

terms.d: A statement of desired outcome mistaken for a strategy. Recognisable because nobody could possibly disagree with it, and because it excludes nothing.
terms.c: “Reach the summit safely and efficiently.” True, agreed, and no help at all at the fork.

terms.d: When a communication tool becomes a commitment register, teams stop learning: changing the plan now requires an apology, so the plan stops changing even when it should.
terms.c: A route you cannot deviate from, in weather that has already changed.

terms.d: Work you are still doing because of a strategy you have already abandoned. Every re-plan should include a deliberate hunt for it.
terms.c: Still carrying the ropes for a face you decided in March not to climb.

steps.t: Write the diagnosis before anything else
steps.out: One page describing the situation honestly
steps.b: Describe where you actually are: what is growing, what is stalling, what customers keep telling you, what competitors have changed, where your team is genuinely strong and where it is not. Include the parts that are awkward to say in front of your boss — a diagnosis that flatters everyone present is not a diagnosis.
steps.do: Include two or three numbers and one uncomfortable sentence. If nothing in it is uncomfortable, keep going.
steps.no: Opening with the vision. Vision without diagnosis produces plans that assume a company you do not have.
steps.snip:
Diagnosis, in four lines
  What is working:        …and why we think so
  What is stalling:      …and what we have ruled out
  What has changed:      market, customers, competitors, cost
  What we are bad at:    the constraint, named plainly

steps.t: Name the constraint
steps.out: One sentence: “the thing holding us back is …”
steps.b: Almost every outcome is limited by one thing at a time. Find it and most of the roadmap writes itself; miss it and you will fund improvements that cannot possibly show up in the results. Test your candidate by asking what would happen if it were suddenly twice as good.
steps.do: Check whether the constraint is even inside your product. Often it is pricing, onboarding, sales capacity or a support process.
steps.no: Assuming the constraint is whatever your team is best at fixing.

steps.t: Make the choice, and say what you are giving up
steps.out: A guiding policy plus explicit anti-goals
steps.b: Choose where you will play and what will let you win there, then write down what that rules out. The anti-goals do most of the work: they are what let a team say no six weeks later without escalating, and they are the part stakeholders will actually argue about — which is the argument you want to have now rather than in month three.
steps.do: Write “we chose X over Y, because Z.” One line per major choice.
steps.no: A strategy nobody could disagree with. If there is no opposing view worth stating, you have not chosen anything.

steps.t: Turn the choice into a small number of bets
steps.out: Three to five bets, each with an outcome and a size
steps.b: Each bet needs an outcome in numbers, a rough size, the assumption it depends on, and what would make you stop. Three to five is the usable range; more than that and you are describing everything you might do rather than what you have chosen. Sequence them so the riskiest assumption gets tested early and cheaply.
steps.do: Give each bet a kill condition written before it starts. It is the only reliable way to stop things.
steps.no: Nine bets. That is a backlog wearing strategy language.

steps.t: Build the roadmap around outcomes, not dates
steps.out: Now / next / later, with confidence decreasing
steps.b: Organise by the problem being solved, with a named outcome per theme. Be specific about the current horizon, vaguer about the next, and directional beyond that — the fading precision is the honest signal, not a weakness. Keep real deadlines clearly marked as deadlines, and everything else clearly marked as intent.
steps.do: Put the outcome and the current baseline on the roadmap itself, next to each theme.
steps.no: Dates on everything twelve months out. You will spend next year defending numbers you invented in a hurry.

steps.t: Write the narrative and take it to the argument
steps.out: A one-pager people have actually read
steps.b: Prose, not slides: situation, choice, what we are not doing, what changes, how we will know. Then go and get it attacked — sales, support, engineering, finance, and the person most likely to disagree. A strategy that has not survived a hostile read has not been tested, and you will discover the objections during delivery instead.
steps.do: Ask each reader: what would have to be true for this to be wrong? Then write the best answers down.
steps.no: Presenting it as finished. People commit to things they were allowed to shape.

steps.t: Review on a rhythm, and hunt the strategy tax
steps.out: A quarterly re-plan with things deliberately stopped
steps.b: Every quarter, check each bet against its outcome and its kill condition, then deliberately look for work still running on assumptions you have abandoned. Stopping things is the hardest muscle in product management and the one that most distinguishes a strategy from a wish list.
steps.do: Report bets as won, lost, or still open — and say what the loss taught you. Publicly killing one bet buys credibility for the rest.
steps.no: Adding the new quarter's bets on top of the old ones. Capacity does not care how good the reasoning was.

cases.kind: A strategy with a no in it
cases.title: The scheduling tool that stopped serving everybody
cases.sub: Flat growth, a roadmap full of requests from four different markets, and a diagnosis nobody wanted to write down.
steps: A scheduling product sold to clinics, salons, tutors and repair firms. Retention differed enormously by segment — clinics retained at 91% annually, tutors at 44% — but the roadmap was an evenly split queue of requests from all four. The uncomfortable sentence: “we are four mediocre products with one login.”
Not engineering capacity. The constraint was that every feature had to be built generically enough for four workflows, which roughly doubled design and QA cost and made none of them good.
Where to play: clinics and allied health. How to win: the compliance and reminder features nobody else would build for a small market, and integrations with two practice-management systems.
Written down explicitly: no new tutoring features, no marketplace, no consumer-facing booking app. Three of these had active internal champions and one had a signed pilot.

Four bets: no-show reduction (target 30% fewer), two named integrations, an audit-trail feature required by regulation, and a pricing change to reflect the new positioning. Each with a kill condition.
Tutoring customers, 22% of revenue, were told plainly there would be no new work for them. Roughly a third churned over a year, which was forecast and accepted in writing.

No-shows fell 34% for clinics, which became the sales pitch. Net revenue grew despite the churn, and quarterly growth moved from 3% to 14%. The roadmap got shorter and shipped faster because everything only had to work for one workflow.

verdict.p: The positive half of this strategy was not clever — “focus on your best segment” is advice anyone could give. The work was in writing down the three things they would not do while two internal champions were in the room, and then holding it for three quarters.
verdict.lesson: A strategy is only real once it names what you are giving up, in writing, in front of the people who wanted it.

cases.title: Twelve months of dates, defended to the end
cases.sub: The roadmap was committed to a customer in January. By April everyone could see it was wrong, and it shipped anyway.
steps: To close a large enterprise deal, a dated twelve-month roadmap with nineteen named features was attached to the contract as an appendix.
Usage data showed the customer's teams were not using the two features that the next six months of the plan built upon. The workflow assumption behind the whole sequence was wrong.
Changing the plan now meant reopening a contract appendix, so it became a legal and commercial conversation rather than a product one. The safest individual choice for everybody was to keep shipping.
Seventeen of nineteen features delivered close to the dates. Adoption of the six-month block: under 4% of licensed seats. The customer did not renew, citing “low internal adoption”.

The failure was structural. A roadmap is a communication tool; the moment it becomes a commitment register, learning becomes expensive and teams optimise for keeping the promise rather than for being right.

Roadmaps moved to outcomes with three horizons. Enterprise contracts got a different instrument: two named outcomes with agreed success measures, quarterly reviews, and an explicit right to change the how. Two later deals closed on that basis.
This is harder in enterprise sales than product people admit. Some buyers require dates. The workable version is committing to a small number of dated items and keeping the rest as outcomes.

verdict.h: They kept every promise except the one that mattered
verdict.p: Nobody behaved badly. Sales needed certainty to close, the customer wanted assurance, and the team delivered what was written. The only thing missing was any mechanism for the plan to respond to what April taught them.
verdict.lesson: Never let a roadmap become a contract. Commit to outcomes and review dates; keep the right to change how you get there.

quiz.q: Which of these is closest to an actual strategy?
o: “Become the leading platform for small businesses by 2027”
“We will win mid-market clinics by building the compliance features generalists won't, and we will not build consumer booking”
“Grow revenue 40% while improving NPS”
“Ship the twelve features on the roadmap”
quiz.e: A strategy contains a choice, and a choice excludes something. The second option names where it plays, what wins there, and what it refuses to do — so a team can apply it to a decision nobody anticipated. The others are ambitions, targets and a plan respectively, and none of them rules anything out.

quiz.q: Your roadmap has precise dates for every item twelve months out. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Better stakeholder confidence
The team will learn faster because they are accountable
Changing the plan becomes politically expensive, so learning stops being acted on
Nothing — dates are just estimates
quiz.e: Once dates read as promises, being right becomes less important than keeping them. That is the feature-factory mechanism: teams keep shipping a plan they can already see is wrong, because changing it now costs credibility. Fade the precision as the horizon extends, and mark real deadlines as deadlines.

quiz.q: You have identified the constraint on activation as your onboarding data-import step. What follows?
o: Improve everything in onboarding equally
Concentrate effort on the import step, because improvements elsewhere cannot show up in the outcome
Increase acquisition to compensate
Re-run discovery to confirm
quiz.e: A constraint is the limiting factor: while it holds, gains elsewhere are absorbed rather than realised. Concentrating there is the highest-leverage move available. Test the candidate by asking what would happen if it were suddenly twice as good — if the answer is “not much”, you have the wrong constraint.

quiz.q: What is the most useful thing to put next to each theme on an outcome roadmap?
o: The feature names
The engineering team assigned
The outcome it should move, with today's baseline
The planned delivery date
quiz.e: An outcome with a baseline makes the roadmap arguable in a productive way: people can challenge whether the theme will move that number, and at the end you can tell whether it did. Feature names invite scope debates, and dates invite commitment debates.

quiz.q: A bet is running and its core assumption has been shown to be false. What should already exist?
o: A kill condition written before the bet started
A stakeholder escalation process
A replacement bet ready to go
A retrospective template
quiz.e: Kill conditions are written up front precisely because stopping is much harder in the moment — sunk cost, sponsor commitment and momentum all push the other way. Deciding the exit before you have anything invested is the only reliable version of it.

sections.h: A roadmap is a route, not a railway timetable.
sections.lede: Strategy is three things in order: an honest look at the ground, a choice about how to cross it, and the actions that follow from that choice. Almost every document called a strategy is missing the middle one. This topic is about writing the choice down, including the part where you say what you are not doing.

panel.big: If nothing is excluded, nothing was chosen.
items: Diagnosis first. A plan built on an ambition assumes a company you do not have.
Find the one constraint. Improvements elsewhere get absorbed.
Write the anti-goals. They are what let your team say no in month three.

sections.lede: Richard Rumelt's structure is the most useful thing in the strategy literature, mostly because it is diagnostic: you can hold a document up against it and see immediately which part is missing.
sections.statement: Most strategy documents are a destination and a schedule, with the choice quietly left out of the middle.

cards.p: What is actually going on, including the awkward parts and the constraint. If everyone in the room is comfortable, it is not finished.
The approach you will take in response — broad enough to apply to decisions you have not anticipated, specific enough to rule things out.
Three to five bets that reinforce each other, each with an outcome, a size and a condition under which you stop.

sections.lede: Front: what it means. Back: what it is on the expedition. Click or press Enter to flip.

sections.h: From a blank page to a plan people can follow
sections.lede: Seven steps. The order matters more here than anywhere else in the playbook — steps three and four are impossible to do honestly if you skip one and two.

sections.lede: Hover or tap any part of a diagram for the detail.

items: What is actually going on, including the awkward parts. If everyone is comfortable, it is not finished.
The choice. Broad enough to apply to decisions you did not anticipate, specific enough to rule things out.
Three to five bets that reinforce each other, each with an outcome and a kill condition.

items.p: Hold any strategy up against these three and you can see immediately which part was skipped.

zones: In progress, specific, dates only where a real deadline exists.
Agreed problems and outcomes, ordered, no dates.
Themes and direction, explicitly uncertain. Not a graveyard for quiet no’s.

title: Specs, PRDs & Working with Engineers
one: Writing the document that stops the same five questions being asked in five separate threads.

terms.d: The written answer to “what are we building, for whom, and how will we know it worked.” Its purpose is to stop the same five questions being asked in five separate threads, not to prove you did your homework.
terms.c: The drawing set. Nobody pours concrete from a conversation.

terms.d: The lightweight version: problem, evidence, proposed change, success measure, risks. Enough for most work, and the right thing to write before you know whether the idea survives.
terms.c: The sketch you take to the planning meeting, before anyone pays for structural drawings.

terms.d: Who is struggling, with what, how often, and what it costs them or you. Written first, and written so that someone could propose a completely different solution and still be responding to it.
terms.c: “The kitchen is dark by four o'clock and the family eats in the hall.” A window is one answer, not the brief.

terms.d: The number that should move, its current value, and by how much you expect it to change. Without a baseline it is not a measure — it is a hope with a unit attached.
terms.c: “Enough light to read a recipe at 5pm in November.” Now the drawing can be judged.

terms.d: What this work explicitly will not do. The single highest-value paragraph in any spec, because it is the one people quote back at each other in week three.
terms.c: “We are not moving the plumbing.” Written on the drawing, in the same ink as everything else.

terms.d: The specific, checkable conditions under which the work is done. Written before build, ideally as scenarios: given a situation, when something happens, then this is true.
terms.c: The building inspector's checklist. Signed off against, not debated on the day.

terms.d: The unusual-but-real situation: empty state, one item, ten thousand items, expired card, two tabs open, offline, a name with an apostrophe. Deciding these in the spec costs minutes; deciding them mid-sprint costs a day each.
terms.c: What happens where the new wall meets the old, uneven one. Always the expensive bit.

terms.d: The states a design usually omits and users constantly see. Specify all three or they will be invented at 5pm on a Thursday by whoever is closest.
terms.c: What the room looks like before the furniture arrives, and what it looks like when the power is out.

terms.d: How well it has to work rather than what it does: speed, load, accessibility, privacy, retention, uptime. Cheap to state up front and extremely expensive to retrofit.
terms.c: Load-bearing, fire-rated, and it has to be quiet. Not decisions you make after the walls are up.

terms.d: The team's standing agreement on what “finished” includes — tests, instrumentation, docs, accessibility, monitoring. Agreed once so it does not get renegotiated per ticket when a deadline gets close.
terms.c: Snagged, signed off, and the site cleared. Otherwise “done” just means the builders left.

terms.d: Cutting work so each slice delivers something usable end to end, rather than building all of one layer first. It lets you ship early, learn early, and stop halfway with something real.
terms.c: Finish one room completely rather than half-plastering the whole house.

terms.d: Additions that arrive after the estimate, one small ask at a time, each individually reasonable. It is not caused by bad people; it is caused by a spec that never said what it would not do.
terms.c: “While you're in there…” — the four most expensive words on any building site.

terms.d: Deliberately removing scope to hold a date or a quality bar. Should be planned for: mark in advance which parts are cuttable and what the smallest useful version looks like.
terms.c: Deciding on Tuesday that the second bathroom becomes a cupboard, on purpose, before the tiles are ordered.

terms.d: A shortcut taken deliberately, with interest paid in future slowness. Real debt was borrowed on purpose and has a repayment plan; the rest is just mess, and calling it debt makes it sound like a decision.
terms.c: The scaffolding you left up because you will be back next month. Two years later it is part of the building.

terms.d: A fixed-length investigation to reduce uncertainty before estimating. The output is an answer and a recommendation, not code — and the timebox is the point.
terms.c: Two days with a surveyor before anyone quotes for the extension.

terms.d: Product, engineering and QA reading the same story before it is built. Fifteen minutes here removes most of the ambiguity that would otherwise surface as rework.
terms.c: Architect, builder and inspector standing on the plot together, before the dig.

terms.d: An estimate is a probability distribution, usually reported as its most optimistic point. A commitment is a promise. Turning the first into the second without adding buffer is how teams end up permanently late.
terms.c: “About three weeks” is a forecast. “On the 14th” is a contract. Weather exists.

terms.d: Engineering's written proposal for how to build it, including options rejected. A PM should read it, ask about reversibility and about what it makes harder later, and stay out of the rest.
terms.c: The structural engineer's method statement. Your job is to ask what it costs to change later.

terms.d: A switch that lets you ship code dark, release to a subset, and turn it off without a deploy. It converts one-way doors into two-way doors, which changes how much analysis a decision needs.
terms.c: A door you can wall up again in an afternoon.

terms.d: Specifying the implementation rather than the requirement, which throws away the expertise of the people best placed to find a cheaper route.
terms.c: Telling the builder which brand of joist to use. They know a better one, and now they cannot say so.

terms.d: Work that has been nearly finished for two weeks, usually because acceptance criteria were vague enough that “done” is a matter of opinion.
terms.c: “Just the snagging left.” It has been just the snagging for a month.

terms.d: A long document written to be blameless rather than to be read. Recognisable by its completeness, its passive voice, and the fact that nobody can tell you what page four says.
terms.c: Forty pages of drawings, none of which the builder has opened.

steps.t: Write the problem and the measure before the solution
steps.out: Half a page: who, what, how often, how we'll know
steps.b: Start with the situation, the evidence, and the number you expect to move — including its current value. Write it so that an engineer could read it and propose something entirely different; if that is impossible, you have written a solution and called it a problem.
steps.do: Quote a real user or a real number in the first three lines. It is what makes a spec get read.
steps.no: “Users want a dashboard.” Nobody wants a dashboard; they want to stop being surprised on Mondays.

steps.t: Decide what this will not do
steps.out: An explicit non-goals list
steps.b: Three to six lines. Include the adjacent things people will assume are included — other platforms, bulk versions, admin controls, migrations of old data. This is the paragraph that stops the estimate being quietly doubled by reasonable requests, and the one you will thank yourself for most often.
steps.do: Name the specific asks you are excluding, and where they went. “Bulk edit — not this time, revisit after launch.”
steps.no: Leaving it implied. Everything unstated is assumed to be included, by everyone, in different ways.

steps.t: Bring engineering in while it is still cheap to change
steps.out: A shared understanding, and usually a smaller plan
steps.b: Walk the problem and the constraints through with the tech lead before the solution hardens. Engineers routinely know a route that costs a third as much and gets 80% of the value — but only if they see the problem rather than the specification of an answer. Expect the shape of the work to change here; that is the point.
steps.do: Ask “what would you build if you had a week?” and take the answer seriously.
steps.no: Arriving with finished designs and asking for an estimate. You have just paid full price for a solution nobody stress-tested.

steps.t: Specify the awkward parts
steps.out: Acceptance criteria, edge cases, and the three states
steps.b: Write acceptance criteria as given/when/then scenarios, then deliberately hunt the edges: empty, one, many, huge, offline, expired, unauthorised, concurrent, and every non-Latin name. Specify empty, loading and error states — they are the screens users see most often and the ones designs omit most reliably. Add the non-functional requirements now.
steps.do: Ask the engineers which edge cases they are worried about. Their list is better than yours.
steps.no: “Handle errors gracefully.” That sentence has never once prevented an error being handled badly.
steps.snip:
Given  a trial account with 3 seats used of 3
When   an admin invites a fourth member
Then   the invite is blocked, the upgrade prompt shows the
       exact seat price, and no email is sent

Edge cases decided: 0 seats · seat freed mid-invite · two
admins inviting at once · invitee already has an account

steps.t: Slice it so something useful ships early
steps.out: A first slice you would genuinely release
steps.b: Cut vertically: one complete path through the system for one real case, rather than all of the back end followed by all of the front end. Mark which later slices are cuttable, and write down what the smallest useful version is — because you will need that sentence under pressure, and inventing it under pressure goes badly.
steps.do: Put the instrumentation in the first slice. Shipping something you cannot measure means learning nothing from it.
steps.no: A single three-month slice with nothing releasable until the end. You have removed every opportunity to be wrong cheaply.

steps.t: Read it together before anyone builds
steps.out: Fifteen minutes, three people, no surprises
steps.b: Product, engineering and QA read the same story and try to break it. This is the cheapest quality intervention available — most ambiguity surfaces in the first five minutes, and the alternative is discovering it as rework in week two. Update the document in the meeting, not afterwards.
steps.do: Let QA go first. They find the contradictions fastest because they read for failure.
steps.no: Sending the doc round for async approval. Approval is not comprehension, and nobody reads a doc they can simply thumbs-up.

steps.t: Handle change deliberately, and close the loop
steps.out: A decision log, and a result note after launch
steps.b: Changes will come. Handle each as a trade: what comes out, what moves, or what date shifts — never as a silent addition. Log decisions with dates and reasons so the same question is not reopened monthly. Then, after launch, write two paragraphs on whether the number moved, and revise the estimate you would give next time.
steps.do: Keep the decision log inside the spec. Six months later it is the only part anyone reads.
steps.no: Saying yes to small things because each one is small. Six reasonable additions is a new project with an old estimate.

cases.title: Six lines that saved four weeks
cases.sub: The same team, the same kind of feature, twice. The second time they wrote down what it would not do.
steps: A shared-permissions feature, estimated at six weeks, delivered in eleven. The post-mortem found nine additions during build: audit log, bulk assignment, SSO group sync, an admin override, a second platform. Every one had been agreed in a thread by someone reasonable.
The next spec — team-level billing roles — opened with a problem statement, a success measure with a baseline (invoice-related support contacts, 140/month), and six explicit non-goals.
No SSO group sync. No audit log this release. No bulk role assignment. No mobile app support. No migration of historical invoices. No custom roles — three fixed roles only.

Nine change requests arrived during the five weeks. Each was answered the same way: here is what it displaces, or here is the date it moves. Seven were deferred, two were taken in exchange for named cuts. Nothing was quietly added.

Fifteen minutes on the story surfaced a contradiction nobody had noticed: two admins could remove each other simultaneously, leaving an account with no admin. Cost to fix in the spec: one paragraph. Cost to find in production: a support incident and a data repair.
Shipped in five weeks. Invoice support contacts fell from 140 to 62 a month over the following quarter, against a forecast of “roughly half”.

verdict.h: The list of no's did the work
verdict.p: Nothing about the second spec was longer or more rigorous than the first. The difference was six lines saying what was excluded, which converted every subsequent request from an addition into a trade — and a trade is a conversation people can have without anybody being the obstacle.
verdict.lesson: Write the non-goals before the requirements. They are the only part of a spec that defends the estimate.

cases.kind: A spec that specified the answer
cases.badge: Built as written · three times the cost
cases.title: The real-time dashboard nobody needed in real time
cases.sub: The spec named the implementation. Engineering built exactly that, and mentioned the cheaper option four months later.
steps: “Build a real-time dashboard with live-updating charts via websockets, showing the eight metrics in the attached design.” Nine pages, mostly design annotations.
No problem statement, no evidence, no success measure, and no non-goals. The word “real-time” appeared in the title and was never questioned.
Live updating required a streaming aggregation layer, a new caching tier and a websocket service. Thirteen weeks instead of four, plus an ongoing infrastructure cost of roughly $2,100 a month.
Instrumentation added after launch showed the median session opened the dashboard once, looked for 40 seconds, and left. Fewer than 3% of sessions lasted long enough for a live update to matter.
The conversation that should have happened first

In a retro, the tech lead said a cached view refreshed every fifteen minutes would have taken about a week. They had assumed real-time was a hard requirement, because the spec presented it as one rather than as a choice.
The spec solutioned. By naming websockets, it removed the only people who could have costed the alternatives from the decision — and made questioning it feel like questioning the plan.

The team's spec template gained two mandatory fields: “what problem, with evidence” and “what we are deliberately not doing”. Implementation choices moved to the engineering design doc, where the trade-offs get written down by the people who understand them.

verdict.h: Nobody was allowed to offer the cheap version
verdict.p: Engineering did nothing wrong: they built what was specified, on a reasonable schedule for the thing specified. The requirement — people want to know whether today is going badly — could have been met for a twelfth of the cost, and the spec's format made that sentence hard to say.
verdict.lesson: Specify the requirement, never the implementation. If you name the how, you have quietly excluded everyone who knows a cheaper one.

quiz.q: Which is the most valuable section of a spec, judged by how much rework it prevents?
o: The detailed wireframes
The explicit non-goals
The list of stakeholders
The technical approach
quiz.e: Non-goals convert every later request from an addition into a trade. Without them, each individually reasonable “while you're in there” lands on the same estimate, and there is no shared basis for saying no. It is usually six lines and it protects the whole plan.

quiz.q: You bring engineering finished designs and ask for an estimate. What have you likely given up?
o: Nothing, if the designs are good
The cheaper route they might have proposed if they had seen the problem instead
Their sense of ownership
Design consistency
quiz.e: Engineers frequently know an approach that gets most of the value for a fraction of the cost — but only when they are shown the problem and the constraints. Arriving with a specified solution turns them into estimators of your idea rather than contributors to it, and asking questions then feels like obstruction.

quiz.q: Which three screens are most often missing from a design and most often seen by users?
o: Settings, profile, help
Empty, loading and error states
Onboarding, upgrade, cancel
Mobile, tablet, print
quiz.e: Every new user starts on an empty state, every user sees loading, and errors are more common than any single happy path. Left unspecified they get invented late by whoever is nearest, which is how a product ends up with four different error styles and no empty-state guidance.

quiz.q: A stakeholder asks for one small addition mid-build. Best response?
o: Take it — it's small and refusing damages the relationship
Refuse, citing the spec
Say yes to the trade: name what comes out, what moves, or which date shifts
Add it to the backlog and say nothing
quiz.e: Neither a flat no nor a silent yes is sustainable. Framing it as a trade keeps you a collaborator rather than a gatekeeper, and it moves the decision to the person who owns the priority. It also makes the cumulative cost of six small additions visible while there is still time.

quiz.q: Your team keeps having tickets that are “90% done” for two weeks. Most likely cause?
o: Poor estimation
Vague acceptance criteria, so “done” is a matter of opinion
Too much work in progress
Insufficient testing capacity
quiz.e: When done is not defined in checkable terms, the last 10% expands to hold every unresolved question — edge cases, error states, what counts as good enough. Given/when/then criteria and a standing definition of done fix this far more reliably than better estimates.

sections.h: A spec is a drawing set, not an essay.
sections.lede: The job of a written spec is to make decisions once instead of eleven times, and to make them while changing your mind is still cheap. That means it is mostly about the awkward parts — the edge cases, the states nobody designed, and the paragraph saying what this will not do.

title: Pricing & Packaging
one: The highest-leverage number in the product, and usually the least researched one.

terms.d: The thing you charge by: seats, messages, gigabytes, transactions, bookings. The single most consequential pricing decision, because it decides whether your revenue grows when your customer succeeds.
terms.c: Selling coffee by the cup, by the weight of beans, or by monthly subscription. Same shop, three different businesses.

terms.d: It grows as the customer gets more value, it is easy to understand before buying, and it is hard to game. Seats fail the first test for automation products; API calls fail the second for non-technical buyers.
terms.c: Charging by the cup is obvious and fair. Charging by minutes spent in the shop is neither.

terms.d: What a specific segment would actually pay, which varies enormously between segments for the identical product. Discovering that spread is most of pricing research.
terms.c: The commuter at 8am and the student at 3pm are not the same customer, and both know it.

terms.d: Four survey questions — too cheap, cheap, expensive, too expensive — that produce a plausible range rather than a number. Good for a sanity check, weak as a decision on its own because it asks about a hypothetical.
terms.c: Asking a hundred passers-by what a coffee should cost. Directionally useful, and nobody has bought anything.

terms.d: Showing people realistic bundles at realistic prices and having them choose, which reveals trade-offs rather than opinions. Costs more and is worth far more than direct questions.
terms.c: “Large at £3.40 or medium with a pastry at £4.10?” Now you learn something real.

terms.d: How features are grouped into what people can buy. Packaging usually moves revenue more than the price level does, and it is the cheaper of the two to change.
terms.c: The set menus. Same kitchen, and the menu design decides what most people order.

terms.d: The rule that stops a customer who should pay more from buying the cheaper option: company size, use case, support level, timing, volume. Without fences, tiers collapse into whichever is cheapest.
terms.c: “Lunch menu, before 3pm only.” The fence is what makes two prices survivable.

terms.d: A deliberately expensive top tier that makes the middle look reasonable. It also sells occasionally, which is usually a pleasant surprise for the person who proposed it.
terms.c: The £95 tasting menu exists so the £45 one reads as sensible.

terms.d: Freemium gives a limited version forever and works when usage creates value or network effects. A trial gives everything briefly and works when value is obvious quickly. Choosing both usually means neither converts.
terms.c: Free refills on filter coffee, versus a free espresso today only.

terms.d: Entering cheap on a small team and growing with usage. Requires a value metric that grows naturally, and it is the mechanism behind net revenue retention above 100%.
terms.c: One person's morning flat white becomes the office order.

terms.d: Price from your costs plus a margin. Defensible, easy to explain, and almost always leaves money on the table because your costs are unrelated to the buyer's value.
terms.c: Beans plus milk plus rent plus 30%. Ignores that the airport charges four times as much for the same cup.

terms.d: Price from the economic value the customer receives — money saved, risk avoided, revenue enabled. Harder to research, and it is the only approach that scales with your product's impact.
terms.c: If your coffee is what gets the shift started, it is not priced against milk.

terms.d: How much demand changes when price changes. Most software teams badly overestimate it, which is why cautious price rises so often produce more revenue with less churn than forecast.
terms.c: Ten pence on a flat white loses almost nobody. Everyone in the shop is convinced otherwise.

terms.d: A 10% price increase with 5% churn is usually a large net gain; a 10% discount needs a much bigger volume rise to break even. Always do this arithmetic before a discount, because intuition gets it backwards.
terms.c: Half price does not mean twice the customers. It usually means twice the queue and less money.

terms.d: Pre-agreed limits, approval levels, and something asked for in return — a longer term, a case study, an annual prepay. Undisciplined discounting devalues the list price permanently, and buyers talk to each other.
terms.c: “Staff price” becomes everybody's price by Thursday.

terms.d: Letting existing customers keep old prices when you raise them. Buys goodwill, costs real revenue, and complicates your billing system for years. Time-limit it rather than promising forever.
terms.c: The regulars keep the old price. Ten years later half the shop is paying 2013 rates.

terms.d: Moving existing customers onto new pricing. Usually the hardest part of a pricing change, and the part teams plan last. Sequence it: new customers first, then renewals, then a communicated migration with notice.
terms.c: Changing the menu is easy. Telling the regulars is the job.

terms.d: Rarely a clean A/B test — showing different prices to comparable buyers at the same time creates fairness and legal problems, and word travels. Test with new-cohort changes, geographic rollouts, packaging tests and sales-led experiments instead.
terms.c: Two prices on the same board, and the queue notices in about a minute.

terms.d: Revenue from the same customers a year later, including expansion, contraction and churn. Above 100% means your existing base grows without new sales, which is largely a packaging and value-metric achievement.
terms.c: Last year's regulars, spending more this year without you finding new ones.

terms.d: Gating something users consider basic, which reads as extortion rather than as a tier. Support volume and cancellation notes will tell you within a fortnight.
terms.c: Charging for the lid.

terms.t: Seat pricing on an automation product
terms.d: Charging per user for something whose value is doing work without users. Success reduces seats, so you are billing against your own value proposition.
terms.c: Charging by the number of staff in a shop that just installed a machine.

terms.d: Pricing chosen because it was easy to calculate, then defended for years because it is now “our model”. The commonest reason a product is underpriced by a factor of three.
terms.c: Still pricing on 2019 bean costs while the shop next door charges by convenience.

terms.d: Publishing new pricing without having settled what happens to existing customers. The gap will be filled by rumour, and the rumour is always worse than the plan.
terms.c: New menu on the wall, and no answer for the regular who has been coming since 2016.

steps.t: Write down what value the customer gets, in their units
steps.out: One sentence with a number in it
steps.b: Before touching a price, quantify the value: hours saved per week, revenue enabled per month, risk avoided, cost replaced. Do it in the customer's units and from their evidence, not yours. This sentence becomes the ceiling for any credible price and the backbone of every sales conversation.
steps.do: Get it from three real customers with different sizes. The spread between them is your segmentation.
steps.no: Starting from your cost base. Your costs are a floor, and a floor is not a strategy.

steps.t: Choose the value metric, and test it three ways
steps.out: “We charge per ___”
steps.b: Run every candidate through the three tests: does it grow as the customer gets more value, can a buyer understand it before purchase, and is it hard to game? A metric that fails test one caps your growth at your customer's headcount; one that fails test two lengthens every sales cycle; one that fails test three creates a support problem.
steps.do: Prefer a metric your customer already counts for their own reasons. Bookings, invoices, shipments, tickets.
steps.no: Per seat by default. Ask whether your value actually scales with the number of humans logged in.
steps.snip:
Three tests for a value metric
  1. Grows with the value the customer receives?
  2. Understandable before they buy?
  3. Hard to game?
Seats  — fails (1) for automation; passes (2) and (3)
API calls — passes (1) and (3); fails (2) for non-technical buyers
Invoices sent — passes all three for a billing product

steps.t: Design the packaging before the numbers
steps.out: Two or three tiers with a fence on each
steps.b: Decide who each tier is for, and what rule keeps a larger customer out of a smaller tier. Fences based on identity — company size, industry — are hard to enforce; fences based on need work better: volume limits, admin controls, security and compliance features, support level, integrations. Two or three tiers is usually right; five is a decision you have declined to make.
steps.do: Put the features a buyer needs in order to trust you — SSO, audit logs, SLAs — in the tier bought by people who ask for them.
steps.no: Gating something users consider basic. It reads as a penalty and shows up in cancellation notes within a fortnight.

steps.t: Research willingness to pay properly
steps.out: A defensible range per segment
steps.b: Combine methods, because each is weak alone. Van Westendorp gives a range; conjoint reveals trade-offs; win/loss notes and discount patterns are free, real, behavioural evidence sitting in your CRM. Look for the spread between segments rather than one number — the spread is what packaging exists to capture.
steps.do: Start with your own sales data. The distribution of discounts already tells you where your list price is wrong.
steps.no: Asking customers what they would pay and treating the answer as a plan. Stated intent about price is the least reliable data there is.

steps.t: Do the price–volume arithmetic
steps.out: A break-even table for each option
steps.b: For every candidate change, compute what has to happen to volume for you to break even. A 10% price rise usually survives well over 5% churn; a 10% discount needs a substantial volume increase, and against a smaller margin. Teams are consistently too pessimistic about increases and too optimistic about discounts, and the arithmetic corrects both.
steps.do: Model a bad case: your best guess at churn, doubled. Most increases still win.
steps.no: Approving a discount without knowing the volume it needs to be worthwhile.

steps.t: Plan migration before you announce anything
steps.out: A written plan for existing customers
steps.b: Decide who is grandfathered and for how long, what notice you give, what the sales team says, and what a customer at renewal is offered. Sequence it: new customers first so you learn on people with no expectations, then renewals, then a communicated migration with generous notice. Then write the actual email.
steps.do: Time-limit grandfathering — twelve or eighteen months. “Forever” is a promise you will regret in your billing code.
steps.no: Publishing the new pricing page while the migration plan is still open. Rumour fills the gap, and rumour is worse.

steps.t: Change it, watch the right numbers, and hold your nerve
steps.out: A monitored change with a decision point
steps.b: Roll to new customers first and watch conversion rate, average deal size, sales cycle length, discount frequency and churn at the next two renewal cohorts. Expect a noisy fortnight and some loud complaints — loudness is not volume. Set the decision point and the metrics in advance so you are not reacting to the first angry email.
steps.do: Track revenue per visitor, not conversion rate. A price rise is supposed to lower conversion.
steps.no: Reverting in week one. Almost every price increase feels like a mistake for about ten days.

cases.title: An automation tool that was charging per seat
cases.sub: The better the product got, the fewer seats customers needed. Revenue was being punished by its own value proposition.
steps: A workflow automation product priced at $29 per user per month. Its whole pitch was that work happened without a person doing it — so successful customers removed seats. Two of the five largest accounts had shrunk while their usage tripled.
Interviews with eleven customers put the value at roughly 6–9 hours of manual work saved per 1,000 automated actions. At a blended $28/hour that is $170–250 of value per 1,000 actions.
Actions passed all three: it grows exactly with value delivered, customers already counted their own volumes, and gaming it would mean automating less. Seats failed test one outright.

Three tiers with need-based fences. Starter: 5,000 actions, two integrations. Growth: 50,000 actions, all integrations, role controls. Scale: custom volume, SSO, audit log, SLA. Unlimited seats on every tier — deliberately, because seats now cost nothing and adding colleagues increases usage.
$0.019 per action at Growth volumes — around 9% of the low end of measured value, comfortably inside the range where value-based pricing is normally defensible.

New customers only for one quarter. Then renewals, with a fifteen-month grandfathering window and a calculator showing each customer their new cost. Six accounts were worse off; all six were offered a two-year price lock, and four took it.

Average contract value up 34% at twelve months. NRR from 96% to 118%, almost entirely from usage expansion rather than price. Logo churn moved from 1.4% to 1.6% monthly — measurable, and far cheaper than the growth it unlocked.

verdict.h: The value metric was working against the product
verdict.p: No amount of price optimisation would have fixed this, because the problem was structural: the unit being sold shrank as the product succeeded. Changing what you charge for is harder than changing how much, and it is usually the change that matters.
verdict.lesson: If a customer succeeding with your product reduces what they owe you, no price level will save it. Fix the metric first.

cases.title: The 30% launch discount that worked
cases.sub: It hit its target — signups rose sharply. The arithmetic nobody ran beforehand showed it needed to rise almost twice as much.
steps: Growth was 4% below plan. A 30% discount for twelve months was approved in a Thursday meeting to “get volume moving”, with a target of +20% signups.

At a 72% gross margin, cutting price 30% cuts gross profit per customer by about 42%. Break-even therefore needed roughly +43% more customers, not +20%. The target was set below the break-even point and nobody noticed.
Signups rose 22% — a genuine success against the stated goal. Gross profit for the cohort came in 11% below what the un-discounted forecast implied.

At renewal, the discounted cohort faced a 43% jump back to list. Renewal rate for that cohort was 58% against 81% for the previous quarter's full-price cohort. The discount had recruited price-sensitive buyers and then priced them out.
The discount leaked. Two enterprise deals in negotiation asked for the public 30% and got it. Sales spent the following two quarters explaining why list price was list price.

The same money spent on annual prepay incentives — 15% off for paying up front — improves cash without resetting perceived value, and does not create a renewal cliff. It was tried the following year: 19% of new customers took annual, with no measurable effect on conversion.

verdict.h: It hit the target and lost the money
verdict.p: Every step was reasonable in isolation. The target was met, the demand response was real, and the discount genuinely worked as an incentive. The break-even calculation takes about four minutes and would have shown that the target was set below the point where the whole exercise paid for itself.
verdict.lesson: Never approve a discount without the break-even volume next to it, and never without deciding what happens at renewal.

quiz.q: Your product automates work. Which value metric is most misaligned?
o: Per automated action
Per seat
Per integration connected
Per gigabyte processed
quiz.e: Seat pricing on an automation product bills against your own value proposition: the better it works, the fewer humans need access, so successful customers shrink. A metric should grow as the customer gets more value — actions, transactions or volume all do; seats actively do not.

quiz.q: A 10% price increase is proposed. Churn is forecast at 4%. Roughly what happens?
o: Revenue falls, because you lose customers
Revenue rises substantially — a 10% rise survives far more than 4% churn
It is about break-even
Impossible to say without knowing CAC
quiz.e: On a 10% increase, every remaining customer pays 10% more while you lose 4% of them, so revenue rises by roughly 5–6% and gross profit by more, since the lost customers also had costs. Teams routinely overestimate elasticity, which is why careful price rises so often beat forecast.

quiz.q: You want two tiers at different prices. What makes that survivable?
o: A large feature difference
A fence — a rule that stops a bigger customer buying the smaller tier
Clear marketing
A discount policy
quiz.e: Without a fence, everyone who can buy the cheaper tier does, and your tiers collapse into one price. Need-based fences work best: volume limits, admin and security controls, support levels, integrations. Identity-based fences like company size are hard to enforce and easy to resent.

quiz.q: Why is a straight A/B test of two prices usually a bad idea?
o: Prices need more traffic than tests can provide
Charging comparable buyers different prices at the same time creates fairness and legal problems, and word travels
Price effects take too long to measure
Conversion rate is the wrong metric
quiz.e: Simultaneous differential pricing to comparable buyers is a reputational and often legal problem, and buyers compare notes — especially in B2B. Use new-cohort changes, geographic rollouts, packaging tests, or sales-led experiments, and measure revenue per visitor rather than conversion.

quiz.q: When should the migration plan for existing customers be written?
o: After the new pricing is announced, based on the reaction
Before anything is announced
At the first renewal after launch
Only if customers complain
quiz.e: The gap between announcement and a migration answer gets filled by rumour, and rumour is always worse than the plan. Decide grandfathering and its time limit, notice periods, the sales script and the renewal offer first — then publish. Sequencing to new customers first lets you learn on people with no expectations.
