title: Analytics & Instrumentation
one: Where the numbers on the dashboard actually come from, and why two dashboards disagree.

terms.d: A record that something happened: who, what, when, and a few properties. The unit of behavioural analytics, and the thing everyone under-specifies.
terms.c: A meter reading on one pipe. Useless alone, and the whole system once you have enough of them in the right places.

terms.d: Context attached to an event: plan, source, device, item count, error code. Properties are what let you answer the next question without shipping new tracking.
terms.c: Not just “water flowed” but how much, how hot, and which tap.

terms.d: The document listing every event, its properties, its types, its trigger and its owner — written before implementation. Without it you get four names for the same action within a quarter.
terms.c: The plumbing schematic. Retrofitting one from the walls is possible and nobody enjoys it.

terms.d: Client-side sees intent and UI detail but loses 10–30% to ad blockers, crashes and flaky networks. Server-side is far more reliable but blind to anything that never reached your server. Money should be tracked server-side.
terms.c: A meter at the tap versus one at the mains. One knows what was asked for; the other knows what actually flowed.

terms.d: A single place events are declared and then fanned out to your tools. Prevents each vendor's snippet developing its own private definition of a conversion.
terms.c: One manifold, then branches. Not six separate pipes into the same tank.

terms.d: A consistent naming scheme, usually object–action in one tense and one case: “Invoice Sent”, “Report Shared”. Boring, mechanical, and the difference between a queryable dataset and a landfill.
terms.c: Every pipe labelled the same way, so the next plumber can read it.

terms.d: Hundreds of events, most fired once during a test and never used. It slows queries, hides the useful events, and makes newcomers distrust the whole dataset.
terms.c: Four hundred meters, ninety of them wired to nothing.

terms.d: Metric definitions written once as code and reused by every dashboard, so “active user” means one thing everywhere. The fix for two teams presenting two numbers with the same name.
terms.c: One agreed way to calculate consumption, used by every bill in the building.

terms.d: Connecting one person's activity across anonymous and logged-in states, devices and sessions. Get it wrong and your funnels break, your user counts inflate, and cohorts stop meaning anything.
terms.c: Working out that the meter in the flat and the one in the garage belong to the same household.

terms.d: The anonymous ID belongs to a browser or device; the user ID belongs to a person. The alias call that links them at sign-in is the single most commonly broken piece of instrumentation in existence.
terms.c: A meter number versus a customer account. Someone has to write down which is which, once.

terms.d: An arbitrary window of activity, usually ended by 30 minutes of inactivity. Convenient, comparable across tools, and not a real unit of human behaviour — be careful basing goals on it.
terms.c: “One visit to the tap.” A definition of convenience, not a fact about thirst.

terms.d: A group defined by a shared start time or shared behaviour, then followed. The only honest way to see whether the product is getting better rather than just bigger.
terms.c: Everyone connected to the supply in March, metered as one group.

terms.d: Checking your analytics against an independent source — billing, the database, a manual count. Every metric anyone forecasts from should have been reconciled at least once, with the acceptable gap written down.
terms.c: Comparing the meter to the tank level. If they disagree, you have a leak or a broken meter, and you need to know which.

terms.d: Automatically rejecting or flagging events that do not match the tracking plan — wrong types, missing properties, unknown names. Turns silent data rot into a build failure.
terms.c: A gauge that refuses a reading in the wrong units instead of quietly recording it.

terms.d: How out of date the numbers are, and whether anyone knows. A dashboard that silently stopped updating on Tuesday has caused more bad decisions than one that is obviously broken.
terms.c: A meter that stopped last week but still shows a plausible number.

terms.d: Recomputing history after a definition or pipeline change. Necessary for comparability, and dangerous if undocumented — someone will quote last month's old number from a screenshot.
terms.c: Re-reading the old logs after you discover the meter was mis-calibrated.

terms.d: Conversion through an ordered sequence of steps. Sensitive to the window you allow, whether steps must be strictly ordered, and whether people who skip a step are excluded — all of which change the answer substantially.
terms.c: Following the water from the mains to the tap and finding where the pressure drops.

terms.d: Splitting a number by a property to find where the effect lives. The fastest diagnostic you have, and the easiest way to find a false pattern if you go fishing without a hypothesis.
terms.c: Checking each floor separately. The building average said nothing was wrong.

terms.d: Letting non-analysts answer their own questions. Works only on top of consistent naming, a semantic layer and documented definitions; without those it produces a lot of confident, contradictory answers.
terms.c: Everyone can read the meters, because someone labelled them properly.

terms.d: Tracking added feature by feature with no plan, so the dataset can answer last year's questions and none of this year's. The most expensive kind of technical debt because it destroys history you cannot recreate.
terms.c: Twenty years of extensions, each with its own plumbing standard.

terms.d: Almost always two correct calculations of two different things: different windows, filters, timezones or identity rules. Resolve by comparing definitions, never by picking the number you like.
terms.c: Two meters, both accurate, measuring different points on the pipe.

terms.d: Analysing only the users who reached a step, then concluding the step is fine. The people the step defeated are not in the dataset you are reading.
terms.c: Surveying only the households that still have water.

terms.d: Instrumenting success and not failure. You then cannot tell the difference between “nobody tried” and “everybody tried and it broke”, which is the single most useful distinction in product analytics.
terms.c: A meter that records water delivered and never records a burst pipe.

steps.t: Start from the questions, not the events
steps.out: Ten questions you will need to answer
steps.b: Write the actual questions the team and the business will ask over the next year: where do new teams stall, which segments retain, what does a failed import cost us, who is at risk of churn. Instrumentation designed backwards from real questions is a fraction of the size and answers far more.
steps.do: Include the questions you were asked last quarter and could not answer. That list is your specification.
steps.no: “Track everything, we'll figure out the questions later.” You get bloat and still cannot answer them.

steps.t: Write the tracking plan before any code
steps.out: A table: event, properties, types, trigger, owner
steps.b: One row per event: the name in object–action form, every property with its type and allowed values, exactly when it fires, and who owns it. Include failure events alongside success events. Review it with engineering and with whoever will actually query the data — usually not the person who wrote it.
steps.do: Add a failure counterpart to every meaningful success event. “Import Failed” with an error_code property is often more valuable than “Import Succeeded”.
steps.no: Letting each squad name its own events. You will get signup_completed, Signup Complete and user-registered, all live.
steps.snip:
Event      Invoice Sent
Fires      server-side, after the send API returns 2xx
Properties invoice_id (string)  amount_cents (int)
           currency (enum)      recipient_count (int)
           template_id (string) is_recurring (bool)
Owner      Billing squad
Pair with  Invoice Send Failed (error_code, retry_count)

steps.t: Decide where each event fires
steps.out: A client/server split with reasons
steps.b: Anything financial or contractual goes server-side, where ad blockers and flaky connections cannot delete it. Intent and interface behaviour — hovers, scrolls, abandoned forms — has to be client-side. Write down which is which and expect a persistent 10–30% gap between the two; the gap is normal, and not knowing about it is not.
steps.do: Track revenue events server-side only. Two sources of revenue truth is a finance conversation you do not want.
steps.no: Measuring conversion client-side and revenue server-side, then dividing one by the other.

steps.t: Get identity right on day one
steps.out: A documented identity rule, and a tested alias call
steps.b: Define how anonymous activity links to a person at sign-in, what happens on a shared device, what happens on sign-out, and what identifies a company as opposed to a user. Then test it: sign up in a fresh browser and follow one real person through the dataset end to end. This is the highest-consequence, least-glamorous hour in the whole process.
steps.do: Test the anonymous-to-known transition manually every quarter. It breaks silently during auth changes.
steps.no: Assuming your analytics vendor handles it. They handle it according to assumptions you have not read.

steps.t: Validate at the boundary
steps.out: Schema checks in CI, and alerts on volume
steps.b: Enforce the plan mechanically: reject or flag events with unknown names, missing properties or wrong types. Add volume alerts on your top twenty events, because a 90% drop at 3am is the cheapest possible way to learn a release broke tracking. Without this, data quality decays quietly and confidence never comes back.
steps.do: Alert on unexpected zeroes as well as spikes. Silence is the most common failure mode.
steps.no: Discovering a month later that an event stopped firing. That month is gone; you cannot backfill behaviour.

steps.t: Define metrics once, in one place
steps.out: A semantic layer or a definitions doc every dashboard links to
steps.b: Write each metric once — numerator, denominator, window, exclusions, timezone, identity rule — and have every dashboard consume that definition rather than reimplementing it. Version it, and record the date of every change, because a step in a chart is more often a definition than a product.
steps.do: Put the definition and its last-changed date on the dashboard itself.
steps.no: Ten dashboards each with their own SQL for “active user”. You are guaranteeing the two-numbers argument.

steps.t: Reconcile, then publish
steps.out: A number you would defend, with a known margin
steps.b: Before anyone forecasts from a metric, check it against something independent: the billing system, a database count, a manual tally for one day. Find the gap, explain the gap, write down what gap is acceptable. Then publish the number with a link to its definition — and re-reconcile after any pipeline change.
steps.do: Reconcile revenue metrics against finance quarterly. It is the fastest way to earn the right to be believed.
steps.no: Presenting a funnel where each step was instrumented by a different team in a different quarter and none has been checked.

cases.title: Every new user looked like two people
cases.sub: Signup conversion had been reported at 41% for two quarters. It was 63%. One missing call was inventing a user per signup.
steps: Signup conversion sat at 41% and would not move despite three onboarding projects. Meanwhile monthly active users looked healthy and the ratio of accounts to users was drifting upward month by month.
Reconciliation against the production database — done for the first time when a board pack needed it — showed 28% more users in analytics than in the users table. Nobody had compared the two before.

At sign-in the app called identify with the new user ID but never called alias to connect the pre-signup anonymous ID. Every person therefore existed twice: an anonymous visitor who never converted, and a known user who appeared out of nowhere already signed up.

The funnel counted anonymous visitors at the top and known users at the bottom. Because the two were never linked, most genuine conversions were invisible — the same person could not be followed across the boundary.

Two quarters of onboarding work had been evaluated against a metric incapable of showing improvement. One of the three projects, which internal opinion had judged a failure, turned out on reprocessed data to have moved conversion by about 4 points.

Alias implemented and tested manually in a clean browser. Historical data partly repaired by joining on email hash where available — roughly 70% of the period was recoverable, and the rest is a documented gap in the record.

A quarterly manual identity test: sign up as a new user in a fresh browser, then follow that single person through every dashboard. It takes twenty minutes and has caught two subsequent regressions during auth work.

verdict.h: Two quarters of decisions on a broken join
verdict.p: Nothing about this was visible from the dashboard, which showed plausible, stable, slowly-worsening numbers — the most dangerous kind of wrong. It was found only because somebody finally compared analytics to the database.
verdict.lesson: Test the anonymous-to-known transition by hand, every quarter. And reconcile against a source of truth before anyone plans against a number.

cases.badge: One new event · found a 9% leak
cases.title: The import that failed silently
cases.sub: Everything about the happy path was instrumented. Adding one failure event revealed where a tenth of new accounts were disappearing.
steps: New-account activation was 52% and the drop-off was concentrated at the CSV import step. The step had exactly one event: Import Succeeded. Failures produced an on-screen error and no data at all.

From the dataset, a user who tried five times and failed was indistinguishable from a user who never tried. Those are opposite problems with opposite fixes — one is a motivation problem, the other is a bug.
One event added: Import Failed, with error_code, row_count, file_size and attempt_number. Two days of work, including the tracking plan entry.

9.2% of new accounts attempted an import and failed at least once. 61% of those never tried again. Three error codes accounted for 84% of failures: a date-format mismatch, files over 5MB, and non-UTF-8 encoding from a specific popular tool.
Date-format auto-detection, a chunked upload path above 5MB, and encoding detection with a clear message naming the source tool. Four weeks of work, precisely aimed.

Import failure rate fell from 9.2% to 1.4% of new accounts. New-account activation rose from 52% to 59% over the following two months — a bigger movement than the previous three onboarding projects combined.
Every meaningful success event now ships with a failure counterpart in the tracking plan, and it is part of the definition of done.

verdict.p: The instrumentation was not sparse — this product had over two hundred events. It was simply built entirely around things going well, which is the default, because success is what you are hoping to count.
verdict.lesson: Pair every success event with a failure event carrying an error code. It is the cheapest diagnostic instrument you will ever add.

quiz.q: Two dashboards show different numbers for “active users”. What is the most likely explanation?
o: One of them is broken
Two correct calculations of two different definitions — window, filters, timezone or identity rule
Data latency
Sampling
quiz.e: Nearly always both queries are correct and they are measuring different things: a 28-day versus a 30-day window, one excluding internal accounts, different timezones, or different identity rules. Resolve by comparing definitions line by line, never by choosing the number you prefer.

quiz.q: Which events must be tracked server-side?
o: All of them, for accuracy
Anything financial or contractual — payments, subscriptions, invoices
User interface interactions
None, client-side is richer
quiz.e: Client-side tracking loses 10–30% to ad blockers, crashes and network failures, which is tolerable for hovers and scrolls and unacceptable for money. Intent and interface behaviour has to be client-side because the server never sees it. Expect a persistent gap between the two and document it.

quiz.q: Your import step has an “Import Succeeded” event and nothing else. What can you not tell?
o: How many people succeeded
Whether people who did not succeed tried and failed, or never tried at all
How long the import took
Which plan the user was on
quiz.e: Without a failure event, absence of success has two completely opposite explanations — a motivation problem or a bug — and they need opposite fixes. Pairing every meaningful success event with a failure event carrying an error code is the highest-return instrumentation you can add.

quiz.q: When should you first reconcile a metric against an independent source?
o: When someone questions it
Before anybody plans or forecasts from it
Once a year during audit
Only for revenue metrics
quiz.e: An unreconciled metric is a rumour with a chart. Check it against billing, a database count or a manual tally for one day, find the gap, explain it, and write down what gap is acceptable. Doing this before it appears in a plan is what buys you the right to be believed later.

quiz.q: A dashboard chart shows a clean step change on a date with no release. First hypothesis?
o: A competitor event
A metric definition, filter or pipeline change
Genuine user behaviour change
Seasonality
quiz.e: Clean step changes are the signature of measurement, not behaviour — real user behaviour moves messily. Check the definition history, filters, bot exclusions and pipeline deploys first. Twyman's law: the more interesting the number, the more likely it is a bug.

sections.lede: Analytics feels like a data problem and is almost entirely a naming and identity problem. This topic is about designing instrumentation backwards from the questions you will actually be asked, getting identity right before it silently corrupts two quarters of decisions, and tracking failure as carefully as success.

title: Launch, GTM & Adoption
one: Shipping is the middle of the project, not the end. What happens in the six weeks after.

terms.d: A pre-agreed classification for how much launch machinery a change gets. A tier-three change gets a changelog line; a tier-one gets press, enablement and a webinar. Deciding this early stops every release becoming a negotiation.
terms.c: A staged reading, a preview run, or a full opening night with critics. You decide which before you cast it.

terms.d: A checklist walked with every function a week out: support briefed, docs live, pricing configured, legal cleared, monitoring in place, rollback tested. The point is finding the one unowned item, and there is always one.
terms.c: The dress rehearsal, in costume, with the lighting board. Where you discover the door does not open.

terms.d: A limited release to real users who know it is unfinished, with an explicit end date and a stated purpose. Without those two things it becomes a permanent parallel product nobody will let you retire.
terms.c: Previews. Tickets are cheaper, the audience knows, and the run has a published end date.

terms.d: A customer who builds alongside you in exchange for influence and early access. Extremely valuable, and dangerous if you let one partner's edge case become your product's default.
terms.c: The patron who funds the production and would like a word about the third act.

terms.d: Making sure sales, support, success and marketing can each do their job on day one: what it is, who it is for, what it costs, what it does not do, and what to say when it breaks.
terms.c: Front of house knowing the running time, the interval, and where the exits are.

terms.d: What this is, who it is for, what it replaces, and why it is better for them specifically. Written in one paragraph before any marketing copy, because everything downstream inherits it.
terms.c: The one line on the poster that decides who buys a ticket.

terms.d: One primary claim, two or three supporting claims, and the proof for each. It exists so that ten people describing your launch say roughly the same thing.
terms.c: The blurb, the reviews pulled out in bold, and the quotes underneath.

terms.d: The five things prospects and existing customers will push back on, with an honest answer for each — including “that is a fair criticism, and here is what we are doing”. Fabricated answers are found out in one call.
terms.c: What front of house says when someone asks why there is no interval.

terms.d: Telling your own company before you tell the market. Ignoring this is how a customer learns about a feature from a webinar while your support team learns about it from the customer.
terms.c: The cast and crew read the programme before the audience does.

terms.d: Releasing to a growing percentage: internal, 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%, with health checks at each step. The default for anything that touches money, data or authentication.
terms.c: Previews before opening night, in front of progressively larger houses.

terms.d: A switch that separates deploying code from releasing behaviour, and lets you turn something off in seconds without a deploy. It is what makes a phased rollout practical and a bad launch survivable.
terms.c: Being able to drop the curtain without dismantling the set.

terms.d: Deploying the code to production behind a flag, exercised by internal users or shadow traffic, before anybody outside can see it. Removes deployment risk from the launch date entirely.
terms.c: Running the whole show to an empty theatre, with the lights on.

terms.d: The specific, tested steps to get back to the previous state, including what happens to data created in the meantime. Untested rollbacks are theoretical, and they are only ever needed at the worst possible time.
terms.c: Knowing exactly how to strike the set, and having done it once before an audience was present.

terms.d: How many people, and which ones, a failure would touch. Deciding this deliberately — start with low-value segments, avoid your largest accounts and your noisiest ones — is most of the value of a phased rollout.
terms.c: Which night you schedule the risky technical change. Not the one the critics attend.

terms.d: What share of eligible users have used the thing, over time. Distinguish reach — did they ever try it — from depth, whether they still use it, and whether it moved the outcome you built it for.
terms.c: Bums on seats, then whether they came back for the second week of the run.

terms.d: A prompt, tour, empty state or email that gets an eligible user to the point of value. Usually where most post-launch adoption actually comes from, and usually built after launch rather than before.
terms.c: The usher who tells you the good seats are still free upstairs.

terms.d: Checking, weeks later, whether the outcome moved as forecast — and by how much you were wrong. Teams that measure the shrinkage get their next forecast believed.
terms.c: Comparing the box office to the projection, out loud, with the same people who signed it off.

terms.d: Deliberately retiring something: notice, migration path, a date, and a communication plan. A product with no sunsetting habit accumulates surface area faster than it can maintain it.
terms.c: Closing the run properly, rather than leaving one performance a week going indefinitely.

terms.d: Treating release as the end of the project. Adoption work — nudges, docs, enablement, empty states, follow-up — is where most of the outcome actually comes from, and it needs capacity reserved before launch.
terms.c: Everyone going home after opening night, with three weeks of the run still booked.

terms.d: Everything to everyone at once. Removes your ability to find problems cheaply, and concentrates every risk on a single date, usually one nobody chose for product reasons.
terms.c: No previews. First audience is a full house and the press.

terms.d: Support learning about a change from a ticket. Costs you resolution time, customer trust and internal credibility all at once, and it is entirely preventable with a two-day head start.
terms.c: Front of house discovering the running order from an annoyed customer in the foyer.

terms.d: Reporting press pickup, page views, webinar registrations or day-one clicks as if they were outcomes. They measure the announcement, not the product.
terms.c: Framing the reviews while the second week plays to forty people.

steps.t: Decide the launch tier early
steps.out: A tier, and the machinery that comes with it
steps.b: Classify the change while it is still being built: is this a changelog line, a normal release with an email and docs, or a full launch with press, enablement and a campaign? Agreeing the tier early sets expectations, reserves the right amount of marketing and support capacity, and stops the week-before argument about whether this deserves a webinar.
steps.do: Write down what each tier includes as a standing template. It turns a recurring negotiation into a lookup.
steps.no: Treating every release as a launch. Your audience stops reading and your team stops caring.

steps.t: Write the positioning before the copy
steps.out: One paragraph: what, who, instead of what, why better
steps.b: What it is, who it is for, what it replaces in their life, and why it is better for those specific people. Everything downstream — landing page, sales deck, in-product copy, release notes — inherits this paragraph, so an unclear one multiplies into ten unclear artefacts. Test it by reading it to someone in another team and asking who it is for.
steps.do: Name the alternative it displaces, including “a spreadsheet” and “doing nothing”. Those are your real competitors.
steps.no: Leading with the mechanism. “AI-powered” is not a position; “stop reconciling invoices by hand on Fridays” is.

steps.t: Enable your own company first
steps.out: Support, sales and success ready two days early
steps.b: Each function needs something different: support wants failure modes, known issues and the exact escalation path; sales wants the pitch, pricing and objection handling; success wants who to proactively tell and why they will care. Give them a two-day head start and a single page each, and ask them what is missing — they will find gaps you cannot see.
steps.do: Give support the known-issues list before launch. They will find out anyway, and much less kindly.
steps.no: A single all-company announcement email as your enablement plan.

steps.t: Run the readiness review
steps.out: A signed checklist with owners and one date
steps.b: A week out, walk the list with every function: docs published, pricing configured, billing tested, legal and privacy cleared, monitoring and alerts in place, rollback tested, support macros written, analytics firing. You are looking for the item everyone assumed someone else owned. There is always exactly one.
steps.do: Test the rollback for real in a staging environment, including what happens to data created after the release.
steps.no: Reviewing readiness the day before. Everything you find becomes a launch-day heroics story instead of a fix.

steps.t: Roll out in phases and watch the guardrails
steps.out: A ramp schedule and abort conditions
steps.b: Internal, then 1%, then 10%, 50%, 100%, with explicit health checks between steps: errors, latency, support volume, the key business metric. Choose the blast radius deliberately — not your largest accounts, not your noisiest, not on a Friday. Write the abort conditions before you start so the decision is not made under pressure by whoever is most tired.
steps.do: Put the kill switch behind a flag anyone on call can flip without a deploy.
steps.no: Ramping straight to everyone because the beta went well. Betas are self-selected volunteers and behave nothing like the whole base.

steps.t: Work adoption deliberately for six weeks
steps.out: A drive plan with reserved capacity
steps.b: Reserve capacity after launch, before launch. Empty states, in-product prompts, a lifecycle email sequence, help content, a proactive outreach list for accounts that would benefit most, and a follow-up for people who tried it once and stopped. Most of the outcome you were funded to deliver arrives in these six weeks, not on release day.
steps.do: Split adoption into reach, depth and outcome. Reach without depth means the prompt worked and the product did not.
steps.no: Announcing once and waiting. First-week adoption is a floor, not a ceiling, and nobody is thinking about you.

steps.t: Verify the impact, then say what you got wrong
steps.out: A short note comparing forecast to reality
steps.b: Weeks later, check the outcome against the forecast: what moved, by how much, in which segments, and what your estimate was off by. Effects almost always shrink. Publishing the shrinkage is what makes your next forecast credible — and it is also how you find out whether the thing is worth maintaining at all.
steps.do: Keep a running record of forecast versus actual. Calibration is a reputation you build once and spend for years.
steps.no: Reporting press mentions and day-one clicks. Those describe the announcement, not the product.

cases.title: The feature that launched twice
cases.sub: The build took nine weeks and the launch went fine. Adoption came almost entirely from the six weeks that had been planned in advance.
steps: A scheduled-reports feature for a B2B analytics product. Eligible users: 12,400 account admins. The team's previous launch had reached 8% adoption and stalled there, which is why the plan was different this time.

Tier two: in-product announcement, email to admins, docs, a support macro, no press. Positioning: “stop rebuilding the same Monday report — have it arrive in your inbox instead.” Named alternative: a manual export and a calendar reminder.
Support got the known-issues list, the two failure modes and the escalation path two days early. Success got a list of 340 accounts whose usage pattern suggested they were manually exporting weekly.

Internal, then 5% of admins for two days, then 50%, then all. One issue caught at 5%: reports scheduled for 09:00 in a non-UTC timezone fired at the wrong hour. Fixed before the wider ramp; would have generated several hundred support tickets.
6% adoption — almost identical to the previous launch. The email did roughly what emails do, and the announcement was dismissed by most people in under two seconds.

Weeks two to seven: an empty state on the reports page offering to schedule the report you were already looking at; a three-email sequence to admins who had exported twice in a month; proactive outreach by success to the 340-account list; and a one-question prompt for people who scheduled a report and then deleted it.

The empty state on the reports page — a single in-context prompt — produced more adoption than the launch email and the announcement combined. Proactive outreach converted 38% of the 340 targeted accounts. The deletion prompt revealed a recurring confusion about timezones, which became a copy change.
Week eight adoption 41%. Weekly manual exports by those accounts fell 52%. Support contacts about report building fell by a third.

verdict.h: Launch day contributed about a seventh of the outcome
verdict.p: The build was competent and the launch was unremarkable — the same email, the same announcement, roughly the same first-week number as the failed previous attempt. The difference was two person-weeks of capacity reserved before launch for the work that happens after it.
verdict.lesson: Reserve adoption capacity before you launch, and put your prompts where the user already is rather than in their inbox.

cases.title: A navigation change released to everyone at once
cases.sub: It had tested well with fourteen beta users. Twelve hours after full release it was reverted, and the reasons were all knowable in advance.
steps: A navigation restructure, six weeks of work, validated with fourteen beta users recruited from the community forum. Feedback was strongly positive. Released to 100% at 16:00 on a Friday to “give it the weekend to settle”.

Support tickets rose 340% in the first evening. Three distinct problems: power users could not find two frequently-used admin pages; a keyboard shortcut used heavily by one large customer's team no longer worked; and screen-reader users hit an unlabelled menu region, which was an accessibility regression.

Fourteen self-selected volunteers from a community forum are the least representative group available — enthusiastic, tolerant of change, and unlikely to include an assistive-technology user or a high-volume admin. None of the three problems could have surfaced in that sample.

Support was at weekend staffing. The engineer who could have shipped the shortcut fix was off. The decision to roll back was therefore made by whoever was available, twelve hours later, rather than by anyone with context.

There was no feature flag: the change was structural and deployed. Reverting required a release, which took four hours to prepare and deploy on a Saturday. Two customers had already been sent an email explaining the new navigation.

Behind a flag on the second attempt. Ramp at 1%, 10%, 50%, with support volume and task-completion as explicit abort conditions. Beta cohort constructed rather than volunteered: two accessibility users, three high-volume admins, and a random sample. No releases after Wednesday.

Shipped over eleven days. The 1% step caught the admin-page discoverability issue; the constructed beta caught the accessibility regression before any rollout at all. Support volume rose 12% for one week, then settled below the previous baseline.

verdict.h: Fourteen volunteers are not a sample
verdict.p: The work was good and it eventually shipped almost unchanged. What failed was every part of the release mechanism: an unrepresentative beta, no flag, no ramp, no abort conditions, and a date chosen for the team's comfort rather than for the ability to respond.
verdict.lesson: Construct your beta cohort rather than accepting volunteers, and never release anything structural without a flag and a ramp.

quiz.q: Your beta went well with 20 volunteers from the community. What should you conclude?
o: It is ready for full release
Very little — volunteers are enthusiastic, change-tolerant and unlikely to include your hardest cases
That adoption will be high
That you can skip the phased rollout
quiz.e: Self-selected volunteers are the least representative group you can assemble: they like you, they like change, and they almost never include assistive-technology users, very high-volume users, or the reluctant majority. Construct the cohort deliberately instead, then still ramp.

quiz.q: Week one adoption is 6% against a target of 35%. What is the most likely correct response?
o: The feature has failed; move on
Work adoption deliberately for six weeks with in-product prompts, targeted outreach and lifecycle emails
Send the announcement email again
Add more features to it
quiz.e: First-week adoption is mostly a measure of how many people happened to be paying attention, which is not many. Most of the outcome typically comes from the six weeks afterwards — in-context prompts, empty states, proactive outreach — which is why that capacity needs reserving before launch.

quiz.q: Which team most needs a head start before a release, and what do they need?
o: Marketing — the campaign assets
Support — the failure modes, known issues and escalation path
Finance — the revenue forecast
Legal — the terms update
quiz.e: Support is the function that will meet the consequences first and that suffers most from surprise. Two days and one page — what changed, the known issues, the failure modes, what to say, when to escalate — protects resolution times, customer trust and your own credibility. All the others matter; none is as time-critical.

quiz.q: You are releasing a change that touches authentication. What is non-negotiable?
o: A press release
A feature flag, a phased ramp and a tested rollback
A webinar
A design partner
quiz.e: Anything touching money, data or authentication gets a flag, a ramp with health checks between steps, and a rollback that has actually been tested — including what happens to data created in the meantime. An untested rollback is a theory, and it is only ever needed at the worst possible moment.

quiz.q: Which of these is a real launch outcome metric?
o: Press mentions in week one
Webinar registrations
Share of eligible users still using it at week six, and whether the target outcome moved
Day-one clicks on the announcement
quiz.e: The first, second and fourth measure the announcement rather than the product. What matters is reach (did eligible people try it), depth (are they still using it) and outcome (did the number you built it for actually move). Reach without depth means the prompt worked and the feature did not.

They are unrepresentative betas, surprised support teams, releases with no way back, and the assumption that announcing something is the same as landing it. This topic covers the readiness machinery, the release mechanics, and the six weeks after — which is where most of the outcome actually comes from.

title: Frameworks — Diagnosis & Analysis
one: Root cause, gap, process, feasibility and risk: the toolkit for working out what is actually going on before you commit.

frameworks.name: Root Cause Analysis

items: An observable fact with a number and a date. Not a judgement, not a name.
Built from logs and messages, because memory reorders things helpfully.
Usually several. Write them all down before choosing.
Stop here. If the next answer is human nature, you have gone too far.
viz.cap: Four moves. The last one is the test of whether you actually finished.

frameworks.one: An umbrella term for any structured attempt to get past what happened to why it happened, and to a cause worth fixing.
frameworks.when: Something has gone wrong more than once, or the same class of problem keeps returning under different names. Not for one-off incidents with an obvious cause.
how: Write the problem as an observable fact with a number and a date, not as a judgement.
Assemble a timeline of what actually happened, from evidence rather than memory.
Pick a technique to go deeper — 5 Whys for linear chains, Fishbone for many contributing factors, fault tree for compound failures.
Keep asking until you reach a cause you could actually change, and stop when the next answer is “human nature” or “the market”.
Test the candidate cause: if it were removed, would the problem have happened anyway?
frameworks.with: Choose your technique by shape: 5 Whys for a chain, Fishbone for many contributors, fault tree for combinations, Pareto when you have hundreds of instances.

ex.h: Duplicate charges at a payments team

items: The observable fact. Previously reported as “occasional double-billing complaints”.
Three spikes, all within 20 minutes of a deploy
Built from logs. Nobody had noticed the correlation because complaints arrived days later.
Retry path had no idempotency key
Changeable. This is where the analysis stops.
Two changes, one preventive and one detective.

ex.cap: Four stages of one real analysis.
ex.p: Support had been treating each complaint individually for seven months. Twenty minutes of timeline work turned a customer-service problem into a two-day engineering fix: duplicate rate fell from 0.41% to 0.01%, and the reconciliation job now catches the remainder before the customer does.

frameworks.out: One or two causes, each with an owner and a change that would prevent recurrence.
frameworks.trap: Stopping at the first cause that is somebody's fault. Blame is a satisfying place to stop and it prevents you finding the system that made the mistake easy.

frameworks.name: 5 Whys

items: The symptom, stated as a measured fact.
First why. Still a symptom, just a more specific one.
No format detection in the parser
Second why. Now it is about our code.
Third why. Now it is about our process.
No locale question in the discovery brief
Fourth why, and something you can actually change on Monday.
viz.cap: Five is arbitrary. Stopping at something changeable is not.

frameworks.one: Ask why, five times, following one chain from symptom to something structural.
frameworks.when: A single, fairly linear problem where you suspect the obvious answer is the third or fourth one down. Fifteen minutes with the right people in the room.
how: State the problem factually: “43% of imports failed last month.”
Ask why, and answer with evidence rather than a theory.
Repeat, following the single most load-bearing branch each time.
Stop when you reach something you control — a process, a default, an incentive, a missing check.
Sanity-check by reading the chain backwards: does each “therefore” actually follow?
frameworks.with: If the second why has three plausible answers rather than one, switch to a Fishbone.

viz.note: One change at the fifth why: a locale question added to the discovery template.
viz.cap: The fix was upstream of the code.

ex.p: Three earlier attempts had fixed symptoms — better error copy, then a retry button. Following the chain to the discovery template changed how every subsequent integration was specified, and success rate moved from 57% to 96% with four days of work.

frameworks.out: A short causal chain ending in something changeable, plus the change.
frameworks.trap: Five is arbitrary — sometimes it is three, sometimes eight. The real failure is a chain built from opinions, where each answer is a guess nobody checked.

frameworks.name: Fishbone diagram

viz.head: 43% of imports fail
cats: Nobody owns the import path; three squads have touched it.
No acceptance criteria covered non-UTF-8 files.
No format detection, no error message naming the cause.
Customer exports come from four different tools.
No schema validation in CI, so bad files reach the parser.
One popular source tool changed its export format.
viz.cap: Categories exist to make you think outside your favourite explanation.

frameworks.one: Groups possible causes into categories branching off a central problem, so you find the contributors you were not already thinking about.
frameworks.when: The problem clearly has several contributing causes at once, or a group keeps circling the same favourite explanation.
how: Write the problem at the head of the spine.
Choose categories — for software, commonly People, Process, Product, Data, Tooling, External.
Brainstorm causes into each branch without debating them yet.
Mark each cause as evidenced, suspected or guessed.
Pick the two or three that are both plausible and cheap to verify, then go and verify them.
frameworks.with: Follow with Pareto on the branches you can count, then 5 Whys on the biggest one.

ex.h: Checkout abandonment, causes weighted by evidence

items: Measured from logs. The only branch with hard evidence at the start.
Session recordings showed a postcode validator rejecting valid formats.
Survey evidence only, so it was investigated rather than fixed.

ex.cap: Two branches held 60% of the abandonment.
ex.p: The team's shared assumption before the session was that price was the problem. Categorising by People, Process, Product, Data, Tooling and External surfaced two mechanical causes worth 60% of the loss, both fixable in under three weeks.

frameworks.out: A map of candidate causes with evidence levels, and a shortlist to investigate.
frameworks.trap: Producing a beautiful diagram and treating it as the analysis. It generates hypotheses; it does not test any of them.

frameworks.name: Fault tree analysis

root: The top event, defined precisely enough to test.
kids: Payment succeeded but the response was lost, so the job retried.
Provider re-delivered an event and we had no idempotency key.
Support issued a credit while the scheduled charge was queued.
viz.cap: An OR gate near the top means any single branch is enough. Those are your priorities.

frameworks.one: Works backwards from a failure using AND/OR logic to find which combinations of conditions can produce it.
frameworks.when: A failure needs several things to go wrong together — payments, data loss, security, safety. Overkill for most product problems and essential for a few.
how: Define the top event precisely: “a customer is charged twice.”
Beneath it, list the immediate causes and whether they are AND or OR conditions.
Expand each branch until you reach basic events you can observe or guard.
Look for single points of failure — any OR gate near the top is one.
Add a control at the cheapest branch that breaks the most paths.
frameworks.with: Follow with FMEA to rank which branch to guard first when several are live.

ex.h: Routes to a double charge, by observed frequency

items: An OR branch on its own — enough by itself to cause the failure.
Also an OR branch, and closed by the same key.
Needed two things to happen together, so much rarer.

ex.cap: One control closed 93% of the paths.
ex.p: Drawing the tree showed that two of the three routes shared a single missing control. That reframed the work from three separate fixes across two teams into one change, and made the remaining 7% an accepted risk with a detective control rather than a project.

frameworks.out: A logic tree showing every route to the failure, and where one control blocks several.
frameworks.trap: Modelling the system you designed rather than the one that exists. Retries, manual overrides and support tooling create paths that are not on anyone's diagram.

frameworks.name: Pareto analysis

items: Fixing this alone removes two fifths of all failures.
A chunked upload path. One week of work.
Almost all from one popular source tool.
Real, but a long way down the list.
If this bar were the biggest, your categories would be wrong.
viz.cap: Three causes, 84% of the damage. Fix left to right, then re-run it.

frameworks.one: Counts causes by frequency or cost and sorts them, revealing that a small number usually account for most of the damage.
frameworks.when: You have many instances of a problem and limited capacity — support tickets, error codes, churn reasons, failed jobs.
how: Categorise every instance over a meaningful period, using consistent categories.
Count and, where you can, attach a cost to each category.
Sort descending and plot the cumulative percentage.
Draw the line where cumulative cost passes roughly 80%.
Fix left to right, and re-run it a month later — the order changes.
frameworks.with: Always the first step when you have volume. Then 5 Whys on the top category.

ex.h: Six weeks of support tickets, categorised

items: Self-serve reset shipped in nine days.
A downloadable PDF and a clearer line-item breakdown.
If this were the biggest bar, the categories would be wrong.

ex.cap: Two categories, 62% of the volume.
ex.p: Support had been asking for headcount. Two fixes worth about three engineer-weeks removed 41% of ticket volume over six weeks, and the ranking changed afterwards — export failure became the top category, which is why you re-run it.

frameworks.out: A ranked list of causes with the handful that matter separated from the long tail.
frameworks.trap: Categories chosen after seeing the data, or a tail so long it is really a category problem. Also: the biggest category is sometimes “other”, which means start again.

frameworks.name: Blameless post-mortem

items: From logs and messages. Recollection reorders events to make sense.
Separate it from what you know now. Hindsight is the enemy of a useful review.
Why the wrong action looked right
This is the actual question. If nobody can answer it, keep going.
Defaults, alerts, guardrails, checks. Three actions with owners, not twenty.
viz.cap: Blameless means the system is on trial, not the person.

frameworks.one: A written review of an incident that treats the people involved as rational actors responding to the system they were in.
frameworks.when: After any incident with customer impact, and after any near miss you would rather not repeat. Within a week, while memory is intact.
how: Build the timeline first, in UTC, from logs and messages rather than recollection.
Separate what was known at each moment from what is known now — hindsight is the enemy of a useful review.
Ask what made the wrong action look reasonable at the time.
Produce actions that change the system: defaults, alerts, guardrails, checks. Not “be more careful”.
Publish it internally, including the messy parts, and track the actions to completion.
frameworks.with: Feed recurring contributing factors into a Pareto once you have several reviews.

items: Normal process, reviewed, tested. Nothing unusual.
Nobody is looking. This is the gap that mattered.
Detection took 22 minutes and came from outside.
The fix was fast. Finding out was not.

ex.cap: The interesting number is 22 minutes, not 46.
ex.p: The natural conversation would have been about the deploy. The timeline made it obvious that response time was fine and detection was the failure: the alert threshold was set at 8%. Lowering it and adding a deploy-window check cut median detection to under three minutes.

frameworks.out: A timeline, contributing factors and a small number of owned system changes.
frameworks.trap: “Blameless” becoming “consequence-free”, so nothing changes; or the action list being twenty items, which means none of them will happen.

frameworks.name: Process mapping

steps: Where the clock starts, whether or not you are counting.
Median wait here was 14 hours, and it was invisible on every dashboard.
And a second wait, because nobody owned the handback.
viz.cap: Four steps, three boundary crossings, and almost all the time spent between them.

frameworks.one: Draws the actual sequence of steps, decisions and handoffs in a process so you can see where time and information get lost.
frameworks.when: A process spans more than one team or tool and nobody can describe it end to end without arguing. Almost always more revealing than expected.
how: Define the start and end events precisely, and stick to them.
Walk the process with the people who do it, in the order they do it — not from documentation.
Capture every decision point, wait state, rework loop and handoff.
Mark where the process leaves your system entirely, including spreadsheets and email.
Annotate each step with elapsed time and touch time; the gap between them is the opportunity.
frameworks.who: The people who do each step
frameworks.with: Bound it with SIPOC first. Add times and it becomes value stream mapping.

ex.h: Refunds, mapped with real elapsed times

steps: Clock starts here, whether or not anyone is counting.
12 minutes of work, then it waits for the daily finance batch.
4 minutes of work, 31 hours of waiting.
And a second wait, because nobody owned the handback.

ex.cap: Six days of lead time, 40 minutes of work.
ex.p: Everyone assumed finance was slow. Walking the map with the actual people showed two waits created by a daily batch and an unowned handback. Moving approvals to a rolling queue took the median refund from six days to nine hours without anyone working faster.

frameworks.out: A map of the real process with wait states, loops and handoffs marked.
frameworks.trap: Mapping the official process instead of the real one. The real one contains a shared spreadsheet and someone called Priya, and that is the finding.

frameworks.name: Swimlane diagram

steps: Two days, because it waits for a weekly batch.
The customer is now emailing their account manager.
And the loop closes days after the customer expected to start.
viz.cap: Five steps, four crossings. Count the crossings, not the steps.

frameworks.one: A process map with one lane per actor, so every handoff between people or systems becomes visible as a line crossing a boundary.
frameworks.when: The problem smells like a handoff problem: things sitting in queues, work bouncing between teams, nobody able to say who owns a step.
how: List the actors — roles and systems — as lanes.
Place each step in the lane of whoever actually performs it.
Draw every transition between lanes; these are your handoffs.
Count the crossings and measure the wait at each one.
Redesign to reduce crossings, not to speed up individual steps.
frameworks.with: Use it after process mapping when the problem looks like queues rather than steps.

items: Six boundary crossings, four of them waiting on a different team’s weekly cadence.
Provisioning moved into the signing flow and finance reconciled afterwards.

ex.cap: Redesign for fewer crossings, not faster steps.
ex.p: Time-to-first-login went from eleven days to two. Nothing in the process got faster; four handoffs simply stopped existing. Counting crossings rather than steps is what made the redesign obvious.

frameworks.out: A diagram where the number of boundary crossings is immediately countable.
frameworks.trap: Adding lanes for everyone with an opinion. Lanes are for people who perform steps; stakeholders belong on a stakeholder map.

frameworks.name: SIPOC

items: Who provides the inputs — internal teams, customers, third parties.
What each step needs before it can start.
Five to seven steps. No deeper, or the tool stops doing its job.
What comes out, in the form it comes out in.
Who receives each output. Get them to confirm their own row.
viz.cap: A boundary tool. Detail belongs in the process map that comes next.

frameworks.one: A one-page scope frame for a process: who supplies what, the five to seven high-level steps, what comes out, and who receives it.
frameworks.when: Before detailed process mapping, to agree boundaries and stop the exercise expanding to cover the whole company.
how: Name the process and its trigger.
List outputs first, then who receives them — customers, internal or external.
List the five to seven top-level steps, no deeper.
Work backwards to the inputs each step needs, and who supplies them.
Get every named supplier and customer to confirm the row that concerns them.
frameworks.who: 5–6, including a supplier and a customer
frameworks.with: Always before process mapping. It is the cheapest way to stop scope expanding.

ex.h: Monthly invoicing, bounded in one page

items: Contract terms, metered usage, tax rates.
Close usage → rate → generate → review → send. Five steps, no deeper.
Invoice PDF, ledger entry, dunning schedule.

ex.cap: Agreed in forty minutes, and it held.
ex.p: The previous attempt at this had expanded into a review of the whole revenue system and was abandoned. Fixing the boundaries first meant the detailed mapping that followed covered five steps rather than forty, and finished in a week.

frameworks.out: A single agreed page defining what is in and out of scope.
frameworks.trap: Going below five to seven steps. SIPOC is a boundary tool; the detail belongs in the process map that follows.

frameworks.name: Value stream mapping

items: Nobody feels responsible for a queue, which is exactly why it survives.
Speeding this up can recover a fraction of one day out of three weeks.
viz.cap: Three weeks of lead time, four hours of touch time. The opportunity is not in the work.

frameworks.one: Maps a process end to end with time and quality data at each step, separating work that adds customer value from waiting and rework.
frameworks.when: Lead time is the complaint — “why does it take three weeks?” — and you need to show that most of the three weeks is queueing, not working.
how: Pick one product or request type and follow a single real instance.
Record touch time, elapsed time, and first-pass quality at each step.
Compute total lead time against total touch time; the ratio is usually startling.
Mark each step as value-adding, necessary non-value-adding, or waste.
Design a future state that attacks the biggest wait, then re-measure.
frameworks.with: Only worth it once you have a process map. Pair with cost of delay to size the prize.

ex.h: Quote to cash, touch time against lead time

viz.note: 96% of the elapsed time was queueing, and no single person felt responsible for any of it.
viz.cap: Four hours of work inside fifteen days.

ex.p: Two weekly batches accounted for most of the queue. Replacing them with a rolling process took lead time from fifteen days to four, which mattered because the sales cycle was losing deals to a competitor quoting in 48 hours.

frameworks.out: Lead time versus touch time, with the largest waits and rework loops identified.
frameworks.trap: Optimising the steps people can see themselves doing. The waiting is almost always bigger than the work, and nobody feels responsible for a queue.

frameworks.name: As-Is / To-Be analysis

items: Document it honestly, workarounds included, and get the people who live in it to confirm.
Design against a stated goal. If it only works when nobody is busy, it is a diagram.
viz.cap: The work is the list of differences between the two boxes.

frameworks.one: Two pictures of the same process — how it works now, how it should work — with the differences enumerated as work.
frameworks.when: Any change to a workflow that people already have habits and workarounds for. Especially before a migration or a replacement system.
how: Document the As-Is honestly, workarounds included, and get it confirmed by the people who live in it.
Design the To-Be against a stated goal — fewer handoffs, less rework, shorter lead time — not against fashion.
List every delta as a discrete change: system, process, data, role, policy.
Classify each delta by effort and by how much of the goal it delivers.
Sequence the deltas so early ones are useful on their own.
frameworks.who: The people who live in it
frameworks.with: Run impact analysis on each delta before sequencing them.

items: The rework rate was the surprise, and it came from a receipt rule nobody had written down.
Deltas: threshold policy, receipt OCR, retire the second system, retrain 40 approvers.

ex.cap: Four deltas, sequenced so the first is useful alone.
ex.p: The threshold change alone removed 62% of approvals and shipped in a fortnight, before any system work. Splitting the picture into discrete deltas is what made that sequencing visible — the original proposal was a single nine-month platform project.

frameworks.out: Two maps and a numbered list of changes between them.
frameworks.trap: A To-Be that assumes the perfect version of every human involved. If it only works when nobody is busy or confused, it is a diagram, not a design.

frameworks.name: Gap analysis

viz.note: Every gap becomes a sized piece of work, or an explicit decision to accept it.
viz.cap: Borrow the dimensions from outside, or you will score well on everything you already do.

frameworks.one: Compares where you are with where you need to be, on named dimensions, and turns each difference into a sized piece of work.
frameworks.when: You have a target — a compliance standard, a competitor's capability, a service level, a maturity model — and you need to know what stands between you and it.
how: Define the target state in measurable terms, from an external source where possible.
Assess the current state on the same dimensions, with evidence.
Record the gap per dimension, in the same units.
Judge each gap by how much it matters and how hard it is to close.
Turn the shortlist into work, and note explicitly which gaps you are accepting.
frameworks.with: Impact analysis on the gaps you decide to close; feasibility study if any is large.

ex.h: SOC 2 readiness, scored against the control set

items: No quarterly review process existed at all. The largest gap and the cheapest to close.
Already close — documented, just never rehearsed.

ex.cap: Dimensions borrowed from the standard, not invented.
ex.p: Using the auditor's own control list rather than an internal checklist changed the ranking completely: the team had planned to start with logging, which was the visible engineering work. Access review took nine days and closed the biggest gap.

frameworks.out: A table of dimension, current, target, gap, and planned action.
frameworks.trap: Dimensions invented by whoever is running the analysis, so the organisation scores well on everything it already does. Borrow the dimensions from outside.

frameworks.name: Impact analysis

root: Described precisely, including what stays the same.
kids: Every saved query touching the changed columns.
Third parties with contracts. Usually the one nobody remembers.
Scripts and screenshots that will now be wrong.
The month-end file nobody owns until it breaks.
viz.cap: The unbudgeted work is almost never in engineering.

frameworks.one: Works out what else a proposed change touches — systems, data, teams, customers, contracts — before you commit to it.
frameworks.when: Before any change with reach: a data model change, a pricing change, an API change, a policy change, anything customer-visible in a regulated area.
how: Describe the change precisely, including what stays the same.
Trace it outward: upstream systems, downstream consumers, reports, integrations, contracts, support processes, training material.
For each, record the effect, who owns it, and what it needs.
Identify anything irreversible, and anything with an external commitment attached.
Summarise as one page: what breaks, who must act, and what it costs to do nothing.
frameworks.who: PM + one owner per affected area
frameworks.with: Feed the irreversible items into a feasibility study or a one-way-door review.

ex.h: Renaming one field in the data model

root: A one-line change in the schema, estimated at two days.
kids: Owned by three different teams, all breaking silently.
Two under contract. Nobody knew the third existed.
Six macros and eleven screenshots referencing the old name.

ex.cap: Two days of engineering, five weeks of everything else.
ex.p: The change shipped eventually, with an aliased field and a six-month deprecation window. Tracing outward first is what turned a surprise into a plan — the third API consumer was found by searching access logs, not by asking around.

frameworks.out: A list of affected parties and systems, each with an owner and a required action.
frameworks.trap: Only tracing technical impact. The unbudgeted work is usually in support scripts, sales collateral, finance reports and the training deck nobody owns.

frameworks.name: Feasibility study

items: Can we build it with what we have?
Does the value beat the cost, as a range?
Can we support, bill, sell and explain it?
The one teams skip, and the one discovered after launch by the support team.
Can it be done inside the window that makes it worth doing?
viz.cap: TELOS. Five checks, and the fourth is where the surprises live.

frameworks.one: A structured check on whether a proposal is actually possible, across five dimensions: Technical, Economic, Legal, Operational and Scheduling.
frameworks.when: Before committing to something large, novel, regulated or externally dependent. Days of work to protect months of it.
how: Technical: can it be built with what we have, or what we can get?
Economic: does the value exceed the cost, with the assumptions stated and a range rather than a point?
Legal: privacy, licensing, accessibility, sector regulation, contractual commitments.
Operational: can the organisation actually run it — support, billing, onboarding, monitoring?
Scheduling: can it be done in the window that makes it worth doing?
frameworks.with: Pre-mortem afterwards. Feasibility finds what is possible; a pre-mortem finds what will actually go wrong.

items: Go-if — needs 400 accounts to break even
The verdict that stopped it, and the one nobody had checked.
Go — fits before the trade show

ex.cap: Four green, one red, and the red was the cheap one to find.
ex.p: Three of the five dimensions had been assessed informally already. Operational feasibility had not: support was English-only with a 4-hour SLA that was unmeetable across the timezone. The launch moved by a quarter and hired two people first.

frameworks.out: A go, no-go or go-if verdict per dimension, with the assumptions written down.
frameworks.trap: Operational feasibility. Teams check whether it can be built and forget whether anyone can support, bill, sell or explain it once it exists.

frameworks.name: Pre-mortem

items: It is six months later and this failed
Stated as fact, not as a risk. The framing is what unlocks it.
Five minutes, individually. This step is the whole method.
Read them all out before debating
Collect first, argue second, or the first speaker sets the frame.
Change the plan, or add an early check
Two or three failure modes, each with something concrete attached.
viz.cap: Thirty minutes, and it surfaces the objections politeness had suppressed.

frameworks.one: Imagine the project has failed badly, then have everyone write down why — before it starts.
frameworks.when: At the start of anything significant, and especially when the room is unanimously enthusiastic. Thirty minutes, and it surfaces objections that politeness had suppressed.
how: State the plan, then say: it is six months later and this failed completely.
Everyone writes their reasons silently for five minutes, individually.
Read them out without debate, collecting them all first.
Group them, and pick the two or three most plausible and most damaging.
Change the plan now, or add a specific early check for each.
frameworks.with: Any large commitment, right after the plan is drafted and before it is approved.

ex.h: A migration, failure modes by how many people named them

items: Seven of nine people wrote this independently. Nobody had raised it in three planning meetings.
Legacy system still in use after

ex.cap: Silent writing first. The unanimity was the signal.
ex.p: The plan gained a two-week parallel-run and a mapping validation step, which added about 9% to the timeline. The mapping issue was real: 4% of records failed validation in the dry run, which would have been discovered live.

frameworks.out: A ranked list of failure modes, with plan changes or early warning checks attached.
frameworks.trap: Running it as a discussion instead of silent individual writing. The first person to speak sets the frame and the quiet objections stay quiet.

frameworks.name: FMEA

parts: How bad is it for the customer if this happens?
How often would we expect it?
How likely are we to catch it before the customer does?
viz.foot: Improving detection is usually the cheapest lever
viz.cap: Three guesses multiplied. Its only honest use is ordering, not measuring.

frameworks.one: Lists each way a thing can fail and scores severity, likelihood and detectability to produce a priority number for each.
frameworks.when: Safety, payments, data integrity, or anything where a failure is expensive and you need a defensible ranking of what to guard first.
how: List the functions, then the ways each could fail.
For each failure mode, note the effect on the customer and its severity.
Score severity, occurrence and detection, typically 1–10 each.
Multiply for a risk priority number and sort.
Add controls to the top items, then re-score — usually by improving detection first, because it is cheapest.
frameworks.with: Fault tree first to find the failure modes, FMEA to rank which to guard.

viz.foot: detection was the cheapest score to move

ex.cap: The highest severity was not the highest priority.
ex.p: Double charging felt like the worst outcome and scored lower than silent declines, which were frequent and almost undetectable. Adding a decline alert moved detection from 8 to 2 and cut that RPN from 288 to 72 in a week — no product change required.

frameworks.out: A ranked risk register with controls and a re-scored residual risk.
frameworks.trap: Treating the risk priority number as objective. Three guesses multiplied together produce a confident-looking number; its only real use is ordering.

frameworks.name: SWOT

items: Evidence, not aspiration. If a competitor could write it about themselves, cut it.
The uncomfortable box. An empty one means the exercise was decorative.
Things you do not control but could exploit.
Then pair across boxes — that is where any decision comes from.
viz.cap: Four lists are a prompt. The pairing is the output.

frameworks.one: Four boxes: two internal, two external. Useful as a structured prompt, dangerous as a conclusion.
frameworks.when: Early framing of a market or a business unit, or to get a mixed group to surface what they collectively believe. Twenty minutes, not a quarter.
how: Fix the scope first — a segment, a product, a market. A SWOT of “the company” says nothing.
Fill internal boxes with evidence rather than aspiration.
Fill external boxes with things you do not control.
Then do the part everyone skips: pair items across boxes into actions — use this strength against that threat.
Discard anything that could be written by a competitor about themselves.
frameworks.with: Follow with PESTLE for the external boxes and Five Forces if margin is the question.

ex.h: A scheduling tool, and the pairing that mattered

items: The paired action: aim everything at clinics before the generalist enters.
two practice systems have open APIs
a generalist tool is adding bookings

ex.cap: The action came from pairing S with T, not from any single box.
ex.p: Four lists produced nothing for two weeks. Pairing them gave one sentence — use clinic retention and the integrations to become uneconomic to attack — which became the strategy, including the decision to stop serving three other segments.

frameworks.out: Four lists, and three or four cross-paired actions.
frameworks.trap: Stopping at the four lists. An unpaired SWOT is a mood board; the pairing is where any decision comes from.

frameworks.name: PESTLE

items: The letter most likely to have a specific date attached to it.
viz.cap: Specific to your market with a stated horizon, or it is just a list of trends.

frameworks.one: Scans the external forces you cannot control: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.
frameworks.when: Entering a new market or geography, or when planning over a horizon long enough for regulation, rates or platform rules to change under you.
how: Set a horizon — two years, five years — because relevance depends entirely on it.
For each letter, list forces specific to your market, not general trends.
Judge each by likelihood and by impact on your plan.
For the top few, write the leading indicator you would watch.
Review it on a schedule; a one-off PESTLE is out of date within a year.
frameworks.with: Five Forces for market structure; feasibility study once you have candidates.

ex.h: EU expansion, forces with dates attached

items: The only force with a hard date. It moved from a footnote to a roadmap item.

ex.cap: Specific forces with dates beat a list of trends.
ex.p: The first version of this listed “AI” and “remote work” and changed nothing. Forcing every entry to be specific to the market and dated produced two roadmap items and one compliance deadline that would otherwise have been discovered by a customer.

frameworks.out: A short list of external forces with watch indicators and owners.
frameworks.trap: Listing macro trends that apply to everybody. “AI is changing everything” is not analysis; “our sector's data rules change in March” is.

frameworks.name: Porter's Five Forces

left: New entrants
How easily can someone else start doing this?
Substitutes
Including a spreadsheet and doing nothing.
right: Few large buyers means they set the price.
Cloud, data, payment rails, one critical vendor.
viz.cap: Four forces pressing on rivalry. Ask which one sets your margin today.

frameworks.one: Assesses how much profit a market allows: buyer power, supplier power, new entrants, substitutes, and rivalry.
frameworks.when: Deciding whether to enter a market, or explaining why a market with lots of demand has terrible margins.
how: Define the market narrowly enough to be real — a segment, not an industry.
Rate each force high, medium or low, with a reason and evidence.
Identify which force is actually setting your margin today.
Ask what would change that force, and whether you could cause it.
Conclude with a position, not five ratings.
frameworks.with: PESTLE for what is changing around it; strategy work to decide the response.

left: New entrants: high
Two competitors launched in eighteen months. Nothing structural stopped a third.
Substitutes: very high
A phone call and a spreadsheet. The real competitor, and the cheapest one.
right: Thousands of small buyers, none with leverage.
The best 5% of providers had every option and set the terms.

ex.cap: Supplier power was setting the margin, not rivalry.
ex.p: The instinct was to compete on demand-side marketing. The analysis pointed the other way: locking in supply quality through tooling and guaranteed volume was the only force the company could actually change, and it became the year's strategy.

frameworks.out: A view on whether the market can be profitable, and what your position must do.
frameworks.trap: Applying it to a product rather than a market, and treating the forces as fixed. Products routinely change substitution and buyer power — that can be the strategy.

quiz.q: Your 5 Whys chain ends at “because the engineer didn't check.” What is wrong with stopping there?
o: Nothing — that is the root cause
It stops at a person rather than the system that made not checking easy or likely
Five whys were not completed
It needs more evidence
quiz.e: A cause you cannot change is not a root cause. “Someone didn't check” invites blame and prevents the next question: why was checking manual, why was there no alert, why did the deadline make skipping it rational? Keep going until you reach a default, a process or a guardrail you could actually alter.

quiz.q: You mapped a three-week process and found 4 hours of actual work. What does value stream mapping tell you to attack?
o: The four hours of work — make each step faster
The waiting between steps
Both equally
The number of people involved
quiz.e: When lead time is three weeks and touch time is four hours, essentially all of the opportunity is in queues, handoffs and rework loops. Speeding up the work itself can only ever recover a fraction of a day, and nobody feels responsible for a queue, which is exactly why it survives.

quiz.q: Which dimension of a feasibility study do teams most often skip?
o: Technical
Economic
Operational
Legal
quiz.e: Teams reliably check whether a thing can be built and whether the numbers work. Operational feasibility — can we actually support it, bill it, onboard people onto it, monitor it, explain it to sales — is the one that gets discovered after launch, usually by the support team.

quiz.q: A pre-mortem is being run as an open discussion. Why is that a problem?
o: It takes too long
The first speaker frames the conversation and quieter objections stay unspoken
Nobody will be honest in a group
It should be done by leadership only
quiz.e: The mechanism that makes a pre-mortem work is silent individual writing before anything is said aloud. Once someone speaks, anchoring does the rest and you collect variations on one theme. Five minutes of writing, then read everything out before any debate.

quiz.q: You have run a SWOT and produced four lists. What is still missing?
o: Prioritisation of each list
Pairing items across the boxes into specific actions
Competitor comparison
Numerical scoring
quiz.e: The four lists are a prompt, not an output. The decision comes from pairing — use this strength against that threat, close this weakness before that opportunity closes. A SWOT that stops at four lists is the reason the tool has a poor reputation.

families.Feasibility & risk: what it touches, and can we

sections.h: A case board, not a hunch.
sections.lede: These are the frameworks for the part of the job that happens before any decision: establishing what is true, why it keeps happening, what the current process actually is rather than what the documentation claims, and whether the thing you are proposing is even possible. Each entry tells you when to reach for it, how to run it, what you end up with, and how it usually goes wrong.

panel.big: Stop at a cause you can change, not at a person you can blame.
items: Map the real process, workarounds included. The official one is fiction.
Lead time minus touch time is where the opportunity almost always is.
Every framework here generates hypotheses. None of them tests one.

sections.lede: There are more diagnostic frameworks than anyone needs. In practice you are asking one of four questions, and each has two or three tools worth knowing.
sections.statement: A framework is a way of being systematic in public. It has no opinions and it cannot supply evidence you did not gather.

cards.p: 5 Whys for a linear chain, Fishbone when several things contribute, fault tree when a failure needs a combination, Pareto when you have hundreds of instances and limited capacity.
SIPOC to agree the boundaries, process and swimlane maps for the flow and the handoffs, value stream mapping when the complaint is lead time, As-Is/To-Be when you are replacing it.

cards.k: What will this touch, and can we do it?
cards.p: Impact analysis for reach, TELOS for possibility, pre-mortem for the objections politeness suppressed, FMEA when failures are expensive enough to need ranking.

sections.lede: Filter by family, then click any card. Each one is written to be usable on a Tuesday: when to reach for it, the steps, the artefact you end up with, and the specific way it fails in practice.

sections.h: If this is your situation, start here
sections.lede: The shortest possible route from a symptom to a tool.
rows: Fishbone if several causes appear plausible
Chains built from opinion instead of evidence
Optimising the work instead of the waiting
Nobody agrees what the process is
Process map walked with the doers
Mapping the documented process, not the real one
Replacing a workflow people rely on
A To-Be that needs perfect humans
A big, novel or regulated commitment
We are behind a standard or a competitor
Prioritise gaps by impact and effort
Inventing dimensions you already score well on
Fault tree or FMEA if it could recur worse
A twenty-item action list nobody owns
Five Forces on a narrowly defined market
Listing macro trends that apply to everyone
sections.foot: If two tools seem to fit, run the cheaper one first. Most of the value in this topic comes from being systematic at all, rather than from picking the perfect instrument.

sections.lede: One attempt each, with an explanation either way.

title: Frameworks — Decide & Prioritise
one: Scoring models, scope sorting, goal setting and decision rights: the toolkit for choosing, in public, with your reasoning visible.

frameworks.name: RICE

parts: People or events per period, from data where you have it.
3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal — per affected person.
Person-months, from the people who will do the work.
viz.foot: Effort in the denominator is why cheap always wins
viz.cap: Four separate arguments instead of one vague one. That is the actual product.

frameworks.one: A scoring model that forces four separate estimates instead of one vague argument about what matters most.
frameworks.when: You have ten or more comparable items on one product and need an order you can defend to people who each brought a favourite.
