how: Reach: how many people or events per period, from data where possible.
Impact: 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal, per affected person.
Confidence: 100% measured, 80% researched, 50% informed guess, 20% hunch.
Effort: person-months from the people who will do the work.
Score independently first, compare afterwards, and investigate every wide gap.
frameworks.who: PM, tech lead, one commercial voice
frameworks.with: Allocation buckets first, always. Then interrogate confidence on anything large.

items: Reach 9,000 × impact 2 × 90% ÷ 0.5 months. Cheap, certain, and it won.
Reach 200,000 × impact 3 × 40% ÷ 12 months. Ranked last on efficiency.

ex.cap: Scored independently, then compared. The gap was on the rebuild.
ex.p: Impact on the rebuild was scored 3 by engineering and 0.5 by support. Investigating that gap — rather than averaging it — revealed billing errors touched 1.9% of accounts, and the twelve-month rebuild became a five-month targeted fix.

frameworks.out: A ranked list, and — more usefully — a shortlist of hidden disagreements.
frameworks.trap: Effort sits in the denominator, so cheap and certain wins almost automatically. Decide your capacity allocation first, then rank within each bucket.

frameworks.name: ICE

viz.foot: No reach term — never compare across audiences
viz.cap: Fifteen minutes and good enough for experiments on one surface.

frameworks.one: RICE with reach removed: faster, cruder, and fine when everything on the list touches roughly the same audience.
frameworks.when: Ordering experiments or small changes on one surface, in a meeting, where the cost of getting the order slightly wrong is a week.
how: Score impact, confidence and ease out of 10 — or reuse the RICE impact scale.
Multiply.
Sort, then sanity-check the top three against your strategy.
Re-score anything where two people differ by more than 3 points.
Do not compare ICE scores against scores from a different list.
frameworks.with: Fine for experiments on one surface. Switch to RICE the moment audiences differ.

items: Ease 9, but confidence only 0.3 — no evidence either way.

ex.cap: Same surface, same audience, so reach cancels out.
ex.p: Fifteen minutes produced a running order the team stuck to for a quarter. It would have been wrong for cross-product comparison: a niche admin fix scored higher than a change affecting every visitor, because ICE cannot see how many people are involved.

frameworks.out: A rough order, arrived at in fifteen minutes.
frameworks.trap: Without reach, a fix affecting forty users can outrank one affecting forty thousand. Never use ICE to compare across products or audiences.

frameworks.name: WSJF

parts: Value, plus time criticality, plus risk reduced or opportunity opened.
Relative, not absolute. Smallest item is 1.
viz.foot: Maximises value delivered per unit of time
viz.cap: The formally correct order when urgency genuinely differs between items.

frameworks.one: Cost of delay divided by job size — the formally correct answer when you want maximum value delivered per unit of time.
frameworks.when: Items differ sharply in urgency rather than in value: seasonal windows, contractual dates, regulatory deadlines, competitive responses.
how: Estimate cost of delay from three parts: user/business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement.
Score each relatively — smallest item gets 1, others as multiples.
Estimate job size on the same relative scale.
Divide, sort descending.
Re-run when a date moves, because time criticality is the volatile term.
frameworks.with: Estimate cost of delay separately first, or time criticality inflates.

ex.h: Three items with very different urgency

viz.foot: cost of delay = value + time criticality + risk reduction

ex.cap: The regulatory item is small and dated. It goes first.
ex.p: On RICE the onboarding revamp ranked first. WSJF reordered it because the tax change had a statutory date and a fine attached, and the reporting API unblocked two other teams. Both facts were invisible to a model without an urgency term.

frameworks.out: A sequence that maximises value delivered over time rather than per item.
frameworks.trap: Time criticality is easy to inflate and hard to disprove, so everything becomes urgent. Ask what specifically changes on the date, and write it down.

frameworks.name: Cost of delay

curves.label: linear
curves.note: Steady loss. Waiting costs the same every week, so order it by size.

curves.label: fixed date
curves.note: A cliff. Almost all the value is behind one date — a season, a contract, a regulation.

curves.label: expedite
curves.note: Decays fast. If it does not go now, it is not worth doing.

viz.cap: Three shapes. The shape matters more than the number.

frameworks.one: What it costs you per week to not have this yet — the term that distinguishes work that can wait from work that decays.
frameworks.when: Two items look equally valuable and one has a deadline, a season, a contract or a competitor attached to it.
how: For each item, ask what changes if it lands three months later.
Classify the shape: linear (steady loss), fixed date (value drops off a cliff), or expedite (urgent and decaying fast).
Quantify per week where you can, even roughly — a range beats a shrug.
Note whether the cost is revenue, risk, cost avoidance or optionality.
Use it as a term in WSJF, or as a tiebreak.
frameworks.with: Feeds WSJF. On its own it is a tiebreak, never a ranking.

items: Full peak season. The only version where the business case holds.
Almost worthless until next year, and a year of maintenance in between.

ex.cap: A fixed-date shape, not a linear one.
ex.p: Framing it this way changed the decision from “is this worth building?” to “is this worth building by October?”. The answer was yes at reduced scope, and the team cut two of five sub-features rather than slipping.

frameworks.out: A per-week cost and a decay shape for each item.
frameworks.trap: Ignores effort entirely, so it cannot rank on its own. A high cost of delay on a two-year project is not a reason to start it this week.

frameworks.name: MoSCoW

items: Keep it under about 60% of capacity or you have no room to absorb anything.
The only bucket anyone remembers. Write it down and circulate it.
viz.cap: A scope tool for a fixed date. It says nothing about relative value.

frameworks.one: Sorts scope into four buckets against a fixed date, with the fourth bucket doing most of the work.
frameworks.when: A deadline is genuinely fixed — a launch, a contract, a regulation, an event — and the negotiation is about scope rather than order.
how: Define what happens if the date is missed; if nothing happens, use a different tool.
Must: without this, there is no point shipping. Be brutal — if everything is a must, nothing is.
Should: painful to omit, survivable.
Could: nice, first to go.
Won't: explicitly excluded this time, written down and communicated.
frameworks.who: PM, tech lead, and whoever owns the deadline
frameworks.with: Cost of delay to confirm the date is real before you start.

items: First pass had 24 Musts at 112% of capacity. Cutting to 12 took two hours and one escalation.

ex.cap: Must must fit inside about 60% of capacity.
ex.p: The first draft was undeliverable and everyone knew it privately. The forcing question was “if we shipped without this, would we be non-compliant?” — which is answerable. Twelve items were, and the release landed nine days early.

frameworks.out: Four labelled lists, and an agreed minimum viable scope.
frameworks.trap: Must lists that cover 90% of the work. A useful rule: Must should be under about 60% of capacity, or you have no room to absorb anything.

frameworks.name: Kano model

curves.label: must-be
curves.note: Absence causes damage that presence can never repay. Fix these first.

curves.label: performance
curves.note: More is linearly better. Invest here where you actually compete.

curves.label: attractive
curves.note: Delighters. High upside, and they decay into expectations within a few years.

viz.cap: Three response curves, three different investment logics.

frameworks.one: Classifies features by how satisfaction responds: basic expectations, linear performance features, and delighters.
frameworks.when: Choosing between table stakes and differentiation, or explaining why a beloved feature idea will not move any numbers.
how: Survey users with paired questions: how do you feel if this is present, and if it is absent?
Classify each feature: must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, or reverse.
Fix must-be gaps first — their absence causes damage that presence cannot repay.
Invest in performance features where you compete.
Add one or two delighters, knowing they decay into expectations within a few years.
frameworks.with: Opportunity scoring covers similar ground with less survey design.

items: Absence caused lost deals. Presence was never once mentioned as a positive.
Where the team competed, and where more genuinely was better.
Delight now. An expectation within two years, so priced in as temporary.

ex.cap: Three categories, three different investment logics.
ex.p: The roadmap had been treating all nine as equivalent features to rank. Reclassifying moved SSO and audit logging from “nice for enterprise” to “blocking every deal over 200 seats”, which reordered the whole quarter.

frameworks.out: Features sorted into categories with different investment logic for each.
frameworks.trap: Categories migrate. Every delighter becomes an expectation eventually, and a Kano study from three years ago will tell you to build something customers now assume.

frameworks.name: Eisenhower matrix

cells: Important, not urgent. The box that gets eaten, and the one that compounds.
Important and urgent. Also: ask why it became urgent.
Neither. Stop reporting on it as well.
Urgent but not important. Someone else, or a script.
viz.cap: If the top-right is full every week, the real problem is upstream.

frameworks.one: Two axes, four boxes: do, schedule, delegate, delete. A personal triage tool that also works on a chaotic backlog.
frameworks.when: The list is dominated by things that feel urgent, and important work keeps being displaced by it.
how: Place each item by urgency and importance, honestly.
Important and urgent: do now, and ask why it became urgent.
Important, not urgent: schedule it, and defend the slot.
Urgent, not important: delegate or automate it.
Neither: delete it, and stop reporting on it.
frameworks.with: If box one is always full, run a 5 Whys on why work becomes urgent.

ex.h: One PM week, hours by quadrant

cells: Strategy, discovery, writing. The first thing displaced every week.
Escalations and unblocking. Almost half the week, and most of it was preventable.
Two recurring meetings and a report nobody read.
Status updates and triage that a rota could own.

ex.cap: Four hours a week on the work that compounds.
ex.p: Logging a week honestly is the whole exercise. Nineteen hours of urgency traced back to two upstream causes — an unowned triage queue and a weekly report with no owner. Fixing those returned about eight hours a week.

frameworks.out: Four groups with different handling, and a visible measure of how much urgency you are absorbing.
frameworks.trap: Everything drifts into urgent-and-important because urgency is socially rewarded. If box one is full every week, the real problem is upstream.

frameworks.name: Weighted scoring

viz.foot: set the weights before you look at any option
viz.cap: Its integrity is entirely in the order: weights first, options second.

frameworks.one: Your own criteria with your own weights, applied consistently across options.
frameworks.when: The decision has several genuinely different dimensions — strategic fit, revenue, risk, effort, customer commitment — and no borrowed formula captures them.
how: Agree the criteria and their weights before seeing any options or scores.
Score each option per criterion on a fixed scale with defined anchors.
Multiply and sum.
Run a sensitivity check: change one weight and see whether the winner changes.
Publish the weights alongside the result.
frameworks.with: Cost-benefit on the winner before committing real money.

viz.foot: weights agreed before any option was scored

ex.cap: Three points apart, which is itself the finding.
ex.p: A near-tie meant the model could not decide it, and saying so was more useful than pretending. The conversation moved to the one criterion where the options genuinely diverged — strategic fit — and the decision was made explicitly on that, in writing.

frameworks.out: A transparent, auditable ranking that shows what your organisation values.
frameworks.trap: Weights tuned after the fact until a favourite wins. Setting them before you look at options is the entire integrity of the method.

frameworks.name: Opportunity scoring

cells: High importance, low satisfaction. This is the entire point of the exercise.
Important and already working. Protect it, do not invest in it.
Low importance, low satisfaction. Genuinely fine to leave.
You are spending on something people do not care much about.
viz.cap: Write the rows as outcomes in the customer’s language, never as features.

frameworks.one: Surveys users on how important an outcome is and how satisfied they are with it today; the gap is your opportunity.
frameworks.when: Choosing where to invest across a mature product and wanting evidence rather than internal opinion about which areas are underserved.
how: List desired outcomes in the customer's language, not features.
Survey importance and satisfaction for each, on the same scale.
Compute opportunity as importance plus the gap between importance and satisfaction.
Rank, and look for high importance with low satisfaction.
Segment the results — the top opportunity often differs sharply between segments.
frameworks.with: Follow the top opportunity into discovery interviews before designing anything.

items: Importance 9.1, satisfaction 4.4. The gap nobody had articulated.
Spot a problem within a day
High satisfaction already, and low importance. Two quarters of requests had been about this.

ex.cap: Outcomes in the customer’s words, never features.
ex.p: The request tracker had customisation as the top theme by volume. Scored against importance and satisfaction it came last. The winning outcome became a data-confidence feature that nobody had ever requested by name.

frameworks.out: A ranked list of underserved outcomes with evidence attached.
frameworks.trap: Writing outcomes as features. “A better dashboard” is not an outcome; “know within a minute whether today is going badly” is.

frameworks.name: Buy-a-feature

items: Funded first, and three people pooled coins to get it.
Bought by two enterprise participants immediately.
Everyone wanted it. Nobody would pay for it.
The reasoning in the debrief is the real output.
viz.cap: A budget forces trades. A survey lets people approve everything.

frameworks.one: Give people a fixed budget and price the options, so they have to trade rather than approve everything.
frameworks.when: Stakeholders or customers keep saying yes to every item. Works as well internally with executives as it does with customers.
how: Pick eight to twelve candidate items and price them roughly by effort.
Give each participant a budget covering perhaps a third of the total.
Let them buy individually, then allow pooling for expensive items.
Record what got bought, what got argued over, and what nobody funded.
Debrief on the reasoning — that is the actual output.
frameworks.with: Great before a MoSCoW when stakeholders will not accept a Won’t list.

items: Four people pooled to afford it. The pooling conversation was the most useful part.
Requested in writing by three of the people who then refused to fund it.

ex.cap: The debrief matters more than the tally.
ex.p: Themes had been on the roadmap for two quarters because everyone said yes when asked. Given a budget, nobody spent on it. The reasoning — “I would use it, I would not pay for it” — is the distinction a survey cannot draw.

frameworks.out: A funded shortlist, and a clear picture of what people will trade away.
frameworks.trap: Treating the result as a vote. It is a structured conversation about trade-offs; the reasoning matters more than the tally.

frameworks.name: OKRs

root: Objective: trial users reach value in one session
Qualitative, memorable, and it says what will be different rather than what will be done.
kids: A number with a baseline. Somebody could look at this and say you missed.
Two or three key results. Four means nothing was chosen.
Chosen because it can embarrass the objective.
viz.cap: If you could hit every key result and no customer noticed, they are deliverables.

frameworks.one: A qualitative objective with two or three measurable key results, set for a quarter or a year, scored honestly at the end.
frameworks.when: You need several teams pointed at the same outcome without prescribing their plans. Poor for routine operational work, which belongs in KPIs.
how: Objective: what will be different, in plain language, ambitious and memorable.
Key results: two or three outcome metrics, each with a baseline and a target.
Check none of them is a list of deliverables in disguise.
Add at least one counter-metric so the objective cannot be gamed.
Score at the end, publicly, and write what you learned rather than defending the number.
frameworks.time: Half a day to draft, 2 hours to review
frameworks.with: Metric tree to find candidate key results; KPIs for anything you are only maintaining.

viz.note: Scored 0.73. Missing an ambitious OKR is normal; the number is information, not a verdict.
viz.cap: Baseline, target, actual. All three published.

ex.p: Two of three key results landed; the counter-metric held flat, which mattered because the obvious way to hit the number would have degraded it. Publishing a 0.73 rather than reframing the target is what made the next quarter's forecast believable.

frameworks.out: A short, public, scoreable commitment owned by a named person.
frameworks.trap: Key results that are really a project plan (“launch X, ship Y”). If you could hit them all and nothing improved for a customer, they are outputs.

frameworks.name: KPIs vs OKRs

items: Numbers you keep healthy. They get alerts, not ambitions.
Numbers you are deliberately trying to change. Attention is the scarce resource.
viz.cap: Fourteen goals allocate no attention at all.

frameworks.one: KPIs are the numbers you always watch. OKRs are the small set you are deliberately trying to change this period.
frameworks.when: Whenever a goal-setting exercise has produced fourteen items — most of them are KPIs that were never supposed to be goals.
how: List every number currently called a goal.
Ask of each: are we trying to change this, or keep it healthy?
Keep-healthy numbers become KPIs with thresholds and alerts.
Change numbers become key results with baselines and targets.
Cap the second list at three per team.
frameworks.with: Do this before any OKR-setting session, or you will draft fourteen goals.

items: Uptime, latency, ticket volume, churn. Watched, not chased.
Only these got roadmap capacity. The other eleven stopped appearing in planning.

ex.cap: One question per number: changing it, or keeping it healthy?
ex.p: The team had been reporting fourteen numbers monthly and moving none of them. Splitting the list took an hour and freed most of the planning conversation, because eleven of the fourteen simply needed a threshold and an alert.

frameworks.out: A dashboard of KPIs and a very short list of OKRs.
frameworks.trap: Promoting every KPI to a goal each quarter. Attention is the scarce resource, and fourteen goals allocate none of it.

frameworks.name: North Star framework

root: Value received by customers, with a time window. Not revenue.
kids: One team, one input, one baseline.
Tested for causation, not just correlation.
The input that quietly decides everything.
viz.cap: One metric, a handful of owned inputs, and a chain you can argue with.

frameworks.one: One metric representing value delivered, with a small set of inputs that drive it and a team behind each input.
frameworks.when: Multiple teams need to see how their work connects to one outcome, and you keep getting local optimisation instead.
how: Define the North Star as value received by customers, with a time window.
Identify three to five inputs that provably move it.
Assign each input to a team, with its own baseline.
Add counter-metrics at the North Star level.
Review monthly: which input moved, and did the North Star follow?
frameworks.time: 1–2 days, plus a month to validate
frameworks.who: PM, analyst, and the leads who will own inputs
frameworks.with: Metric tree to build it; A/B testing to prove an input is causal rather than correlated.

ex.h: A marketplace, with the inputs owned

root: Replaced total registered users, which had grown 212% while this grew 6%.

ex.cap: One metric, four owned inputs, each with a baseline.
ex.p: Within a quarter the roadmap was unrecognisable: an incentivised referral scheme was cut and the account wall came down. Match rate was deliberately paired with post-match cancellation so that “matching more” could not be achieved by matching badly.

frameworks.out: One metric, a handful of owned inputs, and a visible causal chain.
frameworks.trap: Inputs that are correlated with the North Star but not causal. Test each one by asking what happens if you move it deliberately and nothing else changes.

frameworks.name: Metric tree

viz.foot: if the parts do not multiply out, it cannot diagnose anything
viz.cap: When the top number moves, the tree tells you which branch did it.

frameworks.one: An arithmetic decomposition of one metric into the parts that multiply or add to produce it.
frameworks.when: A number moved and nobody can say why, or you need to find where a team could actually intervene.
how: Write the top metric and decompose it into terms that genuinely reconstruct it.
Keep decomposing until each leaf is something a team could move this quarter.
Attach current values so the arithmetic checks out.
Use it as a diagnostic: when the top moves, find the branch responsible.
Revisit the structure yearly; business models change shape.
frameworks.with: North Star framework to assign owners; A/B testing to move a leaf.

parts: Traffic was slightly up, which is why the drop was confusing.
The branch that did it. Reorder rate had fallen after a delivery change.
viz.foot: the arithmetic reconciles, so it can diagnose

ex.cap: Four branches, one culprit.
ex.p: Two weeks of debate had focused on conversion and acquisition because those are the numbers people watch. The tree located the drop in reorder frequency in under an hour, and traced it to a delivery-window change shipped six weeks earlier.

frameworks.out: A tree whose arithmetic reconstructs the top metric, with owned leaves.
frameworks.trap: A tree of loosely related KPIs that does not actually multiply out. If the numbers do not reconcile, it cannot diagnose anything.

frameworks.name: DACI

items: One person, and not necessarily the most senior one.
Two approvers is the situation you were trying to fix.
Consultation is not a veto. Say so explicitly.
Publish the decision, or it gets re-opened next month.
viz.cap: Four roles for one decision. The scarce one is a single approver.

frameworks.one: Names four roles for a specific decision so that “who decides this?” stops being the reason it takes three weeks.
frameworks.when: A decision is stuck, or several people believe they own it, or a group keeps re-opening something already settled.
how: Write the decision as a question with options.
Driver: one person who runs the process and sets the deadline.
Approver: exactly one person who decides. Not a committee.
Contributors: people whose expertise is needed, with a stated deadline for input.
Informed: people who need to know afterwards. Publish the decision and the reasoning.
frameworks.with: RAPID instead when vetoes are real and cross-functional.

items: Ran the process, set a Friday deadline, wrote the options.
One name. Previously three people each believed they held this.
Input due Wednesday. Stated explicitly as input, not veto.
Told afterwards, with the reasoning, so it stayed decided.

ex.cap: Five weeks stuck, six days to a decision.
ex.p: Nothing about the pricing analysis changed. The decision had been re-opened four times because two executives each believed they were the approver, and each conversation started from scratch. Naming one approver ended it in a week.

frameworks.out: A named approver, a date, and a written decision with its rationale.
frameworks.trap: Two approvers, which is the situation you were trying to fix. Also: contributors mistaking consultation for a veto.

frameworks.name: RAPID

items: Keep this list short and justified by a specific accountability, never by seniority.
Involve them before the decision, not after it.
viz.cap: Its value is naming vetoes up front instead of meeting them in week six.

frameworks.one: Bain's decision-rights model, separating who recommends from who must agree, who will do the work, and who decides.
frameworks.when: Cross-functional decisions in larger organisations, where “agree” is a real constraint — legal, security, finance can veto rather than merely advise.
how: Recommend: who builds the proposal and drives it.
Agree: who holds a genuine veto, and on what grounds. Keep this list short and explicit.
Input: who is consulted, without a veto.
Decide: one person.
Perform: who executes once decided — involve them before, not after.
frameworks.who: Sponsor + the functions with real vetoes
frameworks.with: DACI is lighter and usually enough below about 200 people.

items: Two genuine vetoes, named up front. Previously they appeared in week six and reset the process.
Consulted before the decision, not handed it afterwards.

ex.cap: Naming vetoes early is the whole value.
ex.p: The previous vendor selection had reached contract stage before security raised a data-residency objection that eliminated the chosen option. Listing the two real vetoes at the start cut the second process from eleven weeks to four.

frameworks.out: Explicit decision rights, with vetoes named up front instead of appearing late.
frameworks.trap: An “agree” list that grows until nothing moves. Every veto should be justified by a specific accountability, not by seniority.

frameworks.name: Cost-benefit analysis

viz.note: Present ranges, not points, and name the two assumptions that dominate everything.
viz.cap: If the pessimistic case still works, you have an answer rather than a spreadsheet.

frameworks.one: Totals the quantifiable costs and benefits of an option over a defined period, usually with the assumptions doing all the work.
frameworks.when: A single significant investment decision needs a defensible economic case — a build-versus-buy, a platform migration, a major hire.
how: Set the time horizon and be explicit about it.
List costs: build, run, opportunity, migration, training, decommissioning.
List benefits: revenue, cost avoided, risk reduced, time saved — with sources.
Present ranges, not points, and state the two or three assumptions that dominate.
Run the pessimistic case; if it still works, you have an answer.
frameworks.with: Expected value when the risk profiles differ; feasibility study if delivery is uncertain.

ex.h: Build versus buy, three years, pessimistic case

viz.note: Build was +£210k in the base case and −£40k pessimistic, because the dominant assumption was two engineers staying.
viz.cap: Ranges, and the assumption that dominates.

ex.p: The base case favoured building by a wide margin. Running the pessimistic case exposed that the whole advantage rested on retaining two specific engineers for three years. Stated that plainly, the decision changed in one meeting.

frameworks.out: A range for net benefit, with the dominant assumptions visible.
frameworks.trap: Precision as persuasion. A single number to two decimal places from six estimates is less honest than a range, and much easier to attack once one input is questioned.

frameworks.name: Expected value / decision tree

kids: Four in five. Ask whether you can survive this outcome.
viz.cap: Expected value assumes many attempts. Check the downside separately.

frameworks.one: Multiplies each outcome by its probability and sums, so a risky option can be compared with a safe one on the same scale.
frameworks.when: Choosing between options with genuinely different risk profiles — a bet with a 20% chance of a large payoff versus a certain small one.
how: Draw the decision, then the possible outcomes of each branch.
Assign a value and a probability to each outcome; state where the probability came from.
Multiply and sum per branch.
Check the downside separately — expected value ignores whether you can survive the bad case.
Test how wrong a probability would have to be to change the answer.
frameworks.who: 2–3, one of whom challenges the probabilities
frameworks.with: Always look at the downside separately. Pre-mortem if the downside is severe.

kids: Cash runway is £1.4M. The 80% branch is close to fatal.
Lower ceiling, and the company still exists in the 80% case.

ex.cap: Expected value assumes you get repeated attempts.
ex.p: The bet was the obvious answer on the arithmetic and the wrong answer for this company. Checking survivability separately from expected value is what made that visible — and the same bet would have been correct with two years of runway.

frameworks.out: Comparable values per option, plus an explicit view of the downside.
frameworks.trap: Expected value assumes you get many attempts. For a company-threatening downside, the arithmetic is right and the decision is still wrong.

frameworks.name: Now / Next / Later

items: Committed, in progress, specific. Dates only where a real deadline exists.
Agreed problems and outcomes, ordered, no dates.
Directional themes, explicitly uncertain. Not a graveyard for quiet no’s.
viz.cap: The fading precision is the honest signal, not a weakness.

frameworks.one: Three horizons with deliberately decreasing precision, so a plan can communicate intent without pretending to certainty.
frameworks.when: Communicating a plan to stakeholders who want dates, in a world that changes faster than your planning horizon.
how: Now: committed, in progress, specific, with dates only where a real deadline exists.
Next: agreed problems and outcomes, no dates, ordered.
Later: directional themes, explicitly uncertain.
Attach an outcome and a baseline to each item rather than a feature name.
Move items between horizons openly at a fixed review cadence.
frameworks.with: Outcome-based roadmapping; OKRs for the outcomes each theme should move.

zones: In flight, specific, one real deadline among the four.
Stated as outcomes, ordered, no dates. Two moved to Now mid-quarter without an apology.
Direction only. Two were later dropped, which was the point of not dating them.

ex.cap: Precision fades with distance, deliberately.
ex.p: The previous roadmap had eighteen dated items twelve months out, and the team spent review meetings defending slippage. Three horizons moved the conversation to whether the outcomes were the right ones — and two Later themes were dropped without a crisis.

frameworks.out: A roadmap that can change without anybody needing to apologise.
frameworks.trap: “Later” as a graveyard for things you have decided not to do. If it is a no, say no — otherwise you have created a queue of false hope.

quiz.q: Your team scores everything with RICE and consistently ships small things. What fixes it?
o: Better effort estimates
Higher impact scores on big items
Deciding capacity allocation first, then ranking within buckets
Switching to ICE
quiz.e: Dividing by effort means cheap and certain items win structurally, no matter how good your estimates are. Allocation — deciding in advance that, say, 60% of capacity serves this quarter's outcome — is what stops efficiency outranking strategy. Then score inside each bucket.

quiz.q: When is MoSCoW the right tool rather than RICE?
o: When you have many comparable items and need an order
When a date is genuinely fixed and the negotiation is about scope
When items differ in urgency
When stakeholders keep saying yes to everything
quiz.e: MoSCoW answers “what fits before the date”, not “what is most valuable”. It only works when missing the date has a real consequence — otherwise Must expands to cover everything. The urgency case is WSJF, and the say-yes-to-everything case is buy-a-feature.

quiz.q: A key result reads: “Launch the new onboarding flow and ship the checklist.” What is wrong with it?
o: It is not ambitious enough
It has two items in one
It measures output, not outcome — you could do both and improve nothing
Nothing, it is specific and measurable
quiz.e: Shipping is the plan, not the result. A key result should be a number with a baseline that only moves if something got better for a customer — “activation from 41% to 55%”. If you could hit every key result and no customer noticed, they are deliverables in disguise.

quiz.q: A decision has been re-opened three times in a month. Which framework addresses that directly?
o: RICE
DACI or RAPID
Kano
Cost of delay
quiz.e: Repeated re-opening is a decision-rights problem: nobody is unambiguously the approver, so every conversation is a fresh opportunity. DACI and RAPID fix it by naming exactly one decider up front, distinguishing consultation from veto, and publishing the decision with its reasoning.

quiz.q: A bet has a 20% chance of a $10M payoff and would cost $1M. Expected value says take it. When is that wrong?
o: Never — the arithmetic is the arithmetic
When losing the $1M would threaten the company, because expected value assumes repeated attempts
When the probability came from a survey
When the payoff is over three years
quiz.e: Expected value is the right answer over many independent attempts. For a one-shot decision where the downside is existential, a positive expected value can still be a bad bet — which is why you examine the downside separately rather than only comparing the sums.

sections.h: One truck, a yard full of pallets.
sections.lede: Every framework here does the same underlying job: it makes the basis of a choice visible so the decision can be argued with on its merits rather than settled by whoever is most senior or most tired. None of them will tell you the answer, and the ones that look most like arithmetic are the ones to be most careful with.

panel.big: A score locates the disagreement. It does not settle it.
items: Set weights and allocation before you look at the options.
If everything is a Must, nothing is.
Name exactly one approver, or the decision will be re-opened monthly.

sections.lede: These frameworks get used interchangeably and they are not interchangeable. Each answers one question, and using the wrong one is how prioritisation acquired its reputation.
sections.statement: Any model that turns four guesses into one confident number has hidden three arguments you needed to have.

cards.p: RICE, ICE, WSJF, weighted scoring, opportunity scoring. All comparative, all sensitive to the assumptions you feed them, all blind to strategy unless you constrain them with allocation.
MoSCoW against a fixed date, Kano for table stakes versus delight, Eisenhower when urgency is eating importance, buy-a-feature when nobody will trade.

cards.k: What are we trying to change?
cards.p: OKRs for the few things you are changing, KPIs for the many you are keeping healthy, North Star and metric trees to connect a team's work to an outcome.
DACI and RAPID for decision rights, cost-benefit for a single investment, expected value when the risk profiles genuinely differ.

sections.lede: Filter by family, then click any card for when to reach for it, the steps, the artefact, and the specific way it goes wrong.

sections.h: Grade an OKR in thirty seconds
sections.lede: Eight checks that separate a commitment from a slogan. Tick what is honestly true of an OKR you are actually working with — yours, or your team's.

sections.h: If this is your situation, start here
sections.lede: The shortest route from a stuck conversation to a tool.
rows: Allocation buckets, then RICE within each
Interrogate confidence on the biggest items
Fixed launch date, too much scope
Write the “Won't” list and circulate it
A Must list larger than 60% of capacity
Some items have deadlines, others don't
Inflated time criticality with no stated trigger
Debrief the reasoning, not the tally
Treating the result as a vote
Cap at three key results per team
Assign one input metric per team
Inputs that correlate but do not cause
RAPID if vetoes are real and cross-functional
A risky bet against a safe option
One-shot decisions with an existential loss
sections.foot: Pick one model per list and use it for the whole list. Switching instruments item by item is how a favourite ends up with a favourable measurement.

sections.lede: One attempt each, with an explanation either way.

title: Frameworks — Structure, Measure & Change
one: Structuring a problem, measuring experience, mapping the people, and making a change actually stick.

frameworks.name: CIRCLES Method

items: Product, users, constraints, why now. Be brisk.
Pick one persona and one need, and say why. Half the marks are here.
Three or four genuinely different ones, not variations.
Against criteria you stated before you saw the options.
A recommendation, and how you would measure it.
viz.cap: Seven steps, unequal weight. Cut and Evaluate carry the thinking.

frameworks.one: Seven steps for answering an open product question out loud without missing anything obvious: Comprehend, Identify, Report, Cut, List, Evaluate, Summarise.
frameworks.when: Product design interviews, and genuinely useful for structuring a first pass at a vague brief — “what should we do about retention?”
how: Comprehend the situation: what is the product, who uses it, what constraints exist, why now.
Identify the customer: pick specific personas rather than “users”.
Report their needs as jobs or job stories, in their language.
Cut through prioritisation: choose one persona and one need, and say why.
List solutions — three or four genuinely different ones, not variations.
Evaluate trade-offs against stated criteria, then Summarise with a recommendation and how you would measure it.
frameworks.with: JTBD for the needs step; GSM for the measurement you promise at the end.

ex.h: “Design a feature for a food delivery app”

items: Marketplace, three sides, growth-stage, mobile-first. Constraints stated, then move on.
Chose two of five personas: the courier and the late-evening solo orderer.
Three job stories, in their words, with triggers.
One persona, one need, and said why the other four wait. Half the marks are here.
Three genuinely different solutions, not three versions of one.
Against criteria stated before the options.
A recommendation and the metric that would prove it.

ex.cap: Unequal time on purpose. Cut and Evaluate carry it.
ex.p: The commonest failure is spending twelve minutes on Comprehend and ninety seconds on Cut. Interviewers are listening for whether you can choose and defend a choice — everything before Cut is context-setting.

frameworks.out: A structured recommendation with the reasoning and the trade-offs visible.
frameworks.trap: Performing all seven steps at equal length. Cut and Evaluate are where the thinking is; Comprehend and Report should be brisk.

frameworks.name: Jobs to be Done

items: Specific and actionable, and the only layer most teams ever hear.
The situation — every Monday I rebuild the same table
Where frequency, cost and emotion live. Only reachable by asking about the last time.
The job — my manager trusts the number without me
Change the solution freely at this layer. It is usually cheaper down here.
viz.cap: Three layers. Feature requests are written from the top one.

frameworks.one: Frames demand around the progress someone is trying to make in a situation, rather than around demographics or features.
frameworks.when: You keep hearing feature requests and want to find the underlying goal, or you are trying to work out who you actually compete with.
how: Interview around a specific recent purchase or behaviour change, and reconstruct the timeline.
Identify the trigger, the struggle, the alternatives considered and the anxieties.
Write the job as: when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].
List the current alternatives, including spreadsheets and doing nothing — these are your real competitors.
Design against the job, and check whether your solution reduces the anxieties too.
frameworks.with: Discovery interviewing to gather it; opportunity scoring to size the jobs you find.

items: The request, from 22 support conversations. Specific, unanimous, and a workaround.
“I spend an hour making it look considered”
The situation. Triggered by a birthday, with a deadline and real anxiety about effort showing.
“They should know I made an effort”
The job. Competing with a handwritten card, not with other printing apps.

ex.cap: Three layers. The competitor set changes at the bottom.
ex.p: Reframing at the job layer produced an auto-layout that assembled a considered-looking book in four minutes, plus a printed note in the sender's handwriting font. Neither had ever been requested. Completion rate rose from 34% to 58%.

frameworks.out: Job statements with triggers, alternatives and anxieties attached.
frameworks.trap: Writing job stories from your desk. Without the interviews they are just user stories with better grammar.

frameworks.name: Working Backwards

items: One page, plain language, dated at launch, naming the customer and the problem.
What customers will ask, including price and what it does not do.
Unit economics, dependencies, why now, why us, what could fail.
Only once it has survived several rounds of demolition.
viz.cap: If the internal FAQ has no uncomfortable answers, it has not been written.

frameworks.one: Write the press release and the FAQ for a finished product before building anything, then work backwards to what would have to be true.
frameworks.when: A large, ambiguous initiative where the team is arguing about implementation before agreeing what success looks like.
how: Write a one-page press release in plain language, dated at launch, naming the customer and the problem.
Write the external FAQ: what customers will ask, including price and limitations.
Write the internal FAQ: the hard questions — unit economics, dependencies, why now, why us, what could fail.
Circulate, and expect several rounds of demolition.
Only after it survives, plan the work backwards from it.
frameworks.with: Feasibility study on whatever the internal FAQ exposes as uncertain.

ex.h: A PR/FAQ that killed its own project

items: Written in an afternoon. Read well, and everyone liked it.
Price surfaced the first problem: the obvious price was below the support cost.
Unit economics negative beyond about 400 accounts. This is where it died.
Six weeks saved, and one genuine insight kept.

ex.cap: The internal FAQ is the part that has to hurt.
ex.p: Two questions ended it: what does this cost to serve per account, and why has nobody done it? Answering them honestly took four days and prevented two quarters of work. The team kept one finding and shipped a much smaller version a year later.

frameworks.out: A narrative document that forces agreement on the customer and the outcome first.
frameworks.trap: The internal FAQ being where honesty goes to die. If it does not contain at least three uncomfortable answers, it has not been written properly.

frameworks.name: Double Diamond

labels: Diverge on the problem. Research, data, alternatives, and no solutions yet.
Converge on one clearly stated problem worth solving.
Diverge on solutions. Several genuinely different ones.
viz.cap: The commonest failure is starting in the third phase.

frameworks.one: Two cycles of diverge-then-converge: first on the problem, then on the solution.
frameworks.when: Framing a piece of work at the start, and especially for explaining to stakeholders why you are not designing yet.
how: Discover: diverge on the problem space — research, data, alternatives.
Define: converge on one clearly stated problem worth solving.
Develop: diverge on solutions, several genuinely different ones.
Deliver: converge on one, build, test, iterate.
Guard the boundary between diamonds — the commonest failure is starting in Develop.
frameworks.with: Design sprint to compress the second diamond into a week.

ex.h: A reporting redesign, with the first diamond held open

labels: Interviews and log analysis. No designs allowed, which was the hard part.
One sentence: people cannot tell whether today is going badly.
Three different answers: a digest email, a single status view, an alert.
The status view won on testing, and shipped.

ex.cap: Four weeks before anyone drew a screen.
ex.p: The original brief was “redesign the reports page”, which assumes the answer. Holding the first diamond open produced a problem statement that made two of the three candidate solutions cheaper than a redesign — and the winner was not a report at all.

frameworks.out: A stated problem, then a chosen solution, with the divergence visible in between.
frameworks.trap: A single diamond in practice: teams skip the first divergence entirely and spend all their creativity on solutions to an unexamined problem.

frameworks.name: Design sprint

items: Map the problem, pick a target
With the decider in the room, or do not start.
Individually and silently, before any discussion.
A facade that looks real. Not a product.
Booked before day one. Then decide what you now believe.
viz.cap: Five days, six people, one tested decision.

frameworks.one: A five-day structured process from problem to tested prototype with real users at the end of the week.
frameworks.when: A significant, uncertain decision where the team is stuck, and you can genuinely clear five days for the right six people.
how: Day 1: map the problem and pick a target.
Day 2: sketch competing solutions individually.
Day 3: decide, and storyboard one.
Day 4: build a realistic-looking prototype — a facade, not a product.
Day 5: test with five target users and decide what you now believe.
frameworks.with: Only worth it on a decision that is genuinely stuck and genuinely important.

ex.h: A pricing page, in five days

items: Target: the moment a self-serve buyer decides which tier they are.
Six people, six solutions, silently. Two were unlike anything discussed before.
Decider chose a usage-calculator approach and storyboarded it.
Clickable facade. No real pricing logic behind it at all.
Five target buyers. Four self-selected correctly; one could not find annual billing.

ex.cap: A tested decision by Friday afternoon.
ex.p: Four months of internal disagreement about tier structure ended in a week, because the argument moved from opinions to watching five buyers try. The calculator shipped a month later and mis-tier support tickets fell by roughly two-thirds.

frameworks.out: A tested prototype and a documented decision, in a week.
frameworks.trap: Running it without a decider present, or without the five users booked before day one. Both turn it into an expensive workshop.

frameworks.name: AARRR

items: Healthy. Adding more here just makes the leak below it wetter.
The worst conversion. Every stage below inherits it.
viz.cap: Find the worst conversion, fix it, then re-measure. The bottleneck moves.

frameworks.one: A funnel of five stages — Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral — used to locate where growth is actually leaking.
frameworks.when: Growth is flat and the team is arguing about which end of the funnel to work on. Best used to find the worst conversion, not as a reporting template.
how: Define one metric per stage, with a precise denominator.
Measure the conversion between consecutive stages, not just the absolute numbers.
Find the worst conversion relative to a sensible benchmark for your model.
Fix that one before spending on the stage above it.
Re-measure; the bottleneck moves once you fix it.
frameworks.with: Metric tree for the level below; A/B testing to fix the leak you find.

ex.h: A fitness app, stage by stage

items: The leak. Two thirds of sign-ups never reached the thing the product does.

ex.cap: Activation, not acquisition, was the constraint.
ex.p: Paid acquisition was about to double. Doing this first showed that spend would have bought more people to lose at the same step. A guided first workout took activation from 21% to 38%, which was worth more than the entire planned budget increase.

frameworks.out: Five stage conversions and one identified bottleneck.
frameworks.trap: Pouring money into Acquisition while Activation leaks. More traffic through a broken funnel just makes the leak bigger, and it flatters the vanity numbers while doing it.

frameworks.name: HEART framework

items: Self-selected responders, and it moves with mood. Handle with care.
Pair it with time on task, or you reward people struggling for longer.
viz.cap: Pick two or three. Using all five means you have not chosen.

frameworks.one: Five categories of user-experience metric — Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success — designed to be paired with goals and signals.
frameworks.when: You need to measure the quality of an experience rather than the volume of it, and “satisfaction” keeps being asserted rather than measured.
how: Pick two or three categories that matter for this feature; using all five is a sign you have not chosen.
For each, define the Goal, then the Signal (an observable behaviour), then the Metric (the ratio you will track).
Prefer ratios to counts, so growth does not flatter you.
Set a baseline before you change anything.
Pair task success with time on task, or you will optimise for people struggling for longer.
frameworks.with: GSM is the engine inside it. Use HEART to choose which categories matter.

ex.h: A new editor, three categories only

viz.foot: task success paired with median time on task

ex.cap: Three of five. Using all five means not choosing.
ex.p: Task success alone rose from 81% to 89% — and median time on task rose 40% at the same time, meaning people were grinding through a worse experience. The pairing caught it before launch, and the fix was a default nobody had questioned.

frameworks.out: Two or three GSM rows with baselines you can actually track.
frameworks.trap: Measuring Happiness with an in-app survey and treating a 4.2 as a fact. Survey responders are a self-selected minority and satisfaction scores move with mood.

frameworks.name: Goals-Signals-Metrics

items: What should be different for the user, in one sentence.
The observable behaviour that would change if it worked — and if it did not.
The exact ratio: numerator, denominator, window.
viz.cap: Skipping the middle is how teams end up measuring whatever the tool already tracks.

frameworks.one: The engine inside HEART: state the goal, name the observable behaviour that indicates it, then define the exact metric.
frameworks.when: Any time someone asks you to measure something abstract — quality, delight, trust, confidence, ease.
how: Goal: what should be different for the user, in one sentence.
Signal: what behaviour would change if the goal were met — and what would change if it were not.
Metric: the precise ratio, with numerator, denominator and window.
Sanity-check: could this metric improve while the goal got worse?
Write down the counter-signal too.
frameworks.with: Use inside HEART, or any time someone asks you to measure something abstract.

items: People share externally without worrying who can see it.
They stop opening permissions afterwards to check, and stop using expiring links defensively.
Post-share permission checks per share, plus share-to-revoke rate within 24h.

ex.cap: The counter-signal was written down too.
ex.p: “Feels safe” had been asserted in three reviews and measured in none. Naming the behaviour first produced two numbers already in the data. Revocations within a day fell 44% after a permissions preview, which nobody would have thought to measure.

frameworks.out: A three-column table linking an abstract goal to a concrete number.
frameworks.trap: Skipping Signals and jumping from a goal straight to whatever your analytics tool already tracks.

frameworks.name: Stakeholder mapping

cells: High power, low interest. Neglected because they ask for nothing — until a surprise makes them interested.
Regular, direct, individual. Usually already in your calendar.
Low power, high interest. Often your most useful allies.
viz.cap: Map people, not job titles, and redraw it when the org changes.

frameworks.one: Plots everyone affected by your work on two axes — how much power they have, how much they care — to decide how to engage each.
frameworks.when: Before any change that crosses team boundaries, and at the start of any role in a new organisation.
how: List everyone affected, including people who will only be affected indirectly.
Place each by power over your outcome and interest in it.
High power, high interest: manage closely — regular, direct, individual.
High power, low interest: keep satisfied, briefly and reliably; do not surprise them.
Low power, high interest: keep informed, they are often your best allies. Low/low: monitor.
Re-draw it when the org changes, because it always changes.
frameworks.with: Salience model when many groups compete; comms plan to turn it into a cadence.

cells: High power, low interest. They asked for nothing for six weeks, then asked everything at once.
Weekly, direct, individual. Already in the calendar.
Low power, high interest, and the best allies in the process.

ex.cap: The top-left quadrant is where launches die.
ex.p: A fortnightly three-line note to the CFO and GC — total effort perhaps ten minutes — meant the migration plan was already familiar when it needed sign-off. The previous pricing change had lost three weeks to a late legal objection.

frameworks.out: A grid with a named engagement approach per person or group.
frameworks.trap: Mapping job titles instead of people, and never updating it. Also: a private map that reads as cynical if it leaks — write it as you would defend it.

frameworks.name: Salience model

items: Does it need attention now? The fastest-changing of the three.
viz.cap: More discriminating than two axes when many groups compete for attention.

frameworks.one: Classifies stakeholders by three attributes — power, legitimacy and urgency — which is more discriminating than two axes when many groups compete for attention.
frameworks.when: Large programmes with many stakeholder groups, or when you need to justify why one loud group is not getting priority.
how: For each stakeholder, assess power, legitimacy of claim, and urgency.
Those with all three are definitive stakeholders: they get priority.
Those with two are expectant: they need active management.
Those with one are latent: monitor, respond if attributes change.
Note that urgency changes fastest — re-check it, not the whole model.
frameworks.with: Use after a power/interest map when the map has fifteen groups on it.

items: The one team with a hard external deadline
viz.cap: Three groups got priority, and it was defensible.

ex.p: One extremely vocal internal group had urgency and no legitimate claim — their deadline was self-imposed. Being able to say that out loud, with a framework behind it, is what let the programme deprioritise them without a political fight.

frameworks.out: A tiered stakeholder list with a defensible reason for each tier.
frameworks.trap: Confusing loudness with urgency. A group can be extremely noisy with no legitimate claim, and quietly essential with no volume at all.

frameworks.name: RACI

viz.foot: exactly one A per row — if you cannot pick one, that is the finding
viz.cap: Build one only for the handful of things currently being dropped or fought over.

frameworks.one: A grid of tasks against people, marking who does the work, who is answerable, who is consulted and who is told.
frameworks.when: Work spans several teams and things are being dropped at the boundaries, or two people believe they own the same thing.
how: List the deliverables or decisions down one side, the people across the top.
Exactly one A per row. If you cannot pick one, that is the finding.
R can be several people; A cannot.
Keep C short — consultation is expensive and easily mistaken for a veto.
Circulate it and let people object to their own cell; silence is not agreement.
frameworks.with: DACI for one-off decisions; RACI for recurring deliverables.

ex.h: A release process that kept dropping things

viz.foot: the rollback row had no owner at all before this

ex.cap: Four rows, because only four things were breaking.
ex.p: Rollback had been everyone's and nobody's, which is why one incident ran 46 minutes. Naming a single accountable engineer per row took half an hour. Nobody built a RACI for the other thirty release tasks, and nothing needed it.

frameworks.out: A grid with a single accountable person per row, agreed by the people in it.
frameworks.trap: A RACI for everything, which nobody reads. Build one only for the handful of things currently being dropped or fought over.

frameworks.name: Communication plan

viz.foot: bad news uses the same channel and cadence as good news
viz.cap: A cadence you can sustain beats an ambitious one that goes quiet.

frameworks.one: Who hears what, how often, through which channel, from whom — decided once so it is not improvised weekly.
frameworks.when: Any programme longer than a few weeks with stakeholders outside your immediate team.
how: For each stakeholder group, note what they need to know and what decisions they influence.
Choose a cadence and a channel per group — weekly written, monthly forum, quarterly deep dive.
Standardise the format so it is skimmable and comparable week to week.
Include bad news in the same channel as good news, at the same cadence.
Ask, after a month, which parts anyone actually reads, and cut the rest.
frameworks.with: Build it directly from a stakeholder map so the cadence matches the quadrant.

viz.foot: same channel and cadence for bad news as for good

ex.cap: Four rows, sustained for six months without a miss.
ex.p: The previous programme had a weekly all-hands update that became fortnightly, then stopped in month three — and the silence was read as trouble. A smaller cadence that never slipped generated far more trust than an ambitious one that decayed.

frameworks.out: A small table of audience, message, channel, cadence, owner.
frameworks.trap: A cadence you cannot sustain. A weekly update that becomes fortnightly, then silent, does more damage than a monthly one that never misses.

frameworks.name: ADKAR

items: Do they know why? Communicate the reason, not the plan.
Do they want to? Where most changes fail, and never fixed by more training.
Do they know how? Training, docs, examples.
Can they do it in real conditions, under real pressure?
What makes it stick? Defaults, incentives, removing the old path.
viz.cap: Diagnose which state is blocking before choosing an intervention.

frameworks.one: Five sequential states each individual must pass through for a change to stick: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
frameworks.when: Rolling out a change that requires people to work differently — a new tool, process, or way of planning. Diagnostic as much as prescriptive.
how: Awareness: do they know why the change is happening? Communicate the reason, not the plan.
Desire: do they want to participate? This is where most changes fail, and it is about what is in it for them.
Knowledge: do they know how? Training, documentation, examples.
Ability: can they actually do it in their real conditions? Practice, support, time.
Reinforcement: what makes it stick? Incentives, defaults, removing the old path.
frameworks.with: Force field analysis on the state that is blocking, especially if it is Desire.

ex.h: A new planning process, by state

items: Everyone knew why. Three all-hands had covered it.
Three training sessions. This was never the problem.
The blocker. Planning added four hours a fortnight to people already at capacity.
And nothing made the new way easier than the old way.

ex.cap: Two low bars, and neither is fixed by training.
ex.p: The instinct after resistance was a fourth training session. Diagnosing by state showed Desire and Reinforcement were the gaps: the fix was cutting two existing meetings to pay for the time, and retiring the old spreadsheet so there was no path back.

frameworks.out: A per-group diagnosis of which state is blocking, and an intervention aimed at that state.
frameworks.trap: Treating a Desire problem with more Knowledge. Resistance almost never dissolves under further training, and repeating the deck is the default response.

frameworks.name: Kotter's 8 steps

items: And a strategy for reaching it.
Far more often than feels necessary.
Remove the obstacles people actually name.
The step where changes quietly revert.
Processes, hiring, incentives. Otherwise it was a campaign.
viz.cap: Declaring victory at step six is the classic failure.

frameworks.one: An organisational sequence for large change: urgency, coalition, vision, communication, enabling action, short-term wins, consolidation, anchoring.
frameworks.when: Change at organisational scale rather than team scale — restructures, new operating models, major strategic shifts.
how: Establish genuine urgency, with evidence rather than exhortation.
Build a guiding coalition with real authority across functions.
Form a clear vision and a strategy for reaching it.
Communicate it far more often than feels necessary, and remove obstacles people name.
Engineer visible short-term wins, consolidate them, then anchor the change in processes, hiring and incentives.
frameworks.with: ADKAR for the individual level underneath it; 7S if execution keeps failing.

ex.h: An operating-model change that stalled at step 7

items: Urgency, coalition, vision, communication, enablement, two visible wins.
A celebration email in month four. The coalition disbanded a fortnight later.
Nothing was anchored in hiring, incentives or process. Reverted within two quarters.

ex.cap: Six of eight is not 75% of a change.
ex.p: The first six steps were executed well, which is exactly what makes this failure common — it looks like success right up to the point where it quietly unwinds. The second attempt kept the coalition until the change was in the onboarding docs and the review template.

frameworks.out: A sequenced change programme with a coalition and early wins planned in.
frameworks.trap: Declaring victory after the first short-term win. Steps seven and eight are where changes quietly revert, and they are the least interesting to work on.

frameworks.name: Lewin's change model

items: Make the case that the current state is not sustainable, and surface the fears.
Move, with support and sponsorship, accepting a dip in performance.
Change defaults, tooling, metrics and onboarding. Remove the old path.
viz.cap: Almost every reverted change skipped the third box.

frameworks.one: Three stages: loosen the current way of working, make the change, then make the new way the default.
frameworks.when: You want the simplest useful frame for why a change reverted — almost always because nothing was refrozen.
how: Unfreeze: make the case for why the current state is not sustainable, and surface the fears.
Change: move, with support and visible sponsorship, accepting a dip in performance.
Refreeze: change the defaults, the tooling, the metrics and the onboarding so the new way is the path of least resistance.
Remove the old path deliberately — parallel running is the enemy of refreezing.
Check six weeks later whether anyone has drifted back.
frameworks.with: Force field analysis to find what to remove; ADKAR for individual diagnosis.

items: Clear case, real problems with the old tool, fears aired.
Migration completed, training delivered, dip in throughput accepted.
Old tool left read-only “just in case”. Within six weeks 40% of work was back in it.

ex.cap: The old path was still there, so it was still used.
ex.p: Nothing about the first two stages was weak. Under a deadline, people used the tool they knew. The second attempt set a hard read-only date, moved the reporting that mattered to the new tool, and updated onboarding — and it held.

frameworks.out: A change with an explicit refreeze plan rather than an assumed one.
frameworks.trap: Leaving the old way available “just in case”. People under pressure use the path they know, and the change never completes.

frameworks.name: Force field analysis

left: Exec sponsorship
Strong, and cheap to add more of. Which is why it gets over-used.
Clear benefit
Real, but only for the people not doing the extra work.
right: No amount of enthusiasm removes a real cost. Remove the cost.
Under pressure, people use the path they know.
viz.cap: Prefer removing a restraint to adding a driver. Pushing harder creates tension, not movement.

frameworks.one: Lists the forces pushing a change forward and those pushing back, weighted, so you can see whether to add push or remove resistance.
frameworks.when: A change is stalled and you cannot tell whether you need more advocacy or fewer obstacles. Usually the latter.
how: State the change precisely.
List driving forces and restraining forces separately.
Weight each by strength.
Compare totals, then ask which single restraint is cheapest to remove.
Prefer removing restraints to adding drivers — pushing harder against resistance creates tension, not movement.
frameworks.with: Run it on whichever ADKAR state is blocking. Usually Desire.

left: Sponsorship: 4
Strong, and the thing everyone reached for. Adding more changed nothing.
Clear benefit: 3
Real, but mostly for people not doing the extra work.
right: The heaviest restraint, and the only one anyone could remove.
Under pressure, people use the path they know.

ex.cap: Restraints outweighed drivers, 9 to 7.
ex.p: Two more rounds of advocacy would have made the totals 9 to 9 and changed nothing. Cancelling two meetings and retiring the spreadsheet moved the balance to 9 against 2, and adoption went from 41% to 89% in three weeks.

frameworks.out: Two weighted lists, and a shortlist of restraints to remove.
frameworks.trap: Adding more communication as a driving force when the real restraint is that someone's workload doubles. No amount of enthusiasm removes a real cost.

frameworks.name: McKinsey 7S

items: Where to play and how to win.
Who reports to whom, and which boundaries the work has to cross.
Processes and tooling. Usually the cheapest thing to change.
How leaders actually behave, as opposed to what they say.
Who you have, and who you need.
What the organisation is genuinely good at.
viz.cap: Seven filled boxes tell you nothing. A named misalignment tells you everything.

frameworks.one: Seven interdependent elements — strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff, skills — used to check whether an organisation can actually deliver a change.
frameworks.when: A strategy keeps failing in execution and you suspect the problem is organisational alignment rather than the plan.
how: Describe the current state of each of the seven elements honestly.
Describe the state each would need to be in for the strategy to work.
Find the misalignments — usually structure, incentives or skills.
Note that shared values sit in the middle for a reason; changes fighting the culture need far more energy.
Sequence the changes, because moving one element alone tends to spring back.
frameworks.with: Kotter to sequence the changes it exposes.

items: Clear, written, understood. Not the problem.
Squads organised by system, but the strategy needed them organised by customer segment.
Leaders still reviewing feature lists, not outcomes.
No commercial or pricing capability anywhere in product.

ex.cap: Three misalignments, named.
ex.p: Three quarters of “execution problems” had been treated as delivery and motivation issues. Two of the three real misalignments were structural and one was a hiring gap — none of which more roadmap pressure could have fixed.

frameworks.out: A misalignment list explaining why execution is failing.
frameworks.trap: Using it as a description rather than a diagnosis. Seven filled boxes with no named misalignment tell you nothing you did not know.

quiz.q: Your AARRR funnel shows acquisition healthy, activation at 22%, retention flat. Where do you spend?
o: Acquisition — more volume compounds
Activation — the worst conversion, and every stage below inherits it
Referral — it is cheapest
Evenly, to avoid over-focusing
quiz.e: Fixing the worst conversion first is the entire point of the funnel view. Adding traffic above a leak increases the absolute number of people you lose while flattering your top-line numbers. Once activation improves, re-measure — the bottleneck will have moved somewhere else.

quiz.q: You are measuring “task success” for a new flow. What must you pair it with?
o: Number of sessions
Time on task, or you will reward people struggling for longer
Net promoter score
Feature adoption
quiz.e: Success rate alone can improve because determined users grind through a worse experience. Pairing it with time on task, or error and retry counts, is what makes it a quality measure. This is the counter-signal step in GSM, and it is the step most often skipped.

quiz.q: A team resists a new planning process despite three training sessions. Which ADKAR state is blocking?
o: Knowledge
Ability
Desire
Awareness
quiz.e: More training is a Knowledge intervention, and resistance that survives three sessions is almost always Desire — they understand it and do not want it, usually for a rational reason about their own workload, status or autonomy. Diagnose which state is blocking before choosing the intervention.

quiz.q: What is the most common reason a change reverts within two months?
o: Poor communication at launch
The old way was left available, so nothing was refrozen
Insufficient executive sponsorship
People forgot the training
quiz.e: Lewin's refreeze is the stage that gets skipped, because it is unglamorous: changing defaults, retiring the old tooling, updating onboarding and metrics. Leaving the previous path available means that the first time someone is under pressure, they use the route they know.

quiz.q: On a power/interest grid, who is most often under-served by PMs?
o: High power, high interest
High power, low interest — they need brief, reliable updates and no surprises
Low power, high interest
Low power, low interest
quiz.e: High-power, low-interest stakeholders get neglected precisely because they are not asking for anything — until a surprise makes them interested at the worst moment. They need short, predictable, boring updates. The high-power, high-interest group is rarely neglected; they are usually in your calendar already.

sections.h: A relay is won and lost in the handoffs.
sections.lede: The frameworks here cover the parts of the job that are about other people: structuring a problem so a group can think about it together, measuring an experience rather than its volume, working out who has to be brought along, and making a change survive contact with everybody's Tuesday. This is where most good product work quietly fails.

panel.big: Resistance is rarely a knowledge problem, so more training rarely fixes it.
items: Fix the worst conversion in the funnel before buying traffic above it.
Pair every success measure with something that catches struggle.
Remove the old path, or the change will not complete.

sections.lede: These get lumped together as “PM frameworks”, but they do quite different work and are needed at different moments.
sections.statement: You can be right about the product and still lose, because being right is not the same as being adopted.

cards.p: CIRCLES for an open question, JTBD for the underlying demand, Working Backwards when a group is arguing about implementation, Double Diamond and design sprints for framing and testing fast.
AARRR to find where growth leaks, HEART and GSM to turn abstract quality goals into ratios with baselines and counter-signals.
Power/interest and salience to decide who gets what attention, RACI when things are being dropped at boundaries, a comms plan so updates are not improvised.
ADKAR to diagnose which state is blocking an individual, Kotter for organisational scale, Lewin and force field analysis to explain why it reverted.
